en: Homage to the one who is beautiful with the moon as a chowrie kissing his lofty head!
To Śambhu, the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.
I bow to Umā, whose eyes are closed in the bliss of embracing the neck of Hara.
As if she had fallen into a swoon from contact with the Kālakūṭa poison.
Salutation to that Vyāsa, the omniscient creator of poets.
He performed meritorious deeds at the Sarasvatī, just as Bhārata did for a year.
Generally, in this world, bad poets have their vision dominated by passion.
Like cuckoos, they are born talkative and acting according to their own desires.
There are countless beings belonging to various species in every house, like dogs.
There are not many poets who are creators, like śarabhas.
By the transformation of any other color, and by the concealment of the marks of bondage.
One who remains unspoken among the virtuous is perceived as a thief of a poet.
Among the Northerners, poetry consists mostly of verbal play (śleṣa); among the Westerners and the Gauḍas, it consists of the mere sense alone.
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is found among the Southerners, while verbal bombast (akṣara-ḍambara) is found among the Gauḍas.
A novel theme, a non-vulgar genre, unstrained punning, and a manifest sentiment;
And the composition of difficult syllables—all this is difficult to achieve in a single place.
Of what use is the poetry of that poet, when [his fame] reaches the end of all narratives?
What kind of speech could it be that does not pervade the three worlds?
They are untiring even at the end of a breath, in whose mouths Sarasvatī resides.
How could those lords of poets, who are the authors of this narrative, not be worthy of veneration?
The pride of poets surely melted away because of the Vāsavadattā.
As if by her own power, she had gone within the range of Karna's vision for the sake of the sons of Pandu.
Resplendent with the binding of the feet, captivating, and established in the sequence of the variegated colors.
The prose composition of Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra acts as a king.
Sātavāhana rendered it imperishable and refined from vulgarity.
Like a treasury filled with pure-born jewels, [he was filled] with well-spoken words.
The fame of Pravarasena has spread forth, radiant as a white water-lily.
Just as an army of monkeys crossed to the further shore of the ocean by means of a bridge.
By means of multi-storied dramas whose productions were undertaken by master architects.
He gained glory through his banners, as the sun gains splendor through its rays.
Or rather, from whom have they not emerged—these eloquent sayings of Kālidāsa?
Joy arises as if toward flower-clusters thick with sweet nectar.
She has kindled the god of love and performed the adornment of Gaurī.
Whom would this Bṛhatkathā not cause wonder, since it has been taken away from us?
Even by remembering the efforts made by King Āḍhya, which remain present within the heart.
As if being pulled by the tip of the tongue, it does not proceed toward the state of poetry.
Nevertheless, out of devotion to the king and fearing [his displeasure], he was anxious to bring the matter to a conclusion.
I perform the playful leaping of my tongue within the ocean of narrative tales.
She is playful with easy awakening, resplendent with ornaments fashioned of gold.
A narrative shines by means of words, just as a bed does by means of its supports.
Victory to him who protects the world with a rampart of blazing fire that is his radiant majesty!
Harṣa is a mountain of glory for the fulfillment of all the desires of his friends.

Thus it is heard that in ancient times, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, while presiding over his own realm, sat upon a blossoming lotus-seat surrounded by hosts of gods led by Indra (Sunāsīra). Engaging in discourses on Brahman and cultivating various other faultless assemblies of learning, he once took his seat. While he was thus seated—worthy of the gaze of the three worlds—all the Prajāpatis, headed by Manu, Dakṣa, and Cākṣuṣa, as well as all the great sages led by the Seven Seers, attended upon him; some chanted *ṛc* verses, being skilled in praise.
Some recited the *yajus* verses that receive ritual honor;

some sang the *praśaṃsā-sāmans*; others explained the mantras whose sacrificial procedures and systems were laid open. And there, among them, disputes regarding their respective branches of knowledge arose, caused by contradictions in their learning.

Now, the sage Durvāsas—the son of Atri, a brother of the Lord of Stars (the Moon), and by nature exceedingly irascible and a performer of great austerities—was quarreling with another sage named Mandapāla; blinded by rage while singing a *sāman* chant, he broke into discordant notes. While all the other sages remained silent out of fear of his curse, and while the Lotus-born Lord Brahmā was treating the matter with indifference through the sport of conversation with others, the divine maiden Kumārī, standing at an age where childhood had slightly passed and fresh youth was beginning to adorn her, stood fanning the Grandfather with a fly-whisk held in her swaying, creeper-like arm.

She was resplendent with two sprout-like feet that were naturally reddish, as if flushed with passion born from scolding and beating; her feet were made vocal by a pair of anklets resonant with rhythmic steps, like a pair of disciples;
and she bore a pair of shanks that possessed the graceful appearance of the two pillars of the gateway to the city of Love.
Gracefully resting the sprout of her left hand upon her girdle-string, which resounded with the sweet warbling of a flock of eager swans;
her body sanctified by a sacred thread hanging from her shoulder as if it were the multitude of her virtues clinging to the abode of her wise mind;
and wearing a necklace with a radiant central gem followed by many others, like the path to liberation (apavarga-mārga) accompanied by numerous [disciples].
She was radiant with her throbbing lower lip, pale-red as if by the lac-dye from the feet of all the sciences that had entered her mouth;

she bore cheeks that displayed the reflection of the black antelope skin of Brahmā seated upon his lotus-throne, appearing as if the deer of the moon had descended to listen to the sweetness of her Sāman chants;
and she had one creeper-like eyebrow raised askance with a look of disdain.

As if washing with the stream of tears flowing from the corners of her eyes one ear that was defiled by hearing discordant sounds, and as if laughing with the other ear adorned by a blossoming cluster of white *sindhuvāra* flowers, she— her body veiled in a garment as fine and pure as the expanse of her wisdom,
scattering the light of the moonbeams of her teeth throughout the ten directions like the stainless realm of speech— the Goddess Sarasvatī laughed upon hearing this.

And seeing her laughing in that manner, the sage said, "Ah, you evil-doer! You who are ill-favored by the arrogance of a mere fragment of poorly acquired knowledge, do you mock me? Having spoken thus, he seemed to drench the ten directions with the liquid of the fire of his wrath through the radiance of his mass of matted locks—locks whose tawny hue was slightly enhanced as their binding knots came loose from the shaking of his head.
He knit his brow into a frown that darkened the surface of his forehead like a gambling board where the time for the final throw had arrived;
under the guise of the luster of his teeth, he seemed to arrest speech as it fled in fear of his mercilessly bitten lip;
and he adjusted the knot of his black antelope skin, which was slipping from his shoulder, so that it resembled a decree of a curse.
His every limb was occupied by gods, asuras, and sages who, reflected in the beads of sweat upon his skin, had sought refuge with him out of fear of a curse;

with a hand whose fingers trembled from the agitation of anger, he cast aside his rosary—which seemed to cling to him as it sought his favor—and having sipped water from his water-pot, he took up the water for the curse.
There, seated near the self-existent Svayambhū, was the Goddess herself in bodily form, wearing the bark-garment of a *kalpa* tree that was as white as a mass of nectar-foam.
Her waist-knot was tied between her high breasts with a garment made of lotus fibers;
the courtyard of her forehead shone with three lines of ash-marks that resembled the victory banners of the three worlds conquered by the power of her asceticism;
and she wore a yogapaṭṭaka (meditation band) draped across her shoulder like a white foam of nectar, which, through the majesty of her penance, had been coiled like the stream of the Gaṅgā.
With her left hand she held a crystal water-pot like a lotus bud from which Brahmā was born;
with her right hand she raised it, encircled by a rosary of beads, its ring-finger bristling with a conch-shell bracelet and flickering with a threatening gesture, crying out:
"Ah, you sinner!"
O you who are struck down by anger,
evil-souled one, ignorant one!
O you who do not know the self, O wretched Brahmin, O scoundrel of a sage!

"O outcaste, O wretch! How can you, embarrassed by your own transgression, desire to curse the blessed Sarasvatī— the mother of the three worlds and the one worthy of worship by the hosts of gods, asuras, sages, and men?"— thus she spoke.

Sāvitrī rose from her seat, leaving behind her grass mat along with the four Vedas incarnate, who had abandoned their seats of reed-mats out of anger; whose mouths were resonant with the sound of *oṃ*; who filled the quarters of the sky with the weight of their matted locks swinging as they tossed them about; who made the day seem darkened by the shadows of the voluminous black antelope skins whirled during their circumambulations; who caused the world of Brahmā to tremble with the vibrations of their sighs of indignation; who seemed to pour out moon-nectar under the guise of perspiration; whose foreheads were radiant with the sacred ashes of the *agnihotra* sacrifice; who wore rags and bark garments adorned with beautiful chowries of *kuśa* grass fibers; and who carried their water-pots as if they were weapons.
Then, even though he was entreated by the gods, saying, "O Blessed One, do not be indignant; this is no ground for a curse," [he replied],
"O Preceptor..."
Though being propitiated by his own disciples with joined palms who said, "Forgive this one transgression," and though being dissuaded by Atri who said,
"Son,
do not create an obstacle to your asceticism," [he remained firm].
Overcome by a fit of rage, Durvāsas cried out, "O ill-behaved woman! and discharged that water of his curse;
meanwhile, Sāvitrī, who was prepared to utter a counter-curse, said, "Friend," [to him].
"Restrain your anger;
even those whose minds are unrefined are worthy of respect by virtue of their very birth as twice-born," said Sarasvatī herself, thus restraining him.

Then, seeing Sarasvatī cursed in that manner, the venerable Grandfather (Brahmā) appeared, bearing a body clad in a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) like a lotus-fiber stalk clinging to his birth from the lotus.

With his right hand—whose mass of emerald rays from the rising, clear finger-rings resembled a bundle of *kuśa* grass for quelling the calamities of the three worlds—he warded off the clamor of the curse;
casting with his exceedingly pure and long rays of light, as if laying out the measuring lines for the commencement of the future Kṛta Yuga across the quarters;
and filling the directions with his voice, like a festive drum for Sarasvatī’s departure.
Sudhīra said, "O Brahmin,
this path which you have set out upon has certainly not been followed by the wise; it leads to one's destruction in the end."
For the dust stirred up by the horses of the senses running unrestrained defiles the vision of those who have not conquered their senses.
To what great distance can the eye see?
Those of perfected intellect perceive all objects, whether non-existent or existent, through a purified mind.
This coexistence of righteousness and anger in one place is naturally opposed, like that of water and fire;
why do you plunge into darkness, casting aside light?
For forgiveness is indeed the root of all asceticism.
Like an angry vision skilled at perceiving the faults of others, your intellect does not perceive the fault of its own passion;
where is the exhaustion from the burden of great asceticism, and where is this partiality?
One who is excessively prone to anger is like a blind man, even if he possesses sight;
for an intellect clouded by rage does not discern what ought to be done or what ought not to be done.
In one who is provoked, even knowledge first becomes darkness.
Then, O Bhrukuṭī, at first passion assails the sense-faculties, and finally the eye.
At the outset, asceticism melts away;
afterwards, the water of sweat flows,
while first, infamy flashes forth.
Immediately after, the lower lip—

how has it become like the matted hair and bark garments of a poison tree for the destruction of the world? Indeed, this mental disposition of yours, like a string of pearls, is utterly unsuited to this ascetic garb.
Like an actor, you vainly wear the artificial garb of an ascetic with a mind devoid of true tranquility;
I do not see even the slightest trace of virtue in you.
Because of this extreme lightness, you still float upon the very surface of the ocean of knowledge.
Indeed, these great sages are certainly not deaf, mute, or dull-witted;
yet, when their own hearts—the seat of the fault of anger—should have been restrained, for what reason did you restrain the innocent Sarasvatī?
These are the signs of one's own negligence, stumbling, and embarrassment.
"By these words the clever man incurs censure," having said this, he spoke again: "Child Sarasvatī, do not despair.
This Sāvitrī follows after you and will console you when you are pained by separation from us; moreover, this curse of yours shall last only until the sight of the lotus-face of your own son."

Having spoken thus, he dismissed the assembly of gods, demons, sages, and men; placing his hand upon the shoulder of Nārada, who had approached him in agitation, he rose to perform his customary daily rites.
Sarasvatī, too, though cursed, stood with her face slightly cast down, casting a glance upon her breast that was variegated white and black like a streaked skin of black antelope;
she seemed to be drawn away by swarms of bees clinging to the fragrance of her fragrant breath, as if they were the syllables of the curse incarnate.
With her hand loosened by the grief of the curse,
her path for descending to the world of mortals being pointed out by the web of light from her downward-turned nails,
she returned home together with Sāvitrī, followed by the flocks of domestic swans summoned by the tinkling of her anklets, as if by the hearts of the inhabitants of the Brahma-world.

In the meantime, as if to announce the news of Sarasvatī’s descent, the sun descended to the middle world; and as the day gradually waned, the lake became despondent at the calamity of its clusters of closing lotuses,

while the Lord— the sole eye of the world— descended more swiftly upon the mountain peak, glowing like the ruddy hair of a young monkey, as if being cast down by the side-glances of amorous women whose brows were curved with the intoxication of spring.

In the precincts of divine hermitages, which were whitened by streams of milk flowing from herds of sows with dripping udders— as if washed by the surging waves of the Ocean of Milk at the rising of the moon—
the elephant Airāvata, his tusks reddened by striking the golden slopes as he wandered at will in the late afternoon, began to graze upon the banks of the celestial river;
meanwhile, the path of the stars displayed a rosy hue, as if smeared by the lac-dye from the feet of thousands of Vidyādhara women hastening to their trysts.

When the sun, offered the evening libation by the Siddhas who have set out upon the path of the stars, has descended; when the liquid red sandalwood paste, glowing like safflower that colors the quarters of the sky, flows as if it were the perspiration of the Twilight rising from her prostration before Śiva; when the world of Brahmā shines forth like a multitude of lotus-pools gathered to serve the lotus-born Creator, filled with the rows of saluting hands joined in twilight prayer by throngs of gods and sages; and when Brahmā has chanted the Veda for the third daily libation— [The sentence continues: ...the day was passing away. The city of Ayodhyā appeared like a woman whose husband had gone abroad, her face—the orb of the moon—having its beauty eclipsed by the sun, the lord of the day, which had set; her eyes—the lotuses—shut fast; her breasts—the temples of elephants—darkened by the pollen of the ketaka flowers; her lips—the water-lilies—closed; her cheeks—the moonstones—melting away under the touch of the rays of the setting moon; her waist—the river Ganges—filled with the waters of the evening twilight; her arms—the Yamunā—reddened by the saffron of the twilight; her feet—the earth—covered with the dust raised by the hooves of the horses of the sun; her forehead—the sky—marked by the fading streaks of the twilight clouds; her hair—the darkness—disheveled; her earrings—the stars—drooping; her necklace—the Milky Way—broken; her bracelets—the constellations—scattered; her garments—the stars—fallen; her body—the night—exhausted; her sighs—the breezes—blowing cold; her tears—the dew-drops—falling; her heart—the moon—waning; her speech—the silence—prevailing; her thoughts—the dreams—disturbed; her hopes—the desires—fading; her fears—the anxieties—increasing; her sorrows—the griefs—deepening; her joys—the pleasures—departing; her virtues—the merits—diminishing; her vices—the sins—growing; her friends—the virtues—leaving her; her enemies—the vices—approaching; her prosperity—the fortune—slipping away; her adversity—the misfortune—advancing; her life—the breath—faltering; her death—the end—near at hand. Thus did the day depart, and the night, the beloved of the moon, the lord of the night, approached. The moon rose, the friend of the night-lotuses, the enemy of the day-lotuses, the lover of the night-blooming lilies, the foe of the sun, the kinsman of the stars, the jewel of the sky, the lamp of the world, the crest-jewel of the mountains, the mirror of the ocean, the eye of the universe, the crown of the heavens, the banner of the night, the charioteer of the stars, the lord of the planets, the king of the luminaries, the father of the Rohiṇī, the brother of the Sītā, the son of the Atri, the grandson of the Kaśyapa, the great-grandson of the Brahmā, the light of the world, the joy of the gods, the terror of the demons, the delight of the sages, the refuge of the virtuous, the destroyer of the darkness, the healer of the eyes, the cooler of the heat, the giver of life, the remover of fatigue, the bringer of peace, the source of wisdom, the dispeller of ignorance, the revealer of truth, the knower of all, the witness of all, the ruler of all, the lord of all, the master of all, the sovereign of all, the supreme, the highest, the eternal, the infinite, the unborn, the undecaying, the imperishable, the immutable, the unchanging, the unmanifest, the unperceivable, the incomprehensible, the inconceivable, the indescribable, the ineffable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the unspeakable,

In the dwellings of the Seven Sages, whose courtyards were thick with the flames of kindled sacrificial fires as if they had begun the lustration ceremony for their encampments while engaged in the practice of dharma;
among the ascetics who were light and healthy, their sins and the poisons of disease having been washed away by the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite;

and in the waters of the Mandākinī, whose sandy banks were purified by rows of ascetics seated for the twilight worship, and whose waves were jagged with the laughter of the swans that serve as the vehicle for the Lotus-born Brahmā as he floats upon them.

When the lily grove—serving as a parasol for the water-deities, a palace for the inner apartments of the wives of the flocks of birds, sweet with its own honey-sweet fragrance, and eager to rejoice in the delight of the bees—was about to close;

and when the flock of royal swans—delighted by the drinking of the sweet nectar from the day-fading lotuses, wishing to sleep, their necks curved for the scratch of soft lotus-stalks, and fanning the lotus-pond with the waving of their rows of wings—was about to rest.

When the evening breeze—grey with the pollen of flowers from the creepers on the riverbanks, carrying the fragrance of jasmine from the braided hair of the women of Siddhapura, thin and resembling the sighs of the Night—was blowing; when the swarms of six-legged bees were sleeping within the hollows of the buds of night-lotuses, crowded by the tips of their long filaments rising as they closed;
and when the clusters of stars, resembling the multitude of *kuṭaja* buds in the forest of Śiva’s matted locks tossed up during his dance, were crowding the vault of the sky.
When the twilight had turned coppery, possessing the hue of a ripening palmyra-fruit skin, and when the darkness—thick as a black cloud—was closing over the earth in its fresh youth;
when the clusters of lamp-flames, acting as ear-ornaments of the maiden Night, were blossoming, being most capable of rending the dense veil of youthful gloom;

and when the sky, pale with the lovely light of the thin rays of the moon, was making the darkness wane at the face of the quarters, appearing like the sandy bank of the dark-blue Yamunā whose waters had receded and dried up.

When the darkness—possessing the luster of a blue jay’s wing, like the mass of hair on the forest-dweller Night, which was darkened by her grasping the moonbeams as if they were locks of hair, and which was dissolving like the heart of a proud woman in a lake of blooming blue water-lilies—had vanished; when the divine moon had risen, bearing a body red as the dawn’s glow, as if drenched in the blood dripping from its own deer after being struck by the weapon-like claws of Hari dwelling in the caves and hollows of the ridges of the Eastern Mountain, and as if washed by streams of water falling from moonstones upon the mountain as the gloom was destroyed; ... [the text continues] ...when the night had fled, like a woman whose face is covered with tears, having been seized by the hand by the sun, her garment of darkness cast aside, her earrings of stars fallen, and her tresses of darkness loosened; when the sky, its lotus-face closed, was opening its eyes of stars, as if awakening from sleep; when the world was rising from its bed of slumber, as if from a dream; when the birds were chirping in their nests, as if reciting the morning prayers; when the bees were humming in the lotuses, as if chanting hymns of praise; when the quarters of the sky were emerging from the darkness, as if from a bathhouse; when the sun was shining, as if the very life-breath of the world had emerged from its cave; when the day was unfolding, as if the world were waking from a long sleep; when the light of dawn was spreading, as if the world were being painted with fresh colors; when the world was becoming visible, as if a new creation were beginning; when the sun was rising, as if the eye of the world were opening; when the world was becoming bright, as if a new day were dawning; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being illuminated by a new light; when the world was becoming clear, as if a new vision were appearing; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being awakened from a deep slumber; when the world was becoming manifest, as if a new reality were emerging; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being filled with a new radiance; when the world was becoming luminous, as if a new splendor were unfolding; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being bathed in a new glory; when the world was becoming radiant, as if a new brilliance were spreading; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being suffused with a new vitality; when the world was becoming vibrant, as if a new energy were surging forth; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being enlivened by a new spirit; when the world was becoming animated, as if a new life-force were pulsating; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being invigorated by a new strength; when the world was becoming robust, as if a new vigor were coursing through it; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being fortified by a new power; when the world was becoming steadfast, as if a new stability were being established; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being grounded in a new firmness; when the world was becoming secure, as if a new foundation were being laid; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being anchored in a new certainty; when the world was becoming certain, as if a new conviction were taking root; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being confirmed in a new truth; when the world was becoming true, as if a new reality were being realized; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being validated by a new knowledge; when the world was becoming known, as if a new wisdom were being attained; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being illumined by a new insight; when the world was becoming enlightened, as if a new understanding were dawning; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being awakened to a new perception; when the world was becoming perceived, as if a new awareness were arising; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being made conscious of a new existence; when the world was becoming conscious, as if a new self-awareness were emerging; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being brought into the light of a new consciousness; when the world was becoming conscious, as if a new identity were being formed; when the sun was shining, as if the world were being defined by a new essence; when the world was becoming essential, as if a new core were being revealed; when the sun was rising, as if the world were being centered in a new purpose;
When the lunar disc had begun to fill the ocean like a great ivory crocodile-mouthed conduit carrying forth a flood of milk spilled from Goloka,

and at the clear hour of evening, Sāvitrī said to Sarasvatī, who was weeping and as if meditating on something with a vacant heart: "Friend, before you, who are skilled in giving instruction to the three worlds, my tongue falters and stammers as it speaks."

You surely know how perverse are the crooked workings of fate—which, though occurring toward a virtuous person, are as callous as those toward the wicked; unstable, momentary, difficult to overcome, and not at all pleasant.

Even a single atom of causeless humiliation, when it falls upon one from an unworthy source, turbidizes the mind even of the wise. And grief, being constantly watered by a flood of tears, sprouts a thousandfold like a tree whose leaves have fallen.
The atoms of heat cause even a most delicate person to wither like a *mālatī* flower;
and even a minute affliction falling upon the great is sufficient for torment, like a goad upon elephants.
Furthermore, one's birthplace is difficult to abandon, for it is bound by the ties of the natural snare of affection and is one’s true kinsman.
The separation from beloved people is cruel, tearing the heart like the stroke of a saw.
Moreover, when past karma—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is powerful and stands as the presiding director over the production of its fruit, what occasion is there for grief before the wise?
And how is it that these drops of tears, which are themselves inauspicious, defile your face, which is the unique lotus of blessing for the three worlds?
Therefore, enough of this;
tell me now which region of the earth you wish to adorn,
and in which meritorious place does your heart desire to descend?
Which sacred fords do you desire to visit out of compassion, or in which blessed hermitages do you wish to dwell while practicing austerities?
Here is your beloved, ready to descend to the surface of the earth along with his female companions—skilled in service and made tender by the familiarity of playing together in the dust.

"Having no other refuge, from this very day forth, worship with your mind, speech, and action the three-eyed God, the Lord of Gods and Preceptor of the Three Worlds— the creator and sustainer of all sciences, who purifies the gods and asuras with the dust of his own feet, and whose nectar-like smile is fashioned into an ear-ornament;
in a very short time, he will grant you release from the sorrow of this curse."

Thus addressed, Sarasvatī, her tears as white as pearls that had been released, replied: "Dear friend, as I wander with you, neither the separation from the world of Brahmā nor the grief of the curse will cause me any pain;
only the joy of serving the Lotus-Seated One moistens my heart."

"Moreover, you alone know the abodes of dharma for me in this world, the means for attaining meditative concentration, and the places suitable for yoga where I may dwell. Having spoken thus, she ceased; and with her sleeplessness brought on by restless anxiety, she passed that night with her eyes unblinking.

On the following day, when the Blessed One, the crest-jewel of the three worlds, had risen; when the crest-jewel of the Eastern Mountain had his body reddened as if by the blood spurted from the mouths of his own horses wounded by the sharp-sounding *khaṇakhaṇā* clatter of their hooves; and when the sun was preceded by the dawn-red crests of old cocks—then, not far away, the guardian of the swan-flock belonging to the celestial chariot of the Grandfather (Brahmā), wandering about, sang aloud in the *aparavaktra* meter: "Why do you cause your eye to tremble, O you who are fondled by dwelling in a mind that is longing and yet stainless?"
"Descend, O Kalahaṃsī; you shall go once more to the lotus-pool, your home. Hearing this, Sarasvatī thought again: "Let me be questioned by him as I have been;

I shall honor the sage's word. Having said this, she rose, resolved to descend to the surface of the earth, and—leaving behind her own attendants who were distressed by the separation, disregarding her circle of kinsmen, and alone—she circumambulated the Four-faced One three times. After some effort, having turned back the throng of ascetics who had followed her with entreaties, she departed from the world of Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī.
Then, in due course, she appeared like the cow of dharma that has begun to flow steadily, with her white udders running downward,
emitting a loud sound,
and serving as a garland of *mālatī* flowers for the head of the slayer of Andhaka.
Its banks were obstructed by Vālakhilyas who were clinging to them; its star-like bark was washed clean by Arundhatī;
and its shimmering, trembling, and most brilliant stars were gliding along.

Its sandy banks were bristling with the scattered, sparse offerings of sesame water by ascetics; its shores were whitened by the funeral cakes offered to the ancestors by Pitāmaha (Brahmā) after he had purified himself by bathing; and it indicated a fast observed for the birth-impurity of the Sun by the beds of kuśa grass where the Seven Sages slept upon its banks.

It was variegated by heaps of flowers being spoken of as fit for worship for the Lord of Śacī, who is purified by sipping water; it possessed garlands of Mandāra flowers fallen from the sacred offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva’s city;
and it contained the rocks of the caves of Mount Mandara, split open with disregard.
Its form was caressed by the jar-like breasts of many women belonging to various groups of beautiful leaders;
its current was made resonant by stumbling over rocks and shoals of crocodiles;
and its banks were starred with clusters of spray from the nectar of the moon flowing through the *suṣumṇā* channel.
Its sandy banks were grey with the smoke from the sacrificial fires of the *dhiṣaṇas*;
its *vidyādharas* fled in terror at the sight of the sand-lingas fashioned by the *siddhas* being trodden upon;
it was like the slough cast off by the serpent of the sky.
It was like the playful forehead-mark of the King of Heaven,
the marketplace for the merchandise of merit,
and the ivory bolt upon the gate of the city of hell.
Like a silken turban-band for King Sumeru,
like a silken palanquin-pole for the elephant that is Kailāsa,
and like a path to liberation.
Like the felly of the wheel of the Kṛta age,
she descended to the world of mortals following the Mandākinī, the queen of the seven oceans;
and even while remaining in the sky, she beheld [the city] which was like the splendor of Varuṇa.
Like a cascade of nectar from the Moon-Mountain,
like a flow of moonstone-juice from the Vindhya range, and like a stream of camphor-tree sap from the Daṇḍaka forest.
Like a fountain of the essence of beauty for the quarters of the sky,
like a crystal stone couch for the splendor of the heavens,
he beheld the great river named Hiraṇyabāhu— the offspring of the blessed Grandfather— filled with clear, cool, and delicious water.
Seeing that which people call the Śoṇa,
her heart was captivated by its beauty, and she chose to dwell upon its very bank;
and she said to Sāvitrī, "Friend,"

"The regions on the banks of this great river, which has surpassed the splendor of the Mandākinī, delight me—their trees are strewn with sand from the heaps of flower-pollen, their sweet cries are the songs of peacocks, and they are made charming by the lute-like humming of bees intoxicated by the fragrance;
moreover, my heart inclines to remain right here. Having been thus addressed, and having welcomed his words with "So be it," she alighted upon its western bank.
And in a certain clean vine-cottage on the riverbank, provided with a stone slab, she formed the notion that it was her home;
and having rested there, she rose after no long time and, together with Sāvitrī, gathered flowers for worship.

Then, having established a sand Śiva-liṅga upon the surface of the sandy bank, she, with supreme devotion, performed the eight-fold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) for a long duration, preceded by the five Brahmans, properly accompanied by the binding of ritual gestures (*mudrā*), containing the chanting of the *dhruva* verses, and meditating upon all eight forms consisting of Earth, Wind, Forest, Sky, Fire, Sun, Moon, and the Sacrificer.

She maintained her bodily existence with fruits and roots that required no effort to obtain, and with the cool water of the Śoṇa river, which in its sweetness sought even to surpass the taste of nectar.

Having passed the day, she slept upon a bed of leaves prepared on the stone slab within that bower of creepers; and on the following day as well, she spent both night and day in this very same manner.

As the days passed in this manner and time went by, once, when the sun had risen for only a watch, she heard from the northern quarter a deep yet increasingly piercing sound of neighing horses, filling the forest thickets with its echoes.

Her curiosity aroused, she emerged from her bower of creepers and, looking out, beheld not far away a mass of dust, pale as the inner petals of a blooming *ketakī* flower, rushing directly toward her.
And gradually, as its manifestation approached, he was seen floating like a school of crocodiles in the water amidst that great dust, grey as the belly of a fish;
he was moving forward with his mass of hair tied into a topknot on his forehead by long, curling shoots of hair,
and his cheeks were made to smile by the luster of white ivory ear-ornaments.
He wore a saffron-colored tunic variegated with black by the application of a paste of black aloe-wood;
he had wrapped his head with an upper garment,
and a bright golden bracelet was fastened upon his left wrist.
With a sword hilt fastened by a tight knot in a double-layered silk band,
his body lean and hardened by incessant exercise,
he repeatedly leaped into the air like a herd of wind-deer.
who had leaped over even and uneven ground, ravines, and thickets; who carried a staff and held a sword in his hand.
With various forest flowers, fruits, roots, and leaves gathered by his attendants,
and with a continuous clamor raised by them crying, "Move aside, move aside! Give way!"— thus he proceeded.
He beheld a troop of horses accompanied by a foot-force of about a thousand men, mostly youths;

and in their midst was one whose shadow was protected by a sky-reaching parasol, white as the foam of milk or a conch shell, encrusted with fragments of various gems and adorned with a fringe of pearls in the shape of a half-moon, appearing like the Ocean of Milk itself come in person to bestow Lakṣmī.

He was followed by a multitude of the lustrous radiance of his ornaments, as if by a circle of the quarters of the sky clinging to him out of affection for the sight; he shone with a garland of *mālatī* flowers hanging down from his hips, like a banner of beauty won through the conquest of the entire world;

and his body, roughened by the dust of the road, was being wiped clean—as it were—by the rising, reddish webs of rays from the ruby in his topknot, which appeared like young sprouts held by invisible forest deities.
With a head made beautiful by a garland of Bakula buds arranged in a circle and adorned with clusters of curling locks of hair, he seemed to drink in the day’s sunlight through his closed eyes;

and with the natural luster of his forehead—fashioned as if from the second half of the crescent moon upon the crown of Śiva’s matted locks and embraced by innate beauty—he seemed to smear the very sky with the vermilion-pink radiance of his loveliness.

With the breadth of his eyes—which, through the bold glances of one emboldened by the onset of fresh youth, treated the three worlds as mere straw—he seemed to usher in an autumn that covered the ten directions with thousands of lakes of blooming white, blue, and red lotuses;

and he shone with a long nose-bridge, which acted like a dam across the boundary of the rivers of his wide eyes, appearing as if it were a stream of liquid beauty flowing down from the moonstone surface of his forehead.

With his mouth, which emitted the fragrance of exceedingly sweet mangoes, camphor, kakkola, cloves, and pārijātaka flowers, and was resonant with the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees, he seemed to be vomiting forth the spring season together with the Nandana grove;

with his charming smiles, his face upturned in the spirit of jesting with nearby friends, bathing the quarters of the sky with the moonlight of his teeth, he repeatedly created, as it were, the light of the moon moving through the heavens.

He appeared as if adorned with ear-ornaments of green sprouts and flowers, due to the spreading luster of his swinging three-pronged ear-rings, which featured emeralds set between pairs of pearls as large as *kadamba* buds;
he bore a pair of arms radiant with the leaf-patterns drawn in fragrant musk-paste, resembling two staffs for the banner of the god of love, whose crests were seized by fierce sea-monsters.
He bore a body marked by the white thread of the sacred *brahmasūtra*, appearing like Mount Mandara encircled by the stream of the Gaṅgā in her indignation at the churning of the ocean;

with his chest, which was as if covered in the dust from handfuls of camphor powder and served as a vast sandy bank for the pair of ruddy geese that were his lovely, high breasts, he seemed to spread out the circle of the quarters before him, gathered together by the length of his thick arms.

With his lower garment—a deep green like the *hārītaka* fruit—tightly tucked at the waist, its front corner charmingly tucked slightly below the navel, its trailing hem cast over the back, and its three-fold folds clearly visible where it gathered between the thighs;

with his exceedingly slender waist thus revealed; and with his two pillar-like thighs, which were as thick and beautiful as fresh sandalwood paste, their knees pressed against the formidable, crocodile-mouthed knobs hardened by the flesh built up from incessant exertion, acting as stone pillars supporting the altar-platform of his broad chest—he seemed to mock the length of Airāvata’s trunk.
His shanks appeared exceedingly slender, as if from the exhaustion of bearing the excessive weight of his thighs;

with his two feet, pale-red like a pair of sprouts from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) hanging down on either side, he seemed to be fashioning a row of chowries to adorn a horse with the trembling rays of light from his toenails.

He was mounted upon a great horse, swift as thought, possessing a body with hair as black as the cheeks of a monkey and the color of a blue *sindhuvāra* flower; its hooves, which seemed to rest for a long time high above the ground as they rose upward and turned back in a majestic curve, tore the earth; its harsh bit produced a *khaṇa-khaṇa* sound at every moment as it was gripped and released by the teeth; beautiful golden wheel-ornaments (*cakraka*) rolled upon its forehead, where bees clung to its long nostrils; it shone with a war-chariot of tinkling *śātakaumbha* gold, and its speed delighted the mind.
With two attendants standing close by, their hands gripping the saddle-girths on both sides, he was fanned by a pair of white chowries;

with his moon-like face— its cheek-surface bristling with horripilation as if covered by the filaments and petals of the blue lotuses clinging to his ears— he was relishing the elegant sayings of the bards reciting before him,
appearing like a manifestation of the descent of the two Apsarases of the God of Love.
He seemed to produce a polish made of moonlight, to create a world of living beings consisting almost entirely of grace,
and to fashion another creation composed of nothing but passion.
He seemed to transform the day into one composed entirely of erotic passion, to inaugurate a kingdom of love,
and to act as a magical ointment for the eyes that draws all things toward oneself.
It was like a spell for subduing the mind,
like a powder for inducing possession in healthy beings,
and like a lack of satiety for curiosity.
Like a perfected elixir of good fortune, like the day of rebirth for the God of Love, and like an alchemical potion for youth.
It was like a sole kingdom of loveliness, a pillar of fame for beauty, a root-treasury of grace,
and the fruition of meritorious deeds for the cycle of existence.
Like the first sprout of the creeper of beauty,
like the fruit of Prajāpati’s practice of creation, like the majesty of grace,
and like the flowing stream of elegance;
He saw a youth about eighteen years of age, with a second person by his side whose horse was not touching his own,
who was tall and resembled a pillar of refined gold.
Though advanced in years, his body was hardened by physical exercise; his nails, beard, and hair were kept short,
and he had a bald head with a patch of hair at the back like a conch shell.
With a slightly protruding belly and a hairy chest,
he seemed, by his noble and unostentatious attire, to be teaching even old age how to cultivate modesty.
He seemed to bring his virtues to a state of weightiness, as it were,
and his great majesty to a state of discipleship, as it were;
he was, so to speak, acting as the preceptor of right conduct itself.

Then that youth, having learned from his footmen— who had turned back as they saw him and were speaking with minds full of wonder— that the two maidens possessed divine forms, and seeing a man wearing white trousers with his head wrapped in a band of washed silk cloth, became filled with curiosity; desiring to see them, he urged his horse forward and arrived at the spot of the bower of creepers, wherefrom he dismounted from his horse even from afar.
Having dismissed her attendants, she approached with humility on foot together with that second ascetic.

Once they had both performed the ritual salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*), Sāvitrī received them, along with Sarasvatī, in due order with hospitality appropriate for forest-dwellers—beginning with the offering of seats of young shoots and ending with the presentation of water for the feet (*argha*) consisting of flowers and fruit.
When the two were seated and she herself had sat down, she remained for no very long time and then addressed the elder of the two: "Noble sir,..."
For women whose wealth is innate modesty, addressing them first is a lack of decorum;

especially for noble maidens as innocent as forest deer, it is only their faculty of hearing— uplifted by curiosity— that impels itself forward, longing for the eyes that have already achieved their purpose through the mere act of beholding them.

At the very first sight, a virtuous person offers a kind of gift—friendship—to even a timid person through a powerful display of humility; like honey, it makes the mind speak with ease. Moreover, when a virtuous man is deeply bowed in devotion, confidence, like a string on a bow, effortlessly raises him to the highest pinnacle.
Moreover, the extraordinary creations of the Creator, when seen in this world, produce wonder even in those of most profound intellect, for they have never been seen before;
since this form of his, which surpasses the three worlds, and this supreme essence of benevolence belonging to that great being,
and this exceedingly auspicious nature of the gods, cause one to speak of him, but not the fickleness that arises naturally among young women.

Tell me, which region has been rendered desolate by the arrival of that man who, through his mere report, has caused such a person to experience the agony of separation and become a partaker of demerit?
Or where is he to go;
for whose sake has this youth—whose pride in the *huṃ*-utterance of Hara has been stolen away, appearing like another Ananyaja—been brought here?
What is the name of his father, whose ascetic merit is so abundant, that this [child], like the Kaustubha gem that rains nectar, delights the heart of Hari?
And who is his mother, worthy of homage by the three worlds, who gave birth to him of great splendor as the dawn twilight gives birth to the sun?
And what are the meritorious syllables of his name that enjoy such renown?
When she had said, "This same sequence applies even to the noble thorough knowledge [of reality], for the heart follows its curiosity," he, manifesting his courtesy, replied: "O long-lived lady,
for the virtuous, speaking what is pleasing is indeed a family tradition."
Not only does your face, but your heart as well, gladdens us with words as cool as sprays of nectar, like the moon itself;
for those born of noble character, who are the very artistry of the Creator’s hand in fashioning the virtuous, arise for the most part with auspiciousness.
Far from engaging in conversation with such refined persons, even the mere mingling of one's gaze with theirs elevates one to a great height.
Listen, for this man is indeed the ornament of the lineage of Bhṛgu— the Blessed One who is the crest-jewel of the three worlds (Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ),
who paralyzed the pillar-like arms of Indra by his immense power,
and whose lotus-feet are fondly cradled upon the jeweled stone-slabs of the crowns of gods and demons.
Cyavana, whose life-force had become externalized as his own radiance scorched Puloman, had a son named Dadhīca.
His mother was the princess Sukanyā, a jewel among the maidens of the three worlds, daughter of Śaryāti—who had conquered the world and was followed by many thousands of kings.
Having learned that the queen was pregnant, her father brought her from her husband’s side to his own home for delivery in the month of childbirth.
And there that queen gave birth to him, who was destined for long life;

he grew up right there without delay, delighting his circle of kinsmen. With lotus-like eyes, the child—like the moon, the lord of the stars—was not released by his maternal grandfather from the royal palace, even when his daughter arrived at her husband’s home, for she could never look enough upon this grandson who was such a source of mental delight.
There he studied all branches of knowledge and every art;

and when his maternal grandfather saw that he had reached the bloom of youth, thinking, "Just as I have, may he too experience the joy of beholding the lotus-face of this [prince]," he sent him by some means or other into the presence of his father. May your ladyship also take note of me, a mere atom among servants named Vikukṣi, who am now an executor of the commands of that god whose name is auspiciously invoked, Śaryāti.
As my lord was approaching the feet of his father, I accompanied him;
for this is the family custom of our royal house, and even in one who is dependent, antiquity produces at least some measure of authority over those of high station.
Truly, the treasury of courtesy of the great is inexhaustible;
for about a *gavyūti* beyond this river Śoṇa lies the dwelling of that blessed Cyavana, a forest named Cyāvana—so called after his own name—which rivals the Caitraratha grove.
And this journey of ours has that very place as its limit.
If our heart has grasped this moment with courtesy and without disdain, or if this person is a fit vessel for your favors, or if he is worthy of hearing [your words],
then let not this first request of ours be disregarded;
we too are eager to hear the account of your long-lived selves.
This form of yours does not belie its divine nature;
however, our hearts long to hear your lineage and name, so tell us: what family has been rendered worthy of envy by your birth?
And who is this lady here beside you, appearing like a collection of contradictory things?
For she possesses a radiant form, yet is surrounded by the darkness of her hair.
With a face like a white lotus and eyes like those of a deer, possessing the radiance of the morning sun and a smile like a water lily;
with a voice like the call of the swan and breasts that are full and high.
"Her hands are as tender as lotuses, yet her broad hips are like the rocks of the snowy mountains;
her thighs are like those of a young elephant, yet her gait is languid; she has not yet lost her maidenhood, yet her pupils are full of affection."
She, however, said:
"Noble sir, you shall hear;
our hearts desire to remain here for many more days."
"And this journey is but short;
it will soon reveal itself.
Noble sir, you must not forget this person whom you have encountered by chance," he said, and then fell silent.

Dadhīca, however, spoke very firmly, making the serpent-eaters dwelling in their forest-creeper-homes dance with his speech that resembled the deep thundering of clouds laden with fresh water: "Noble sir, our venerable father will surely show favor when propitiated by you;
let us first see him."
"Arise, let us go.
Having been thus permitted by him with the words "So be it," he rose slowly, offered his salutations, and set forth.
And as he departed mounted upon his horse, Sarasvatī gazed at him with great affection through eyes whose lashes were raised and whose pupils were motionless, as if they were painted there;
and after crossing the Śoṇa, Dadhīca reached his father’s hermitage in no long time.
When he had gone, she remained for a very long time, looking toward that same direction.
With great effort, as it were, he withdrew his gaze;
then, having remained still for a moment and recalled that perfection of her form, his heart was filled with wonder again and again,
and his eyes longed once more for the sight of her.
Her gaze was led, as if by force, toward that very direction; though her mind was not sent forth, it went along with it,
and a passion for him arose somewhere in her heart like a new sprout on a young forest creeper.
From that time forth, she spent her days as if languid, as if vacant, and as if drowsy.

And when the solar light—the embodiment of the three Vedas, possessing the copper-hued brilliance of a cluster of *lāṅgalikā* flowers, with a radiance as red as the head of a mature crane—was setting, its orb tumbling toward the west;
and when the mass of darkness, spreading through the sky and darkening it like the deep green of young *tamāla* leaves, had pervaded the firmament.
As the moon, following the tinkling of the anklets of the wandering *siddha-sundarīs*, slowly ascended the vault of the sky like a swan of the Mandākinī, Sāvitrī—
having performed her salutations at twilight and cast off her limbs even at the onset of night— remained upon a bed of sprouts;
and she too, having completed the evening round of rituals as was her custom, took to a bed of leaves at the proper hour for sleep.
Having fallen asleep, she slept soundly;
but the other, though her eyes were closed, found no rest as her limbs tossed repeatedly upon the bed of young shoots, and she thought: "The world of mortals is indeed above all worlds."
In whom such jewels as these arise— ornaments of the three worlds, heavy with the weight of every excellence;
for indeed,
the moon is but a single drop from the flow of the stream of beauty of his face.

The glances of his eye were like pools of blooming white, blue, and red lotuses; the rays of his ruby-like lower lip were like rows of flowering bandhūka forests; and the God of Love was the means by which the excellence of his body was brought to perfection.

Blessed are those eyes, minds, or youthful charms that are feminine, for whom he has become an object of sight even for a moment; yet by showing him to me, it is as if I have reaped the fruit of unrighteousness born from a previous birth.
Thinking, "What is my course of action now?", she finally fell asleep after a long time, somehow or other overcome by drowsiness;
and while sleeping, she beheld that long-eyed one in a dream.
Having obtained a second vision in her dream, she was struck mercilessly in the heart by the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāma), who drew his bow back to his ear; then she awoke.
And as if to obtain news of her who had been struck by the arrows of Madana, restlessness came upon him;
for from that time forward, even though not struck by the forest creepers white with the pollen of flowers, he experienced a pang of pain.
Though her eyes were not stained by the pollen of flowers shaken by the gentle breeze, she shed tears;
though not sprinkled by the red spray scattered by the wind from the palm-fans of swan-wings, she became moistened;
and though not carried away by pairs of swaying kādamba birds, she reeled upon the swings of the waves of the forest lotus-pools.

Though untouched by the smoke of sighs from separation, the sky attained a dark hue by the vapors released by pairs of *cakravāka* birds parting; though unbit by swarms of bees, it quivered as if stung by the pollen of flowers grey with dust.

Then, at the end of many nights, Vikukṣi, returning by that very same path and arriving at that place, approached just as before, having dismissed his retinue and accompanied only by his umbrella-bearer.

But Sarasvatī, seeing him approaching from afar, rose with affection and agitation to meet him; looking at him like a wild doe with her neck outstretched, she seemed to bathe him, who was weary from the road, with her gaze that whitened the ten directions.
When he had accepted a seat, Sāvitrī asked him with affection, "Noble sir, is the prince well?"
He said, "O long-lived lady, he is well and remembers you both."
Only in these days does he bear a body that seems somewhat thinner,
and he displays an unrecognizable and causeless emptiness, as it were;
moreover—
"A young woman named Mālatī will surely arrive shortly to learn news of you;
she is eager for the prince's breath of life.

Hearing this, Sāvitrī spoke again: "The prince is indeed of exceedingly noble character, since he maintains such a bond of intimacy even toward a person seen but a moment ago, whose identity remains unknown."

For as he was passing by, his mind, like a garment, somehow became attached to us for a moment among the creepers of the path; indeed, the nobility of your master’s son is not devoid of kindness. Alas, the world is truly sluggish, in that it does not purchase with anything at all the hearts of the great, which are so easily won over by friendship.

"This is some extraordinary excellence of magnanimity among great souls, unattainable by ordinary men, by which they make the three worlds their own instruments"— having spoken thus with various discourses for a long while, Vikukṣi departed for his desired destination.

On the following day, as the divine sun— the jewel of the sky— was rising with unrestrained splendor, having chased away the stars, dispelled the darkness, and was intent upon expanding the day-lotuses, she came along after crossing the Śoṇa river.
Under the guise of the radiance emanating from her trembling body, she seemed to bring forth the entire river’s crystal-clear water as if it were blood;
she stood upon a great, white horse whose luster was like that of a cluster of blossoming *atimuktaka* flowers, appearing like Gaurī mounted upon a lion with a thick mane.

She was drawing along, as it were, groves of red *aśoka* saplings that had sprouted on both sides out of a longing for the pleasure of being struck, by the streams of exceedingly crimson luster radiating from her pair of feet—feet which were gracefully placed upon her breast-band, whose anklets were heard tinkling loudly as she tilted her ears like a horse, and whose soles were made to blossom with thick *piṇḍālaktaka* dye and whose backs were tinged with saffron;
while her hips resounded with a girdle that seemed to proclaim a public notice for the forcible abduction of the hearts of all living beings.
Her slender body was concealed by a short, ankle-length bodice made of white, washed silk that was lighter than a snake’s slough;

with her limbs visible through the opening of the bodice, white as dried sandalwood paste, she resembled a lake in which stalks of lotus fiber are discernible within its clear waters. Wearing a *caṇḍātaka* garment rosy with the dye of safflower and variegated with patterns of pleats, she appeared like a floor of crystal revealing a treasure of jewels within.
With her necklace of smooth, round pearls from *āmalaka* fruits, she was like the autumnal sky veiled by a thin layer of white clouds, shimmering with the stars of its thick clusters of planets;
and over her two jar-like breasts, she wore a string of jeweled pendants whose sprout-like rays were red and green, appearing like the forest-garland of some fortunate man bound to enter his heart.

She was followed, as if out of fear of Lakṣmī, by the masses of her rays—which turned the horizons green—each ray resembling a golden bracelet resting upon her forearm and adorned with an emerald dolphin-shaped mount;
she seemed to vomit forth the darkness swallowed by her moon-like face along with the twilight glow from her lip-cup, which was darkened by the thick stain of betel-juice;
and the lower half of her face was veiled, as it were, by a net of blue silk, by the swarm of bees that had settled out of curiosity upon her blooming blue-lotus eyes.
She shone like lightning with a tooth-ornament resting upon her left ear— a dark blue leaf from a black cloud, possessing the deep azure of indigo dye and the blackness of a peacock’s throat—
while her two exceedingly tender creeper-like arms were being sprinkled by a downward-hanging pair of pearl pendants, resembling *bakula* fruits, which seemed to rain down streams of light;

and the surface of her cheek was being licked, as it were, by the longing for her beauty, by the streak of the inner petal of a *ketakī* flower serving as an earring on her right ear, resembling a tongue of moonlight.
Bearing a face that seemed as if sealed with a circular mark of musk, dark as the *tamāla* tree and exuding its fragrance—the very essence of the God of Love;
her head veiled, as it were, by the flickering web of rays rising from the restless, four-cornered *tilaka*-gem resting upon her forehead and kissing her hair-parting;

with the knot of her braided hair loosened by the careless binding that swayed behind her; she was like the banner of the standard of the fish-bannered god, adorned with a crest-jewel in the form of a sea-monster and topped with a blue yak-tail fringe.
Like the family deity of the moon,
like the life-restoring herb of the flower-bowed god,
and like the shore of the ocean of passion.
She was like the moonlight of the rising moon of youth,
like a great river of the nectar of the pleasure of love,
and like the blossoming of flowers from the tree of sexual union.
Like childhood learning to wit,
like the moonlight to beauty,
like fortitude to steadfastness.
Like a guru’s residence for dignity, like the soil for the seed of modesty, and like a gathering for the wise;

She was followed by a female attendant carrying a betel-box who seemed like the very pride of high-mindedness, the very satiety of youth; she had eyes as long as a wreath of blue lotus petals, lips as red as the *pāṭala* flower, teeth as bright as jasmine buds, arms as delicate as a garland of *śirīṣa* flowers, hands as soft as lotuses, breath fragrant as the *bakula*, and a complexion as fair as the *campaka*; she appeared as if made entirely of flowers, and she was mounted upon a mare of immense size.
Mālatī was seen from afar, accompanied by only a few attendants; she appeared as if her heart had been plundered by Sarasvatī out of love for Dadhīca,
and as if drawn away by curiosity.
As if welcomed by her surging waves,
as if embraced by her longing,
and as if drawn within by her heart.
As if bathed with tears of joy,
as if wiped away by her smile, and as if fanned by her sighs;
As if covered by his eye,
as if surpassed by his lotus-face, she drew near to him, as if made a companion by his heart.
Having dismounted from her horse, she made a salutation from afar with her head bowed low;
embraced by the two of them, she sat down with humility,
and being addressed by them with courtesy, she considered herself a partaker of merit.

And she related the message sent by Dadhīca; she offered her salutation with her joined palms placed upon her head, and from the very moment of their meeting, through those various refined and charming conversations, she gradually won over the hearts of both Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī. When midday had passed and Sāvitrī had descended into the Śoṇa river to bathe, Mālatī, having dismissed her attendants, approached Sarasvatī—who was reclining on a bed of flowers—and spoke to her with intent: "O Goddess," she said.
"There is something we wish to communicate to you in private; therefore, I desire that you show us favor by granting your attention for a moment.

Sarasvatī, however, suspecting it might be a message from Dadhīca, wondered what he would say; she covered her heart—its surface bristling with the rays of the nails of her left hand resting upon her breast, as if it were a cluster of sprouts of curiosity breaking forth—with a portion of her upper garment of fine silk and bark-cloth.

With her ear-ornament of *galatā* leaves fluttering as if it were an ear running to hear [him], she clung to a nearby creeper that was swaying in the gusts of her incessant sighs like the hope for life;
flooding the world of living beings with the stream of loveliness from her full-blown moon-like face as if with the essence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*);
and being lifted up by swarms of bees clinging to the fragrance of her flower-ornaments, as if by her own desires—darkened by the burning of the fire of love—which had emerged in embodied form.

Suffering from the fever of Love’s arrows upon her bed of flowers, she rose very slowly and spoke with great composure in a sweet voice: "Friend Mālatī, why do you speak thus? Who am I to grant attention—whether to my body or to my life? As she spoke, she seemed to usher Mālatī, who was reflected on the surface of her cheek, toward the root of her ear as if out of modesty, saying, "Speak in private."
A person who is pleasing to the eye possesses power beyond measure even if not solicited;
you are such a person to me—neither a sister, nor a friend, nor a beloved, nor one equal to my very life.
Therefore, let this little body of mine be employed in whatever task it is capable of, whether small or great.
"My heart is free from blemish and flows toward you with affection; I am devoted to you as your refuge.
O lady of excellent complexion, reveal what you wish to say."
She, however, said: "O Queen,
you surely know the sweetness of sense-objects and the greediness of the collection of the senses."
The intoxication of fresh youth and the restlessness of the mind are indeed well known as the irresistible power of the god of love.
Therefore, you ought not to approach me with reproach;
neither childishness, nor fickleness, nor wandering about is the cause of my loquacity— nothing at all, for it is an extraordinary devotion to my master that compels me.
O Goddess, from the very moment you were seen by the King, desire became his heavy burden, the moon became the lord of his life,
and the Malaya breeze became the cause of his sighs.
Anxiety resides in the inner chambers,
torment is the supreme enemy, and wakefulness is a trusted friend.
Desires pervade everywhere, sighs lead the way for the body,
and death stands by one's side.
Longing is the messenger;
intentions have grown through the instruction of the intellect—
what more can I report?
"He is a worthy match for the queen" is self-aggrandizement;
"he is virtuous" is consistent with the context;
"he is steadfast" is contrary to the circumstances.
"Fortunate" depends on you; "steadfast in affection" is a clever suggestion; "knows how to serve" is unbecoming of one who is not a master.
"He wishes to remain in a state of servitude until death" is the speech of a rogue; "you shall become the mistress of the house" is a seductive lure;
"a woman of merit enjoys such a husband" is partiality toward the master.
"To say 'you are his death' is unpleasant;
to say she was ignorant of his virtues is an insult;
and to say you were frequently shown favor by him in dreams is without witness."
To beg for the sake of preserving one's life is cowardice;
to issue the command "Come there" is an overbearing order; and to come by force even when forbidden is an insult.
Having heard, "Thus you are beyond the range of words," the Goddess remained silent, saying, "You are the authority.
Then Sarasvatī replied with eyes wide with joy: "O friend, I am unable to speak much more."
"I stand here before your words, O you who speak with smiles;

let these life-breaths be accepted," said Mālatī. But she, having replied, "As you command—this is a great favor," and being overcome by intense joy, bowed down and crossed the Śoṇa river on a swift horse.
She went to the hermitage of Cyavana to bring Dadhīca,

while the other, out of affection for her friend, informed even Sāvitrī of what had occurred; then, with a heart fainting under the weight of longing, she somehow managed to pass the remainder of the day as if it were an entire aeon.
When the blessed sun had gone to its setting,
and the darkness was descending more intensely,
the eastern quarter of Indra appeared as if smiling white, like a cave releasing the moon, which is like a lion.

Sarasvatī sat upon the sandy bank of the Śoṇa, which was as pure as fine Chinese silk, rippling like a bed of fine linen, and soft as *dukūla* cloth; there she wore upon her forehead a decorative mark that resembled the moonlight from the toe-nails of Dadhīca, which had adhered to her as she prostrated at his feet in a prayer made during a dream.

Upon the mirror of her cheek, the moon—positioned near her ear—seemed to announce the message of Love as if reflected there: "O lovely-smiling one, here is that person, the beloved of your heart, who has been brought before you."

Fanning with her hand—which, like a cluster of moonbeams turned into a fly-whisk, possessed a circle of radiating rays from her fingernails—his perspiring and clearly visible cheek, she thought to herself:

"No one but Dadhīca shall enter here. She held a young lotus stalk across her breasts like a graceful cane-staff cast obliquely by the God of Love. In her mind she reflected: "If even I, Sarasvatī, have been so utterly brought under the sway of this Mind-born God, what need is there to mention other poor, fickle young women?"
And he arrived like the month of Madhu, bearing fragrant scents; like a swan, possessing the grace of a lotus stalk; and like a peacock, with its face upturned in joy at the clouds.
With his slender body white with fresh sandalwood paste trembling like a Malaya breeze,
he seemed as if being dragged by the Lord of Planets who had seized him by the hand,
and as if being impelled by the southern wind, which is skilled at kindling the god of love.

Dadhīca, accompanied by Mālatī, had his slender body covered as if by a blue veil by a swarm of bees attracted by the fragrance— bees that were like a flood of the passion of love surging within him; and the hollow of one cheek was being whitened by the reflection of the moon, which resembled the conch-shell of the intoxicated elephant of Love throbbing within, appearing like a smile of bashfulness born from the pleasures of their first union.

And having arrived, he addressed her with a voice faltering like that of a swan, as if mingled with the sound of the anklets of his beloved dwelling in his heart; and just as the God of Love commands, so did he delight that charming Rāmā.
And Sarasvatī, having conceived confidence, revealed herself to him.
He spent more than a year with her, which passed for him like a single day; then, by the turn of fate, Sarasvatī conceived a child and,
in due time, gave birth to a son who was delightful in every auspicious mark.

And as soon as he was born, his father granted him this boon: "By my grace, all the Vedas along with their secret doctrines (rahasyas), all the Śāstras, and all the arts (kalās) shall manifest themselves to him spontaneously.
Then, as if to demonstrate the praise due to a good husband by taking Dadhīca within his heart, he ascended to the world of Brahmā together with Sāvitrī, following the command of the Grandfather.

When she had departed, Dadhīca, his heart as if struck by a thunderbolt, entrusted the daughter of a sage named Akṣamālā—the wife of a brahmin born of the Bhārgava lineage—to the care of his own son for the sake of rearing him; then, afflicted by separation, he went to the forest for asceticism.
At the very moment that Sarasvatī gave birth to a son, Akṣamālā also gave birth to a son;
she, however, nurtured those two infants without distinction, nourishing them equally with her breast milk, until they gradually grew up.
Of the two, one was named Sārasvata,
and the second was named Vatsa;
and between these two, there existed a desirable affection like that of brothers born from the same womb.

Then Sārasvata, by the power of his mother’s greatness, having manifested the entire wealth of all branches of knowledge at the very onset of youth, transmitted the entirety of the verbal sciences (*vāṅmaya*) to that dear brother of his own age— one who was as dear to him as life itself and a trusted friend—
and he, having taken a wife, affectionately established for him a residence named Prītikūṭa in that very region; while he himself [remained] at Āṣāḍhī.
Clad in a black antelope skin,
wearing bark garments,
and holding a rosary of beads.
Having become girdled and matted-haired, he went into the presence of his father, who was engaged in ascetic penance;
from that man, whose fame had spread forth due to the exaltation of his own conduct produced by his increasing primordial nature, [the lineage emerged].
Borne upon the head of the Supreme Lord,
profound in all the scriptures of the arts,
and honored by the great sages.

A vast lineage unfolded, capable of withstanding the agitation of opposing forces, finding its future expansion upon the surface of the earth, and as purifying as the unimpeded flow of the Bhāgīrathī.

From whom were born those household sages named Vātsyāyanas, who, though adhering to the Śruti, did not resort to the false chatter of heretics; and though they adopted the conduct of a cock, they did not possess the behavior of a cat.
They had abandoned the ranks of common folk;
they had avoided the pretenses of hypocrisy, greed, and deceit; and they had not embraced the depths of worldly entanglements.
Having cast aside all baseness,
with natures made serene and free from all distortions.
Their minds were turned away from censuring others; their vision was purified by turning back from the three castes; and they had shaken off all entreaties through their firm intellects.
They were of an unshakeable nature,
humble toward those who sought their friendship,
and had stilled all doubts regarding other philosophical systems.
They had unraveled the knots of the meanings of all the texts; they were poets and eloquent speakers.
Free from envy,
addicted to the pleasure of witty conversation,
and skilled in discerning clever jests.
They were skilled through long practice,
not outsiders to dance, song, and instrumental music,
and insatiable in their thirst for traditional lore.
Compassionate,
truthful and pure,
they were esteemed by the virtuous.
Their hearts were moistened by the fluid of affection for all sentient beings;
likewise, they were endowed with every virtue, unvanquished by royal armies,
possessed of patience, and were a source of delight to those who sought refuge in them.
The Vidyādharas are without swords;
the possessors of arts are not dull-witted;
and the stars are without blemish.
They do not afflict others, yet they are radiant; they are without heat, yet they consume offerings; they are free from guile, yet they possess great power.
They were pillars of virtue, abodes of merit;
they were skillful, never neglecting the performance of sacrifices; they were free from malice, having conquered their desires.
The Kaurukucīkas are unique among the twice-born; and while they are thus being born,
they wander through cyclic existence.
As the ages pass,
as the Kali age has descended,
and as the years flow on,
As the days passed and time went by,
the Vātsyāyana lineage flourished, continuously expanding through successive generations of descendants.
In due course, a twice-born man named Kubera was born, who, like Vainateya, was devoted to his preceptor;

he had four sons—Acyuta, Īśāna, Hara, and Pāśupata—who, like the beginnings of the four ages, expanded the progeny produced by the splendor of their Brahmanical power, and who, like the staff-like arms of Nārāyaṇa, delighted the virtuous circle of followers.

Among them, Pāśupata alone had a son named Athapati, who, like the weight of the earth, possessed the stability of the mountain ranges, was as deep as the four oceans, and was a high-souled crest-jewel of the entire circle of the foremost of the twice-born.
He begot Bhrigu, Haṃsa, Śuci, Kavi, Mahīdatta, Dharma, Jātavedas,
and the Kānis while plunging into that very same state of wisdom (vaipaścitī) suited to his own lineage;
and after a long time, he returned once more to that very birthplace of his, the abode of Brahmins belonging to the Vātsyāyana clan.

And there, his arrival greeted like that of a festival day by trusted friends whose affection had been renewed by their long absence and who displayed their kinship through familiarity, he experienced, as it were, the bliss of liberation while standing in the midst of his circle of childhood friends.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Vātsyāyana," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
The *Harṣacarita*, Second Chapter: In the king, who was exceedingly profound like a well from which people cannot descend...
Virtuous kings, acting as intermediaries, bring about the accomplishment of one's desired goals.
The day deposits upon the impassioned lotus the splendor born of the sun.
The virtuous regard helping others as their very duty, regardless of whether they receive any benefit or suffer any loss.

Then, there were dwellings resonant with the sound of Vedic recitation from within, inhabited by young students whose foreheads were pale with ash-marks and whose heads were matted with masses of tawny locks like fires come out of greed for sacrificial offerings; their courtyards were turning green with *soma* plants in the field, tender from being watered.

There were parched grains of *amāka* rice scattered upon black antelope skins for the sacrificial cakes; offerings of wild *nīvāra* grain were being strewn by young girls; and bundles of green *kuśa* grass and *palāśa* wood for fuel were being brought by pure disciples.
The courtyards were crowded with piles of firewood and balls of cow-dung;
the thresholds were scarred by the circles of hooves of the Agnihotra-cows that yielded milk for the daily oblations;
and the ascetics were busily engaged in kneading lumps of clay for their water-pots.
Its surroundings were purified by heaps of branches from *udumbara* trees used for the sacrificial posts at the Vedic altars;
its grounds were whitened by the rows of funeral cakes offered to the Viśvedevas; and the sprouts of the garden trees were turned greyish by the smoke of the oblations.

Where the calves were cherished by the cowherds of the Vatsa clan and moved about most restlessly; where the continuous practice of animal sacrifice was made manifest by the playful young black-spotted goats;
and where the pleasure of granting respite to the preceptors was afforded by the parrots and mainas who had begun their recitations.
Delighting as if in the very groves of the three Vedas, he wandered through the mansions of his long-lost kinsmen and dwelt there in happiness.

While he was staying there, at one point, the Great Time known as Summer unfolded itself, withdrawing the pair of seasons called the Flowering Season; with the white laughter of full-blown jasmine, it showed affection toward the new gardens that drink water like infants, for they had been recently conquered and now lay fallen like the vassal Spring. Thus, the season became mild.
And the scorching summer season, newly arisen, brought about the loosening of all flower-buds throughout the entire earth;
the masses of hair of amorous women were seized by the Flower-Armed God (Kāma) like yak-tail fans moistened by the coronation of the King of Seasons himself;
and the sun, as if in anger at the destruction of all lotus ponds by the frost, set out on a journey toward the Himalayas.

Then, while the sun scorched the forehead, the women were perceived by their moon-like foreheads—as if they were undertaking religious vows to worship the Sun—with the *puṇḍra* marks of *lālāṭika* tilaka applied, draped in the rags of their disheveled hair, and wearing rosaries formed from beads of perspiration.
Pale with sandalwood paste and unable to endure the sight of the sun, those beauties slept throughout the day like night-blooming lilies;
