languid with sleep, their eyes could not even bear the light of the jewels.
How much more so did the moonlit nights— rejoiced over by pairs of cakravāka birds— attain a state of thinness during this season devoid of cold, like rivers under a harsh heat;
and not only was the water fragrant with the fresh, sharp scent of pāṭala flowers, but so too was the air.
Due to the heat of the sun, people gradually developed a desire even to drink the wind as the rays of the sun became harsh and their childhood was brought to an end.
In a drying lake, in failing streams, and in sluggish waterfalls,
Resounding with the humming of crickets, deafening the entire world with the continuous cooing of timid pigeons, and causing all birds to lose their trust;
In the wind that scraped up dried cow-dung, where the creepers were sparse,
and where young lion cubs, curious about blood, were licking the hard clusters of dhātakī flowers;
On mountain slopes where great peaks were groaning under the distress of herds of panting elephants;
where bees were rendered silent as they settled upon the dark stains of ichor drying on the dejected faces of elephants scorched by the sun;
and where the horizon was reddened by the mandāra flowers turning crimson.

In that place, where the crystal rocks were being split asunder by the tips of the horns of great buffaloes, who were bewildered by the doubt of whether they were the mass of trickling water; where the dust was rustled by the heat; and where the scattered birds were terrified by the tossing of the hot sands of the riverbanks.
In the ponds where the water was reduced to a mere speckled residue of mud, with fish tossing on their backs from the feverish cries of ospreys and herons perched on the riverbanks;
in the world that seemed to be performing a lustration ceremony through the forest fires.
While the night-yakṣma was reigning and the summer season was becoming harsh,
those who were like manifest plunderers of the thatched roofs of water-sheds, roaming about in every direction upon the saline wastes, [were seen].
With the restless flicking of clusters of fully ripened *kapikacchū* fruits, they seemed as if suddenly seized by an itch, dragging along gravelly,
stony ground that scattered coarse dust from large stones and was jagged with the tearing of *mucukunda* sprouts.

Their bodies were sprayed with droplets from the mouths of flocks of noisy birds flying all around; they seemed to be swimming in the false waters of mirage-rivers, shimmering under the heat of the most youthful sun; and their shanks were swift and nimble in leaping over desert paths where the dry *śamī* trees rustled with parching sounds.
They were dancers of the *ārabhaṭī* style, commencing their frantic dances with the forceful whirling of circles of dust;
they were soiled by the smearing of the charcoal from forest-burnt ground,
and like those trained in the conduct of Jain mendicants, they were gathering heaps of peacock feathers from the woods.
They were like those on a journey by virtue of the clusters of seeds from old *karañja* and *nañjarī* trees that were jingling;
they were as if possessing new sprouts due to the thick sighs from the nostrils of forest buffaloes distressed by the heat;
and they were as if accompanied by offspring by means of the swarms of leaping, swift deer driven by the wind.
They appeared as if frowning with the curved crests of smoke from the heaps of burning chaff and husks; they seemed to possess waves through the emission of great heat;
and they were as if hairy with the cotton-fibers of decaying *śālmalī* fruits.
They resembled those afflicted with ringworm because of their dragging along heaps of dry leaves;

they were like those covered in veins because of their spreading out of grassy creepers; and they were like those with overgrown beards because of the spikes of awns from grain stalks being whirled up by the wind.
They were like those possessing fangs with hundreds of moving śalala-needles,
like those possessing tongues with the flames of Vaiśvānara, and like those whose crests were crowned by the sloughing skins of rising serpents.
Practicing, as it were, a mouthful for swallowing the essence of the entire world from Brahma down to a blade of grass with the warm honey of lotuses;
instilling terror in the three worlds with the sharp sounds of their cracking dry bamboo forests—sounds like the kettledrums proclaiming the heat that dries up all the waters;
and trailing paths streaked by the rows of wings of falling, trembling blue jays.
Their bodies appeared as if stained by the scorching heat of the sun’s rays, which were like blazing flames; their limbs were marked by sparks and embers resembling cracked *guñjā* berries.
Their movements were terrifying with deep, echoing roars from mountain caves.

Skilled in the sacrificial cooking for the black magic of world-destruction, they gratified the forest fires—those celestial deities—with showers of *pāribhadra* flower clusters as if with offerings of blood.

The winds possessed a speed as shimmering as frost upon hot sands; they smeared the quarters of the sky with the liquid resin of mountain rocks melting from the heat; and they were pungent with the smell of the "puṭapāka" (steaming) of swarms of insects within tree hollows, which were filled with fragments of sparrow eggs being cooked by forest fires.
Mad winds blew from all sides, as if agitated by the kindling of thousands of great bellows, driven by the air flowing from the deep throat-cavities of aged pythons;
in some places, deer roamed at will among the grass.
In some places there were brown mongooses moving through the hollows at the foot of trees; in others, tawny jackals with hanging manes;
and in yet others, hawks swooping down upon the nests of flocks of birds.
In some places the lips were red-hued like dissolved lac-dye;
in some places the arrows had acquired the swift flight of birds' wings; and in some places the extinguished fires had completely burnt away the causes of rebirth.
In some places they were passionate, fragrant with garments scented by flowers;
in some places they were dull-witted, emitting clouds of smoke; and in some places they were voracious, devouring the entire world and covered in ashes.

In some places they were corpulent, consuming all kinds of flavors; in others, fierce, like burnt guggulu resin; and in others, having established their abode upon the motionless Śiva, they had consumed the flower-bearing Madana with the fire of their blazing eyes.

Acting as actors in a fierce performance with the commencement of the dancing of flickering flames, they seemed to perform a ritual for the sun-god with handfuls of flames that rained down parched grains of flavorless wild rice bursting from the paths of dried-up marshes;
and like pitiless beings, they were greedily attracted by the stench of the fat of hard-shelled tortoises being forcibly offered as oblations.
As if out of fear of giving rise to clouds, they even consumed their own smoke;
in the thickets, they were like offerings of sesame seeds with swarms of young insects bursting forth;
and in the dried-up lakes, they were like lepers with white conch shells and oyster-pearls cracking open due to the heat.
In the forests, they were like sweat-dripping bees, with showers of wax dripping from globes of melting honeycombs;
on the vast salt-wastes, they were like bald patches, with their clusters of crests falling away;
and upon the mountain peaks where sun-crystals blazed, they were like those who had seized mouthfuls of rock.
Terrible forest fires were seen.

Now, during such an exceedingly fierce summer season, once while he was staying in his own house, having finished his meal, at the time of afternoon, his half-brother named Candrasena entered and said: "Indeed, this most renowned long-distance traveler has been sent by Kṛṣṇa—the brother of His Majesty the Emperor, the supreme lord Śrī Harṣadeva, the sovereign of all emperors, whose toe-nails have been polished by the friction of the crest-jewels of the entire circle of kings who are the lords of the four oceans—and he stands at the gate."
He said, "Long-lived one,
bring him in without delay. Then, as he was being brought in by him,

His shanks were heavy and sluggish from the great distance he had traveled; his coarse, tattered outer garment was bound together with strips of reddish-brown cloth; and the knots of his patched rags, dangling from his back, had come undone.
He saw a letter-carrier entering, his head covered with a series of lines that formed distinct divisions by means of the deep intervals created by the binding of very thick threads;
and even from afar, he asked him: "Good sir," he said.
"May there be well-being for the venerable Kṛṣṇa, the disinterested friend of the entire world," he said;
and having replied, "May there be well-being," and having bowed, he sat down not far away.
Once rested, he spoke: "Indeed, this letter has been sent by our honorable master. Having unsealed it, he presented it.

Then Bāṇa, having respectfully taken the letter, read it himself: "Having understood the message from Mekhalaka, the wise should remove any delay that might obstruct the fruit; this is the substance of the matter here, while everything else is merely for the purpose of exchanging news. Having grasped the meaning of the letter, he dismissed his attendants and asked for the message.
Mekhalaka replied: "The master says thus: 'The honorable one surely knows, as does the wise man, that whether by virtue of belonging to the same lineage, or...'"
Whether it be equality of birth, equal upbringing,
or residence in the same place;
Either the practice of seeing one another, or hearing of mutual affection, or the sharing of similar character;

As for the causes of this affection: though you are not seen and there is no apparent reason, my heart feels an inexplicable attachment toward you, as if you were a relative standing near at hand; even though you are far away, it loves you just as a bed of night-lotuses loves the moon.
Otherwise, had it not been for you, this emperor would have been led astray by wicked men in various ways.
And yet, that is not so;
for there truly exist those virtuous people for whom friends, neutrals, and enemies do not exist.

Moreover, because your mental disposition is turned away from the fickleness of youth, whatever improper thing has been uttered by some intolerant person, the rest of the world perceives and speaks of it exactly as it is.

Indeed, the minds of those lacking discrimination are as fickle as waters following the contours of the terrain; having had his resolve unsettled by hearing various accounts from many sources, what can the lord of the earth do?

Furthermore, though you were at a distance, you were perceived by us seekers of truth, and the Emperor was informed on your behalf that, generally speaking, childhood is guilty of the restlessness of all in their first stage of life.
"My lord has agreed, saying 'So be it';
therefore, you must come to the royal palace without delay. For you, who have not yet beheld the Supreme Lord, are highly esteemed by me as you dwell among your kinsmen like a tree without fruit."
And you should not be despondent due to the failure of your service, nor should you be afraid of approaching the Supreme Lord;
for even though He does not go so far as to say "Give," when His object arises by His own will, He gives it even at the cost of a hundred hardships of begging.
Out of delusion, he suddenly snatches away even life itself, alas, like the perverse Lord of the Mind (Kāma).
Nevertheless, those other kings were one thing,

while this lord is quite another; he is a nectar-like master who has surpassed Nṛga, Nala, Niṣadha, Nahuṣa, Ambarīṣa, Daśaratha, Dilīpa, Nābhāga, Bharata, Bhagīratha, and Yayāti, and his glances are not tainted by the deadly poison of the *kālakūṭa* of egoism.

There were no voices faltering with the seizure of a throat heavy with pride; no postures whose steadiness was lost through the epilepsy of the fever of excessive arrogance; and no distortions of the body distressed by the violent onset of the burning fever of insolence.

There were no instances of the breaking of limbs produced by the great onset of pride, nor were there any harsh words uttered with lips distorted and faces contorted by the affliction of intoxication;
and likewise, [there were none].
He possessed the perception of jewels toward pure virtuous men, and the intent for adornment toward those white as pearls,
but not toward the burdens of ornaments.
He had faith in the means for performing meritorious deeds,
but he felt great joy in fame, which is the foremost of all things, rather than in elephants or insects.
There was no exertion in adorning the hopes that grasp at life as if it were a withered blade of grass, nor any in their own wives, who were but leather dolls.
One should have the notion of an ally toward a bow possessed of excellent qualities,
and not even toward a retinue of servants who subsist on mere morsels of food.
His own self is the instrument for his friends; his sovereignty is the instrument for his servants;
and his erudition is the instrument for his scholars.
Wealth is for the benefit of kinsmen; sovereignty is for the benefit of the miserly;
and one's entire possession is for the benefit of the twice-born.
The heart is the instrument for recollecting good deeds;
life is the instrument for dharma;
the body is the instrument for daring.
The earth is the instrument for the sword; the royal court is the instrument for diversion;
the enemy is the instrument for majesty.

"Only those with great merit can attain the shade of this tree's sprout, which gives rise to the essence of bliss that surpasses all else"—having heard this, he commanded Candrasena himself: "See to it that he is provided with food and made comfortable.
Then, when he had departed,
When the day had come to a close,
as the afternoon sunlight— reddened like the beak of a young crow— waned and grew faint as if being drunk up by the clashing cups of red lotuses; and when the sun,

pale as a cluster of *japā* flowers, had slackened the speed of its own horses and stumbled as if its sprout-like feet were wounded by the thorns of the lotus-beds, having slipped upon the peak of the western mountain;

As the face of the night approached, its tresses hanging down in flickering fragments of darkness, appearing dark as if from the grief of separation from the moon, he performed his evening devotions and went to his bed; there,
alone, he reflected, "What shall I do?"
Otherwise, I have been esteemed by the King,
who is a friend without cause, and thus instructed by Kṛṣṇa;
yet such service is arduous.
Service is precarious, and the great royal family is exceedingly profound; moreover,
I possess no affection for it established by my ancestors.
There was no destiny inherited through family lineage, no compliance with the memory of past favors, and no affection born of service to the ignorant.
There was no respect for [their] lineage, no courtesy based on previous acquaintance,
and no attempt to entice them with the sharing of wisdom.
There is no curiosity regarding excellence in knowledge, no regard for the beauty of outward form, and no skill in the nuances of service.
There was no proficiency in the art of conversing with learned assemblies,
no mastery over the expenditure of wealth,
and no acquaintance with the king's favorites.

"Surely the Blessed One, the enemy of Tripura and the teacher of the world, will provide everything that is appropriate for me once I have gone there. Having thus resolved, he set his mind on departing;
then, rising on another day—
Having bathed early in the morning,
wearing clean, white silk garments,
and holding a rosary of beads, he—
Having repeatedly recited the hymns and mantra-words appropriate for departure,

and having performed with supreme devotion the worship of Virūpākṣa, the God of gods— preceded by a ceremonial bath of milk and abounding in fragrant flowers, incense, perfumes, banners, offerings, ointments, and lamps—

he offered oblations into the blessed Fire-god, whose crest of flames was made resonant by the flickering tips as the skins of the freshly offered sesame seeds were split open, and whose southern radiance was increased by abundant libations of clarified butter.
Having bestowed whatever wealth was available upon the twice-born,
and having circumambulated the white cow Naicikī while facing eastward, he was anointed with white unguents.
Wearing white garlands and white garments, with ear-ornaments fashioned from mountain-clover flowers strung together with tips of dūrvā grass and young shoots variegated with yellow pigment.

With white mustard seeds fastened to his topknot, he had all the auspicious rites for his departure performed by Mālatī— named after the great goddess Mahāśvetā— who was dressed in white garments, whose heart was moist with affection like a mother, and who was the younger sister of his father;
and he received blessings from the elderly female relatives.
He was welcomed by the female attendants with cries of joy;
permitted by his elders who saluted his feet;
and kissed on the head by the family elders who greeted him.
His enthusiasm for the journey increased through the omens provided by birds;
having satisfied the astrological requirements regarding the lunar mansion according to the opinion of the horologists,

he awaited at an auspicious moment a full water-jar placed upon a sacrificial altar in the courtyard smeared with fresh cow-dung— the jar whose neck was encircled by a garland of flowers other than black, which was white with the five-finger marks of flour-paste, and upon whose mouth were fixed fresh mango sprouts.
Having prostrated before the family deities,
followed by his own brahmins who carried flowers and fruits in their hands and were chanting the *Apratiratha* hymn,
he set forth with his right foot moving first.
He emerged from Prītikūṭa.

On the first day, having slowly passed through the grove of Caṇḍikā—which, though parched by the heat of summer, appeared as if it had sprouted new leaves; which, though devoid of water, seemed thrilled with joy by the thousands of flickering tongues of thirsty beasts of prey lolling out; which, though bare of foliage, seemed bristling with horripilation from the swarms of bees driven away by the smoke of burning ground; and where the images of Kātyāyanī were carved upon the boats entering the port, saluted by travelers—it was uneven with trees stripped of their leaves, and he reached the village named Mallakūṭa.
There he dwelt happily, receiving hospitality from his brother and friend named Jagatpati, who treated him with no distinction from his own heart.
Then, on the following day, having crossed the blessed Bhāgīrathī, he spent the night in a forest village named Yaṣṭigrahaka.
On another day, he reached the royal camp at Upamaṇitāra, which was established along the Ajiravatī river.
And he stopped not far from the royal palace.

Having completed his bath and meal and rested with Mekhalaka, when only one watch of the day remained and the king had finished eating, he proceeded slowly, observing the many encampments of famous monarchs. The air was turning dark with lordly elephants—some brought for the binding of the royal turban, some fetched for mounting the *ḍiṇḍima* drums, some newly captured, some acquired through ransoms, some received as tributes, some sent by the guardians of the elephant-paths, some brought out of curiosity for a first sight, some dispatched by messengers, some driven by the shouts of village chiefs, some summoned for the pleasure of mock battles, some being given away, some being seized, some being released, and some stationed there for a watch—all gathered like mountains for the purpose of building a bridge across the ocean in their desire to conquer all the continents, and made beautiful by their banners, fluttering drums, conchs, chowries, and painted ornaments, appearing like the very days of the consecration of the Puṣya asterism.

The sky was made to ripple by horses whose hooves, incessantly tossing and striking like mṛdaṅga drums, seemed to make the Goddess of Royal Fortune dance; who seemed to mock Ucchaiḥśravas with their loud neighs of joy at the very thought of a collision; and who, out of anger toward the chariot-horses of the Sun, seemed to leap into the air, their rows of ornamental chowries acting as wings.

The city was being turned tawny by herds of camels—some already dispatched, some being sent, and others returning from their missions—which were adorned with rows of cowries on their muzzles that seemed like strings of syllables counting their journeys of many *yojanas*; they were starred, as it were, with fragments of twilight sunlight; they wore ear-ornaments of reddish chowries and appeared like beds of red lotuses due to their fields of red rice; they possessed beautiful golden bells that produced a constant *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound and *ghurughuru* humming; they resembled ancient *karañja* forests with hundreds of rustling dry seed-pods; they were topped with tufts of hair-like matted locks of variegated threads in five colors dangling at the edges of their ears; and they were as brown as the cheeks of monkeys.

It was made white by fragments of parasols that resembled autumnal clouds with bodies white from masses of freshly fallen rain; that were like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpapādapa*) whose circles of shade were stolen by the light arising from clusters of pearls; that were like the lotuses on the navel of Nārāyaṇa embraced by the wings of Garuḍa; that were like regions of the Ocean of Milk with shining, massive coral stalks; that were like the hoods of Śeṣa with large ruby segments shimmering upon them; that were like the sands of the White Ganges frequented by royal swans; that seemed to overwhelm the summer season, to mock the majesty of the Sun, and to drink up the heat; that seemed to create a world of moonlight for the living world, to bring about a time consisting of night-lotuses, and to fashion a day made of moonlight; that seemed to display a heaven made of foam and to produce thousands of untimely moonlit nights; and that seemed to mock the fortune of Indra while appearing white.

The palace was swaying like a swing, its eight directions momentarily appearing and vanishing as if plundering the world; it seemed to compel the day itself to perform a series of arrivals and departures, as if establishing an autumn season with quarters white as blooming, pure groves of *kāśa* grass, thereby manifesting a state of affairs darkened by the stain of association with wicked kings, while making the sky appear as if woven from lotus fibers—all this through thousands of shimmering fly-whisks, white as moonbeams, being brandished. Furthermore, it resembled a flock of swans through the conch-like ears of elephants, and a forest of wish-fulfilling creepers through its plantain trees.
It resembled a forest of ruby trees with its peacock-umbrellas,
a flow of the Mandākinī river with its silken garments,
and the Ocean of Milk with its linen cloths.
It resembled a grove of plantain trees by means of emerald rays; it was as if creating another day with the morning sunlight of rubies;
and it was as if producing another sky with masses of sapphire luster.
It was as if beginning a never-before-seen night with the darkness of great sapphire rays;
it was as if a thousand flowing Kālindī rivers were streaming forth from the expansions of light from emerald gems;
and it was as if it were overspread with glowing coals by the radiance of topaz stones.

Some, unable to gain entrance, stood with downcast faces as if entering their own limbs through the reflection of their countenances fallen upon the nails of their feet out of shame; some offered, under the guise of the clusters of rays from their fingernails scattered over the ground they were scratching with their toes, chowries for service; some, with the flickering bands of sapphire light swaying upon their chests, appeared as if they had tied sword-belts around their necks to appease their master’s wrath; others, whose faces were darkened by swarms of bees circling the fragrance of their breath, seemed to have grown long beards out of grief for the loss of Fortune; still others, with circles of bees flying up from their crests, seemed to have their heads fleeing in fear of the mockery of prostration; though already conquered, they appeared honored, having no other refuge, as they repeatedly questioned with tireless persistence the attendants of the inner chamber-guards who were emerging and entering at intervals, amidst thousands of supplicants running along the path behind them: "Good sir," [they asked].

It was attended on all sides by great feudatory chiefs, conquered by his own arms, who spent their days with the hope of seeing him, thinking, "Today the meal will be finished and the Supreme Lord will grant an audience," or "He will emerge to the outer courtyard";
and it was occupied at leisure by other kings from various regions, drawn there by his majesty and affection, who waited for the opportune moment.

He was being attended by Jains, Ārhatas, Pāśupatas, and followers of Pārāśarya seated in secluded spots; by students of all castes and by people from every land; by barbarian tribes dwelling on the forested shores of every ocean;

and by circles of envoys arrived from all other continents—appearing like the creative ground of all the Prajāpatis, like a fourth world fashioned from the accumulated essence of the three worlds, and possessing a mass of prosperity that could not be described even by hundreds of *Mahābhārata*s.

He went to the palace gate, which appeared as if its layout had been fashioned by thousands of Kṛta-yugas, which possessed a beauty established by millions of heavens, and which was occupied as if by tens of millions of royal fortunes.

And as he was filled with wonder, there arose in his mind this thought: "How could the creators of beings have produced such a vast multitude of living creatures without experiencing exhaustion, or without the great elements being exhausted, or without the atoms being depleted, or without the end of time?"
"Either it is the end of his life,
or the completion of his physical form. But Mekhalaka, recognized from afar by the gatekeeper, was told, "Stay right here for a moment, you fortunate one," and thus unimpeded, he entered forward.
Then, after a mere moment, he appeared tall, with the complexion of a *karṇikāra* flower, his body covered by a fine, seamless tunic.
With a slender waist adorned by a beautiful girdle of shimmering rubies;
with a chest as broad as a slab from the Himalayan mountains;
and with shoulders as massive as the hump of Shiva’s bull.
He wore upon his chest a necklace that seemed like a noose for binding the fickle deer of the senses;

he was resplendent with jeweled earrings resting upon his ears, which appeared as if they were the moon and the sun brought there to ask, "Tell us, has there ever been a king of such a kind, born of the Lunar or the Solar dynasty?";

and he was being drawn along by the rays of the sun, which were swept away by the stream of the beauty flowing from his face, as if those rays were yielding the path out of respect for his high office.

He gladdened [the king] from afar with a long gaze that seemed like a garland of full-blown white lotuses obtained through his favor; he bore a pale turban upon a head that, though established in a station requiring severity, was bowed as if in humility;
and with his left sprout-like hand, he held a sword whose hilt was jagged with an inlay of large pearls.

Followed by a man carrying a polished golden cane—its flickeringness removed by another’s hand like a beaten vine—he went out and said: "This indeed is the gatekeeper named Pāriyātra, who stands next to the great chamberlains and is pleasing to the sight of His Majesty;
may he favor this youth with a fitting reception, for he is intent upon auspicious deeds.
The gatekeeper approached, made his salutation, and addressed him with humility in a sweet voice: "Please, come in."
"Enter to behold him;
the King has shown you favor," said Bāṇa, "I am indeed blessed."
Having said, "If Your Majesty considers me worthy of such favor," he entered the inner apartments while being shown the way by those born in Vanāyu and those born in Āraṭṭa.
By the Kāmbojas, the Bhāradvājas, and those born in the Sandhu country;
And by the Persians, and by the Śoṇas, and by the Śyāmas.
And with white ones, and tawny ones, and green ones.
And with those speckled like partridges,
and those auspicious in five ways,
and those with eyes like jasmine flowers;
With faces tawny like the Kṛttikā stars, their flesh wasted away from long fasting, and their ear-holes not prominent;

With neck-bells attached that were well-rounded, smooth, and well-fitted; with necks curved like sacrificial posts, long and rising to a sharp point; and with shoulder-joints swelling from their full development.

With chests slightly arched, and with hoof-circles that were thick, straight, extended, and as hard as iron pedestals, they bore rounded bellies that seemed as if they had no entrails, fearing they might burst from excessive speed.
With their broad hips revealed by rising girdles,
with young shoots dangling like swings upon the earth,
they were somehow restrained by being fastened on both sides with firm, thick ropes driven deep into the ground.

With their hind legs stretched out behind them as they were extended by the binding of the noose, appearing as if even longer; with the fleshy protuberances on their necks tied with cords of many strands; with eyes closed;

and shaking their limbs—which were covered in throbbing skin and marked by speckles of foam darkened by the juice of *dūrvā* grass—as they scratched themselves while holding and then releasing morsels of grass between their teeth.
with their tails flicking languidly, their hindquarters drooping and slackened from the rest of standing on a single hoof,
and dozing in deep meditation;
With their hooves striking the earth, producing soft, low-sounding grunts at every stumble, and their hoof-tips resonant with the clatter against the ground as they pawed the surface;
longing for fodder, agitated by the envy arising from the taste of the scattered mouthfuls of grain;
and with pupils trembling with extreme fear at the angry roars of fierce outcasts.

Beholding the stable constructed by the king’s favorite horses— horses whose bodies were tawny from being rubbed with saffron and who appeared as if constantly attended by the fires of lustration rites due to their golden hue, with canopies spread above them and their chosen deities worshipped before them.

With his heart captivated by curiosity, having traversed a short distance, he beheld from afar the indistinct temple of the elephant-god (Gaṇeśa), which, on account of its extreme height, seemed to leave no room for the sky itself; its perimeter was surrounded by a vast grove of plantain trees, and it was being filled on all sides by rivers of ichor flowing like streams composed of bees; and it was anointing the sense of smell with a fragrance spreading toward the quarters of the horizon, as if from blossoming groves of *bakula* trees.
And he asked, "What is the King doing here?
He replied, "This is indeed the King’s mount, his external heart, his very self in another form—the lordly elephant.
This great pavilion seen here is his place of residence."
He said to him, "Good sir,
it is heard that Darpaśāta is here;
if this is so, I shall look upon the lordly elephant himself, provided there is no fault."
"Therefore, you ought to lead me there;
I am overcome with curiosity.
"Let it be so," he replied.
"May your honor come;
what is the harm?
Please look at this lordly elephant for a moment."

And having reached that place, even from afar he beheld a great clamor being raised by flocks of *cātaka* birds in the sky with their deep throat-thundering, and by throngs of domestic peacocks on the ground with their mouths resonant with the sweet-sounding warbling of their cries; a world filled with the wine-like fragrance of rutting ichor that rivaled the scent of blooming *kadamba* flowers;
it was like the time of untimely clouds incarnate.
He was casting off the fourth stage of life, which resembled a lake covered with a dense network of lotuses tawny with thick drops of honey;
he seemed to be singing the auspicious commencement of his entry into the fifth stage with the incessant sounds of his ear-ornament shells and the deep resonance of his flapping ears like drums;

and, due to the swaying of his long, expansive body through the graceful rhythmic dances of his constantly moving variegated three-legged stools, he appeared as if lightening his burden for fear of splitting the earth, or as if scratching his own body against the slopes of the walls of the quarters.
With its trunk raised for combat, it seemed to summon the elephants of the quarters;

with its thick and sharp tusk acting as a saw, it appeared to cleave the pillar of the universe (brahmastambha); and though unable to fit within the interior of the palace, it strove to emerge as if it were outside.

He experienced the joy of receiving the seasonal rites appropriate for the summer from his mahouts, who were like forests long-familiar through constant association with bees that clung to every side of the creepers with their fresh sprouts, and who resembled lakes whose waters were mottled by the spreading clusters of moss and lotus stalks scattered about.

Moreover, with his exceedingly massive iron bar of a trunk—whose belly was rippled by very thin lines of wrinkles that seemed like streaks of light counting his many victories in battle, tossed far upward by the wind from the ichor of rival elephants—he appeared to bolt the entire circle of the quarters, including its mountains, oceans, islands, and forests.

He bore in one hand a plantain stalk with its tip like a blue lotus, its base being sprinkled by internal spray as if it were a sprout that had burst forth; while in the other, he held a cane-shaft adorned with a cluster of playfully dangling lotus fibers, which made his arm appear as if bristling with horripilation from the thrill of the passion for battle.

With the luster of his pair of trunk-tusks spreading forth, he seemed to be vomiting out in many ways the beds of night-lotuses he had tasted during his sports in the lake; he appeared to be bestowing upon the quarters of the sky his own mass of glory, mocking lions who were arrogant in their tearing of the lowly *kuka* insects, and fashioning for himself a face-veil from the silken garments of the wish-granting tree (*kalpadruma*).

And in the graceful play of raising his trunk-staffs, with a palate as delicate as red silk that was visible, he seemed to rain down swallowed forests of red lotuses and to vomit forth a heap of fresh sprouts.
He was vomiting, as it were, with his naturally tawny eye—which had drunk the essence of lotuses—the sweet nectar of their beauty;

and through the profusion of ichor flowing from his temples, which resonated with the sounds of mangoes, campakas, lavalīs, cloves, and kakkolas, he seemed to be repeatedly offering up all the groves of Pārijāta trees he had enjoyed, under the guise of the thick fragrance of rut.

Day and night, with his trunk resting in various playful positions, scratched by the itching of half-chewed stalks of red sugar-cane, and resonating with swarms of bees, he seemed to be bestowing upon all the forest elephants the very gifts of those royal tuskers.
He was being cooled by a necklace of shimmering stars composed of fragments of moonstone that dripped incessant drops of water;
he bore his head held very high, beautiful with the binding of the turban signifying his sovereignty over all the lords of elephants;

and, as if out of devotion to his master, he repeatedly fanned the Royal Fortune seated upon the couch of his tusks with his two fan-like ears, which alternately covered and revealed the quarters of the sky.
He was resplendent with a tail that moved like a fly-whisk—the insignia of lordship over elephants—descended through a long line of ancestors;
and under the guise of clear, cool spray, he seemed to discharge again and again from his mouth the rivers swallowed during his conquest of the quarters.

For a moment, all his limbs were rendered motionless as he gave his attention, and at the end of the twisting of his body upon hearing the drum of another elephant, he seemed to announce the pain of humiliation with long, hissing breaths.
He seemed to mourn his own lack of battle;

with three-quarters of his eyes closed by the drowsiness of rut, he accepted morsels of fodder only with great difficulty and with utter indifference, compelled by the neighing of his rider who was angry at being made to release his mouthfuls after having been snubbed;
and because of the abundance of the dark juice trickling from the chewed tamāla shoots, he appeared as if he were discharging a stream of rut even through his mouth.
As if swelling with pride,
as if panting with valor, as if fainting with intoxication.
As if bursting with youth,
as if flowing with generosity,
as if leaping with strength;
As if intoxicated by pride,
as if rising up with energy,
as if fainting with splendor.
As if anointing with loveliness,
as if sprinkling with good fortune,
he was glossy in his nails.
He was harsh regarding his hair, grave in speech, and well-disciplined toward his disciples.
Gentle on the head,
firm in the joints,
and short at the neck-binding.
Long in life, impoverished in the belly,
and constantly engaged in giving.
Balabhadra in his playful intoxications,
the family wife in matters of dependence,
and the Jina in forbearances.
One should employ Vahni in the discharge of wrath, Garuḍa in the extraction of serpents,
and Nārada in the curiosity for quarrels.
He was like a dry thunderbolt in sudden assaults,
a sea-monster in the agitations of an army,
and a venomous serpent in the act of biting.
He was Varuṇa in drawing enemies with the noose of his hand, Yama in ensnaring his foes with his net,
and Kāla in bringing about their transformation.
Rāhu in the grasping of sharp rays, Mars in its retrograde motions,
and a fire-brand circle in the consciousness of circular whirling.
It was a mountain of wish-fulfilling gems for his valor;
a palace with pillars of ivory and pearls for his pride;
and a celestial chariot for his self-respect, enchanting with its ornaments of bells and fly-whisks and capable of moving at will.

It was the abode of intoxication, the palace of egoism; it was a pleasure mountain for arrogance, possessing springs like boulder-strewn slopes; it was a diamond temple for pride, featuring gate-arches like its tusks.
It was a mountain fortress for the kingdom, formidable with its high water-jars, turrets, and watchtowers;
it was an iron wall for the earth, pierced by thousands of openings made for arrows;
and it was a *pārijāta* tree for the earthly paradise, resounding with the humming of hundreds of bees.
And thus, he was a concert hall for the rhythmic dances of his ears,
a drinking pavilion for the swarms of bees,
and an inner chamber for the ornaments of love.
It was a festival of passion for those performing dances of intoxicating grace; it was an unbroken night of the dark fortnight for the circles of star-garlands;
and it was an untimely monsoon season for the mists that filled the great rivers of rut.

He beheld that false cloud, which was merely a display of thundering, and whose pride had been shattered; and it occurred to his mind: "Surely, in the creation of this [cloud], mountains were reduced to the state of atoms."
"How else could there be such majesty?
This is a marvel: 'These are the teeth of Vindhya; this is the trunk of Ādivarāha!'—while he was thus filled with wonder, the doorkeeper said to him: 'Behold!'"

The prosperity of their enemies—who, with minds agitated by the fabrication of means for achieving their goals, had vainly painted it with hundreds of desires and then utterly lost it—has appeared once more in the forest.
How has this lord of serpents, having somehow entered the path of memory for those whose minds are becoming empty, failed to tolerate even the elephants of hope dwelling within their minds?
"Come, you shall see him again;

first, behold the King," he was thus addressed by him. With some effort, he withdrew his gaze—which had fallen upon the elephant's temples smeared with rut-fluid and was as if intoxicated and closed like a bud by the scent of that ichor—and, guided by that same doorkeeper, he passed through three courtyards crowded with thousands of monarchs and stood in the courtyard before the reception hall where the king had finished his meal.

He was surrounded from a distance by a circle of tall, principal bodyguards standing upright, fair as *karṇikāra* flowers, their bodies robust from physical exercise and bearing weapons; they stood in rows like a cluster of golden pillars.

Nearby sat his distinguished and beloved attendants, while he himself was seated upon a couch made of a slab from a pearl-mountain, appearing as if fashioned from moonstone, with legs white as ivory, its surface cooled by frost-like spray and washed with yellow sandalwood juice.
With the entire weight of his body resting upon an arm placed at the edge of his bed,

he was sporting with the circle of kings in a canopy of bodily radiance spreading toward the quarters of the sky, where the rays of jewels were diffused; it was like a lake in the season of heat, its waters entangled with a network of soft lotus stalks,
and he appeared as if fashioned from nothing but the atoms of splendor.

As if forcibly seating upon the lion-throne one who was unwilling, he was embraced in all his limbs by every auspicious mark; having taken up the vow of celibacy, he was embraced by the Fortune of Kingship; and being a royal sage who never spoke falsely, he had undertaken the difficult vow of walking the edge of a sword.
He was firmly established in righteousness as if out of fear of tripping while placing his feet upon an uneven royal road;
he was served with his whole soul by Truth, which had found its voice and was terrified after being abandoned by all other kings;
and he was being saluted by the ten directions—represented by the reflections of the nearby courtesans falling upon his toe-nails—as if they were bowing down before him.
With long glances reaching to the ends of the quarters, he seemed to be scrutinizing the deeds and omissions of the world-protectors;
with his hand resting upon the back of his jeweled footstool, he seemed to be seeking permission from the day to proceed upward;
and even by the mountains that did not bow before him, he was pained by the heat of his valor.
He bore an ocean of loveliness white as sandalwood, as if surging with foam;
through the majesty of his sole sovereignty, he seemed unable to endure even his own reflections held upon the crest-jewels of the circle of kings;
and he possessed the Royal Fortune, who, due to the misery of her pride, seemed to sigh many times under the guise of the breeze from the chowries.
He was embraced by the Goddess of Fortune, who had arisen as if having taken up the entire loveliness of the four oceans;
he seemed to be bestowing upon the kings thousands of rainbows produced from the mass of light radiating from his ornaments, as if they were presents sent by Indra;
and in his conversations, he showered honey even though it had been discarded.
He was one who, even in poetic tales, vomited forth nectar though he had not drunk it; who revealed his heart even when not drawn out by confidential conversations;
and who established, in various places, a fortune that remained steady even during favors.
With his cheeks bristling with thrill during assemblies of heroes, he seemed to be listening in secret to the whispers of the Goddess of War regarding her message of passion;

casting a glance like a shower of affection upon his beloved sword whenever the clamor of past duels was mentioned; and revealing, as it were, the pure heart of the royal assembly—frightened by his great majesty—through the rays of his teeth during their jesting smiles.
Though he dwelt within the hearts of all people, he remained established in justice;

he stood upon a greatness of majesty that was beyond the range of virtues, outside the domain of good fortune, inaccessible to the granting of boons, impossible for blessings, off the path of desires, far removed from the reach of fate, and unachievable by merit—having never before been seen by Fortune.

With limbs as supple as the shoots of the dawn-lotus, thighs as steady as those of the Sugata, a forearm and back as firm as a thunderbolt-weapon, shoulders like a bull’s, lips as radiant as the solar disc, a gaze full of serenity, a face like the moon, and hair as black as jet—by means of such a body, he seemed to manifest the descent of all the deities into a single form.

Moreover, upon a great and precious footstool made of sapphire, its base adorned with a girdle of ruby strings and its surface darkening the earth with a dense mass of rays, he rested his left foot with ease as if it were the head of the Kali age; like the young lotus-eyed Viṣṇu treading upon the circle of Kāliya’s hoods,
he seemed to elevate his own majesty by spreading across the earth a white silken sash— the expansion of the luster from his toenails— resembling the binding cloth of a Great Queen.

He bore two feet that were exceedingly red, as if from the wrath of the world-protectors who had failed to bow before him; they seemed to vomit forth the intensely yellow light of rubies from the garlands upon the crowns of all kings, like the twilight at the setting of the entire circle of luminaries; they appeared to pour forth streams of the sweet nectar from the flowers on the crests of the whole assembly of monarchs; they were never for even a moment separated from swarms of bees wandering about in the fragrance of the wreaths from the topknots of all the vassals, as if those swarms were the heads of his enemies; they fashioned, as it were, dwelling-places for the forest of blooming red lotuses of the Goddess Śrī, who was intent on massaging them; and they seemed to proclaim the marks of his enjoyment of the four oceans, since their soles were adorned with lotuses, conchs, fish, and sea-monsters.

He was resplendent with two pillar-like thighs that were as beautiful as the tusks of the elephant Diṅnāga used for a pestle, which were curved by the obstruction of fierce crocodile mouths; they were like surging currents from the ocean of overflowing loveliness, adorned with the splendor of foam, and served as ruby pillars for supporting the burden of the earth placed upon his heart.

He shone like Mount Mandara encircled by the sloughed skin of Vāsuki, with a lower garment white as a mass of nectar-foam, inlaid with the rays of gems from his girdle, draped across the orb of his hips, washed in pure water, and beautified by the threading of its cords, appearing like the serpent’s own cast-off skin.

He shone with a vast chest-plate of crystal-like whiteness, which was as hard and smooth as if polished by thousands of maces from the tusks of lordly elephants; it was so broad that it seemed insufficient for the expanse of the sky, and it could endure the tumultuous clamor and crush of various armies, making him appear like Mount Kailāsa itself, while the second heaven above, filled with hosts of stars, made the entire world seem radiant.

His neck was encircled by a necklace that resembled the remains of the cord used to divide the enjoyment of the breasts and faces of Śrī and Sarasvatī, and which appeared like the serpent Śeṣa fast asleep in the bliss of rest after bearing the entire burden of the earth upon his pillar-like arms;

and his chest was covered by a mass of rays from the pearls of his necklace, which looked like the white garment of initiation for the great gift of bestowing all one’s possessions at the end of one’s life.

With the ruby-staffed rays of light from his armlets spreading out on both sides—like the arms of the Goddess Śrī, who reclines upon his embrace, stretching forth in her desire to conquer him, or like streams of honey trickling from the ear-lotuses of that same Śrī, or like the emerging paths for the departure of the heat born of his own arms—he appeared like a mountain of rubies with a canopy of jeweled wings spread wide on either side.
