the divine sun, radiant with a mass of matted locks of tawny rays hanging low in the west, is sinking into the great lake of blood at Samantapañcaka like the venerable Bhārgava Rāma. Into this expanse of twilight hues, I shall report tomorrow."
And they all agreed, saying, "So be it.
Before long, having risen, he went to the Śoṇa river to perform his twilight devotions.

Then, as the sun—reddest like the closing of a lotus, licking at the darkness, and hanging low—was setting, the day had closed like a bud in the soft glow upon the cheeks of Mālava women, which were blossoming with the intoxication of honey.
As the darkness in the sky rushed along the path of the sun’s chariot-horses like Yama’s buffalo,

and as the bark garments— hanging from the thatched roofs of the house-dwellers’ huts— were gradually withdrawn along with the fragments of their red glow; and as the smoke from the sacrificial fires, which steals away the sins of the Kali age, nourished the firmament.
While the sacrificers observed their vows of silence,
while the wives wandered about, restless at the hour of the ritual distribution,
and while the sacrificial cows— tawny from the milk used for oblations— were being fed with handfuls of green, dark śyāmāka and śāli rice scattered about;
While the Tanūnapāt oblation was being offered in the sacrificial fire,
and while the matted-haired ascetic sat upon a purified seat of kuśa grass, the young students were chanting their prayers.
While the assembly of yogis sat upon their Brahma-seats in meditation,

while the endless circle of disciples ran about to the sound of clapping hands, and while the crowd of dull-witted, aged Vedic scholars— permitted by the elders— chanted the falling syllables of the sacred texts, the twilight was observed and the starlight emerged in the sky.
When the onset of evening had arrived, he returned to his residence and sat down together with his affectionate kinsmen;
he remained in that very company until the first watch of the night had passed, and then retired to the bed prepared for him in the palace of Gaṇapati.

But as for all the others, though their eyes were closed and they were not yet overcome by sleep, they waited like beds of lotuses for the rising of the sun, and thus, through sheer curiosity, that night somehow came to an end.

Then, having awakened during the fourth watch of the night, that same bard sang these two verses: "Stretching out his hind leg, extending his body high with his back arched, resting his face against his chest with his neck bent, and shaking his mane grey with dust—"
Desiring a mouthful of grass, the horse, its muzzle constantly flickering, rises from its bed and, making a soft sound, scratches the earth with its hoof.
With his back bent, his waist drawn close to his face, and his neck tilted far sideways, he was being struck by a swaying, pollen-dropping mane that scattered sprays of frost.

The horse, with its shell-like ears pressed tight, rubs with its hoof the corner of its eye—a corner stained by the itch of sleep and containing fine particles of chaff from the tips of its twitching eyelashes.

Bāṇa, having heard that, cast off his sleep, rose, washed his face, and performed the worship of the divine Twilight (saṃdhyā). When the blessed sun had risen, he took his betel and remained right there.
In the meantime, all his kinsmen arrived and sat surrounding him.

He too, having understood their intention through their preliminary hints, began to recount the *Harṣacarita* before them: "Listen! There is a place, like a dwelling for the meritorious, which has descended upon the earth—"
The stability of its social order was based on the constant practice of unadulterated speech, and it remained established in the conditions of the Kṛta Yuga;
its fields were being ploughed by ploughs that, due to the abundance of land-lotuses, uprooted the lotus-stalks and raised a clamor of bees as if singing the earth’s essential virtues;
and it was filled without interruption with continuous rows of sugar-cane and *puṇḍra* groves, appearing as if sprinkled by clouds drinking the waters of the Ocean of Milk.
Its boundaries were crowded with heaps of grain that divided every direction like unprecedented mountains, serving as dwellings for threshers;

it was adorned with rice-fields more excellent than even the most fertile lands, and presided over by the surfaces of fields where the abodes of wheat appeared tawny with the bursting pods of mung beans and variegated by clusters of king-beans crumbling in ripeness.

The forest was whitened by herds of cattle—protected by cowherds singing while mounted on the backs of buffaloes, followed by sparrows greedy for swarms of insects, made charming by the tinkling of small bells fastened to their necks—as they roamed about, exuding milk like the Ocean of Milk divided into many portions out of fear that it had been drunk by Śiva’s bull; these herds were satisfied with grass that could be cut by mere breath. The landscape was speckled with black antelopes, numbering in the thousands, which appeared like the thousand eyes of Indra when blinded by the smoke of various sacrificial oblations.

It was adorned with regions that, whitened by the pollen of *ketakī* groves shedding white dust, appeared grey like the entryways to the city of Śiva, stained with the ashes smeared upon the body by the Lord of the Pramathas; its surface of the earth near the villages was darkened by the young shoots of *śāka* plants.

At every step, the exits were made alluring by vine-arbors that served as pavilions for nectar-liquids offered by forest deities; these arbors had travelers sleeping comfortably after drinking the juice of fresh fruits, with their hands massaged by the rows of young elephants' trunks, smeared with the juice of citron petals crushed by those very trunks, and fashioned into flower-beds from saffron filaments gathered at will. Furthermore, the exits were enchanting due to groves of pomegranate trees whose bursting fruits seemed to possess the red hue of parrots' beaks clinging to the juice, and whose flowers were mistaken for the cheeks of the troops of monkeys climbing upon them.

It was delightful with groves where the coconut-liquor was being drunk by forest guards, where clusters of dates were being plundered by travelers, where the sweet-smelling juices of *piṇḍī* fruits were being licked by monkeys, and where *ārūka* fruits were being crushed by the beaks of *cakora* birds;

its forest clearings were never empty, being filled by woodland tracts that served as refuge for hundreds of wayfarers, whose banks were turbid from the descent of herds of cattle and which were surrounded by rows of tall *arjuna* trees;
and it was crowded with camels and lambs being tended by young camel-herders and shepherds.

It was filled with herds of mares wandering at will like wind-haunted deer, who—having rolled upon the ground smeared with the essence of saffron as if to entice the horses of the sun’s chariot in every direction—seemed to drink in the wind with their upturned, snorting nostrils, as if to generate speed for the foals lying within their bellies;
its world was whitened by arrows that, like flocks of swans emerging from the darkness of the smoke of incessant sacrifices, made the earth bright;
and the realm of living beings was made resonant by its riches, which, like peacocks intoxicated by the sound of drums in a musical performance, filled the air with their cries.
It was adorned with virtuous men whose conduct was as pure as moonbeams, like pearls set upon a string;
it was worthy of being approached by all guests, like great trees whose abundant fruit is being plucked by hundreds of travelers;
and it was rendered stable by eminent men covered in deer-skin garments that wafted the fragrance of musk, like the foothills of the Himalayas.

The country named Śrīkaṇṭha was adorned with lakes that resembled the circle of Nārāyaṇa’s navel, filled with the best of birds seated upon thousands of upraised lotus petals; its quarters were filled with great-sounding rivers whose banks were washed by torrents of churned water, resembling the onset of the churning of the Ocean of Milk;
and there, false doctrines perished as if washed away by the tears of smoke from the three sacrificial fires.
Sins became invisible, as if burnt by the fire upon the bricks being baked in the sacrificial hearths;
unrighteousness was torn asunder, as if split by axes cutting the wood for the sacrificial posts;
and the mixture of various castes was washed away, as if cleansed by the torrents from the clouds of smoke rising from the flames of the sacrifice.
As if being shattered by the horns of thousands of cows being given away, Kali fled;
as if cut to pieces by the multitude of chisels from the striking against the stones of the celestial abode, calamities were rent asunder;
and as if pursued by the clamor of the performance of great gifts, misfortunes ran away.
Diseases melted away as if scorched by the heat of thousands of blazing sacrificial kitchens;
misfortunes did not approach, as if terrified by the sharp sound of the holy drums beaten at the marriage of the Bull; and calamities departed, as if deafened by the continuous chanting of the Veda.

In that place, ill fortune did not prevail as if it were overwhelmed by the authority of Dharma; and there, in such a spot, was the commencement of youth for the world, delightful with the fragrant scent of flowers from various groves;
it was like the inner apartments of Dharma, graced by many thousands of buffalo-cows reddened by the smearing of saffron.
With its borders whitened by hundreds of yak-tail fans being waved by the Maruts, it was like a single region of the realm of the gods;
with the ten horizons illuminated by thousands of blazing sacrificial fires, it was like the encampment of the Kṛta Yuga;
and with all ill fortune being quelled through the meditations of Brahman-sages seated in the lotus posture, it was like the first descent of the world of Brahmā.
It was crowded with hundreds of great rivers whose mouths were filled with clamor, like the northern continent of Uttarakuru;
its entire population was unacquainted with the suffering of seeking a lord, as if it were the city of Tripura desiring victory;
and it was white with rows of palaces whitened by the essence of nectar, like a counterpart to the world of the moon.
There was a particular district named Sthāṇvīśvara, which filled the world with the sound of ornaments from women intoxicated by wine, resembling as it were the city of Kubera;
which was called a "penance grove" (tapovana) by the sages.
It is a "pleasure-grove" according to courtesans,
a "concert hall" according to dancers,
and a "city of Yama" according to enemies.
It was a "wish-fulfilling gem" for those seeking objects of desire,
a "field of heroes" for those who subsist on the teachings, and a "preceptor's household" for those seeking knowledge.
It was called a "city of the Gandharvas" by musicians,
a "palace of Viśvakarman" by experts in craftsmanship,
and a "ground for profit" by merchants.
It is a place of gambling, according to the bards; a gathering of the virtuous, according to the righteous; and a diamond cage, according to those who have sought refuge.
It was called a "gathering of parasites" by the clever,
a "fruition of good deeds" by travelers,
and a "subterranean cave of the Asuras" by the garrulous.
It was called "the hermitage of the Śākyas" by those seeking tranquility, "the city of the Apsarases" by those driven by desire,
and "a great festive assembly" by the wandering bards.
And there, the Brahmins accepted the earth as a gift, for there were women who walked like elephants yet were virtuous,
and who were fair-complexioned yet devoted to wealth.

They were dark-complexioned yet possessed of the luster of rubies; their faces were as pure as white lotuses, yet their breath was fragrant with wine; their bodies were as radiant as moonstones, yet their limbs were as delicate as the śirīṣa flower.
They were inaccessible to libertines yet possessed inner chambers;
they possessed the splendor of many wives yet were joined with impoverished husbands;
they were full of loveliness yet spoke with sweet words.

There, the women were vigilant, possessed of bright and radiant passion, free from curiosity, and mature; for these women, their very eyes were a natural ornament of severed heads, while garlands of blue lotus petals were a mere burden.

The reflections of her own face upon the surface of her cheeks serve as unadorned ear-ornaments; the sprouts of the *tamāla* tree are redundant, for the delightful stories of her beloved are themselves the ornaments of her ears; her earrings are mere ostentation, for her cheeks are themselves the source of constant light; and during the nights, her very countenance is the wealth of jewel-lamps that provide illumination.

The swarms of bees drawn by her breath alone constitute her lovely facial veil; the custom of noble women is her net-like screen; her sweet speech alone is the lute; external knowledge is the striking of its strings;
her laughter alone is the most fragrant perfumes; camphor powder is useless.
The glow of her lower lip alone is a more brilliant cosmetic than any other; saffron paste is a mere stain upon her natural loveliness;
her arms alone are most tender, serving as cane-staffs for the playful blows of laughter; lotus stalks are useless;
the beads of perspiration from the heat of youth are themselves the clever ornaments for her breasts, while necklaces are but a burden.
In that very courtyard, the vast, square crystal slabs served as the cause for rest for those filled with passion; the jeweled pedestals of the palace were a signless abode;

the buzzing swarms of bees, lured by the desire for lotuses, served as the resonant ornaments for her feet; the fruitless sapphire anklets were replaced by the appropriate companions for her movement—the palace swans summoned by the sound of her anklets; and the attendants were merely the manifestations of her sovereign power.
And there, he appeared like the thousand-eyed Indra in person, wielding a bow that bore every hue;
he was like Mount Meru in his auspicious nature,
and like Mount Mandara in his power to attract fortune.
He was like the ocean in his adherence to the bounds of propriety,
like the sky in the manifestation of sound,
and like the moon in his gathering of the digits of excellence.
He was like the Veda itself in his natural eloquence,
like the earth itself in supporting the world,
and like the wind itself in removing all the dust of worldly passion from kings.
Guru in speech,
Pṛthu in the chest, Viśāla in mind.
Janaka is in asceticism, Suyātra is in splendor, and Sumantra is in counsel.
Budha was preeminent in the assembly,
Arjuna in fame, and Bhīṣma in archery.
He was Niṣadha in physical form,
Śatrughna in battle, and a hero in the conquest of Śūrasena.
There was a king named Puṣpabhūti, skilled in the business of governing his subjects, who seemed as if fashioned from the massed splendor of all the primordial kings;
he made this earth his queen, as if in rivalry with Pṛthu, who had made the cow the earth.
For the intellect of the great is indeed naturally independent and follows its own inclination;
thus, without being instructed by anyone, he possessed from childhood itself an innate devotion directed toward the Blessed One and away from other deities,
such that he did not take food even in his dreams until he had performed the ritual worship of the Bull-bannered Lord.
Unborn,
undecaying,
the teacher of the immortals,
The enemy of the cities of the Asuras,
the lord of immeasurable hosts,
the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having taken refuge in Paśupati, to whom all the worlds had prostrated themselves, he considered the three worlds to be devoid of any other deity;
and the subjects among his dependents, conforming to the mind of their master, did likewise.
For thus,

in every house the Blessed One, the wielder of the broken-axe (Śiva), was worshipped; and in those holy regions, winds blew, laden with the thick fragrance of guggulu resin melting in the sacrificial fire-pits, scattering droplets of milk used for his ritual bathing, and carrying forth the petals from the garlands of bilva leaves.

The citizens, the ministers who lived at his feet, and the great vassal lords—conquered by the strength of his arm and made to pay tribute—served him with offerings and gifts appropriate for the worship of Śiva;
for instance:

They brought satisfaction to his mind with great sandalwood bulls, white as the peaks of Kailāsa, their tips of horns adorned with golden leaf-patterns; with golden ceremonial jars for ablutions, vessels for the *arghya* offering, incense burners, lamps on jeweled stands, sacred threads, and mouth-covers inlaid with fragments of precious rubies.

Even the women of the inner apartments followed his desire; they themselves began the husking of rice for the sacrificial offerings, their sprout-like hands grew even redder from smearing the temple floors with unguents, and their entire retinue became busily engaged in stringing flowers.
And so it was.

That king, a supreme devotee of Maheśvara, heard from the people that there was on earth another Bhagavat, as it were, Dakṣa-makha-mathana incarnate, a great Śaiva named Bhairavācārya from the Deccan, who filled the world of mortals with thousands of disciples renowned for their mastery of various sciences and virtues;
for cool words bring delight to the heart even when the person is unseen.
For at the very moment he heard this, the king conceived a profound devotion toward that venerable Bhairavācārya—as if toward Śiva himself—even though the teacher had already gone far away;
and he longed with all his heart for a vision of him by any means possible.
Then one day, when the day had declined and was kissing the western mountain, the female door-keeper approached the king in the inner apartments and announced: "Your Majesty,"

A wandering mendicant was sitting at the gate and said, "I have come to Your Majesty by the command of Bhairavācārya. Upon hearing this, the king respectfully asked, "Where is he? Bring him here; let him enter right now."
The female doorkeeper acted accordingly,
and before long, she saw a tall man entering with arms reaching to his knees; though emaciated from living on alms, he appeared robust due to the thick bones of his limbs.
He had a broad head, a forehead marked by deep, prominent wrinkles, hollow cheeks devoid of flesh,
and round eyes tawny like drops of honey.
With a slightly curved nose,
an excessively long lobe on one ear, and rows of teeth as large and prominent as gourd seeds;
His lower lip was slackened by the habitual pulling of the horse's reins;
his chin was pendulous and his mouth was wide;
and he wore a saffron-colored meditation band draped over his shoulder, fashioned into a *vaikakṣaka* cross-strap.
He wore an upper garment made of a piece of cloth, reddened by mineral pigments, which was as if cut into fragments by passion itself, with a knot tied at the center of his chest.

Furthermore, he saw a wandering mendicant (maskarin) whose shoulder was supported by a yogic staff (yogabhāraka) held in his left hand; this staff had its base made motionless by being wrapped with a cord of twisted bark, was bound with bamboo strips and hempen ropes for cleaning clay pots, and had its upper end provided with a loincloth. His alms-bowl was contained within a leather pouch shaped like a date-palm leaf, and his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) was fixed upon three wooden planks arranged in a triangle. Sandals were placed outside [the staff], and a bundle of books secured with thick cords of thread rested against it. In his other hand, he carried a cane seat.
The lord of the earth also received the approaching man with appropriate respect, and once he was seated, the king asked, "Where is Bhairavācārya?

With a mind delighted by the respectful words of the monarch, the wandering mendicant informed him that the teacher was staying in a deserted temple situated in a grove on the bank of the Sarasvatī, just outside the city.

Furthermore, he spoke again: "The Blessed One honors this illustrious man with his blessing. Having said this, he drew from his yogic burden five silver lotuses sent by Bhairavācārya, which were adorned with jewels and filled the inner apartments with intense light. But the king, fearing to break the affection of those dear to him, yet constrained by courtesy and unable to disregard the slight of refusal, stood with a wavering mind; then, overcome by extreme kindness, he accepted them with great difficulty.

And he said, "This devotion to Śiva is the cause for the production of all fruits; it bears fruits that are difficult even for our desires to attain, since by this very means the venerable Bhairavācārya, the teacher of the world, takes pleasure in us.
Tomorrow I shall see the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, he dismissed the wandering mendicant.

He attained supreme joy from this news, and rising early the very next morning, he mounted his horse with a white parasol held aloft and a pair of white chowries being waved before him; surrounded by only a few princes, he set out to see Bhairavācārya, as the moon approaches the sun. Having traveled a short distance, he saw one of the teacher's disciples coming toward him.
And he asked, "Where does the Blessed One dwell?
He replied, "He dwells in the middle of a grove of *bilva* trees to the north of this dilapidated mother-house.
Having gone to that place, he dismounted from his horse.
And he entered the grove of bilva trees,
where, in the midst of a great multitude of pilgrims, he had already bathed at dawn and offered the eightfold flower-oblation.
Having performed his fire-rites,
he was seated upon a tiger skin spread over the ground smeared with green cow-dung, having arranged a circle of ash to ward off evil;
under the guise of his black woolen cloak, he seemed to be practicing the art of dwelling in the darkness of Pātāla out of fear of entering the subterranean abyss of the Asuras.
He was anointing the circle of his disciples with the golden-brown luster of his own eyes as they opened, which—purchased by the sale of his great flesh—seemed like an ointment of red arsenic;

with a topknot bound upward, from which a portion of matted hair hung down and a rudrākṣa bead and conch-shell fragment dangled, he seemed to bind the Siddhas who moved above him, arrogant in their pride of learning;
and by virtue of a few white hairs among his locks, he appeared to have passed fifty-five years of age.
His hairline was receding with the rows of hair on his temples thinning, the regions of his earlobes were hairy,
and the surface of his forehead was broad.
He seemed to produce the illusion of white streaks on his skull-bones, cracked by the heat of burnt guggulu resin held repeatedly above his head, due to the horizontal ash-mark upon his forehead;

he bore a single, continuous brow-line created by the meeting of his eyebrows—which, being naturally furrowed by the wrinkles of his forehead, caused the tufts of hair between them to contract—possessing a tawny luster.

With a pair of exceedingly long eyes—whose pupils were slightly clouded by a film of cataract, whose rays of light issued from the corners of his reddish eyes and spread outward like a rainbow with a white band across their centers—he seemed to be painting great circles of manifold colors all around; he appeared to be scattering in every direction the offerings to Śiva, variegated with rows of white, yellow, and red banners.
His nose-tip was curved like the beak of Garuḍa, and his cheeks were drawn inward by his widely parted lips.

He was whitening the expanse of the quarters with the light of his teeth, which emerged with a slight unevenness as if it were the radiance of the moon upon Śiva’s crest ever-present within his heart;
his lips hung down slightly, as if weighed down by the immense burden of all the *Śaiva-saṃhitās* resting upon the tip of his tongue;

and he seemed to be pursued by Śukra and Bṛhaspati—manifesting as two crystal earrings swinging from the lobes of his long ears—out of a desire for the mastery of the sciences possessed by gods and demons.

On one forearm, he wore a conch shell fragment—broken by the Blessed Lord Śiva like the tooth of Pūṣan—which was adorned with devotion and served as an ornament; it was encircled by a copper bracelet and bound with a series of threads upon which various medicinal herbs and mantras were tied.
With his right hand, he twirled a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, which resembled a water-clock (ghaṭīyantra) for drawing up the entire well of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
And with the mass of his beard, its tips slightly reddish-brown, swinging against his chest, he seemed to be sweeping away the internal dust of his own passions.
He bore a region of the chest covered with an extremely dense circle of dark hair, appearing as if consumed by the light attained through meditation;
his belly was being bound by a slightly loosened circle of folds, and the masses of flesh on his buttocks were growing full.
His loincloth was covered with white, sacred linen;

he was being circumambulated by his yogic bandage, which was white as the foam of nectar and encircled him in a firm cross-legged posture, appearing like the serpent Vāsuki manifested through the power of various unimpeded mantras;

and with the stainless networks of rays from the nails of his pair of feet—whose soles were as delicate as the petals of a red lotus—he seemed to be shattering the subterranean realm (rasātala) out of a desire to unearth a great treasure.

He was attended at his feet by a pair of washed sandals, pure and rinsed with water, which clung to his feet like a pair of swans that had come along from their familiarity with pilgrimages to the Ganges;

he shone with a bamboo staff topped with a crooked iron spike driven into its end, which stood constantly by his side like a goad for removing the Vināyakas who obstruct the attainment of all branches of knowledge;
and he was one who spoke but little.
Smiling gently,
beneficial to all,
and a celibate from his youth.
One who has practiced great austerity, possesses a lofty mind,
and has diminished anger.
It was free from meager affection,
adorned by its noble nature like a great city,
and possessed a delicate luster like Mount Meru with its mass of sprouts from the Kalpa-tree.
Like Mount Kailāsa, its summit purified by the dust from the feet of Paśupati;
like the realm of Śiva, followed by the hosts of Maheśvara’s attendants;
like the ocean, its body washed by thousands of rivers and streams.
Like the current of the Ganges, pure with many holy bathing places and shrines,
it was the abode of dharma and the source of truth.
A treasury of the wholesome,
a port of purity,
and a hall of ethical conduct.
It is the field of forbearance,
the paddy-field of modesty,
and the abode of steadfastness.
The support of fortitude,
the mine of compassion,
and the abode of wonder.
A garden of loveliness, a palace of serenity,
a home of dignity.
The assembly of goodness,
the source of sincerity,
and the very time of the Kali age.
He beheld Bhairavācārya as if he were Virūpākṣa, the Blessed One himself, in person.
But Bhairavācārya, seeing the king from afar, stirred like the ocean at the sight of the moon;

rising before his circle of disciples had even stood up, he went forward to meet him. Offering a *śrīphala* fruit as a gift, he uttered a blessing with a voice as deep as the roar of the Ganges' current surging from the ears of Jahnu.

The king also, with eyes whose whiteness was expanded by joy as if returning vast groves of white lotuses, and displaying—as it were—the favor of Maheśvara through the emergence of a third eye in the form of the crest-jewel emitting rays from his forehead-plate, performed a fresh salutation while bowing low from afar; his ears were bent down so that the bees fled toward the sprouts of his ear-lobes, as if he were being liberated from every last fragment of sin uprooted by his service to Śiva.
The Teacher also said, "Come, sit here," and displayed his own tiger-skin.

But the king, having displayed his courtesy, spoke these words, as sweet as the voice of a rutting swan—stuttering yet melodious—and like the flow of a great river rich with honey: "O Blessed One, you ought not to treat me with contempt for the transgressions of other kings.
This is surely a fault of character or a malady of wealth belonging to this ruined Fortune, neglected by all the world's monarchs, that my lord behaves toward me in such a manner."
This is not the proper ground for formalities;
enough with excessive constraint,
for this person remains a disciple of your heart's desire even though standing at a distance.

"Since he is worthy of honor like a preceptor, he ought not to violate the teacher’s seat; let your majesty sit here instead. Having spoken thus, Bhairavācārya sat down upon the garment brought by his attendants, while the king himself took his place there. Following the king's command, which was impossible to disregard out of affection, the teacher resumed that same tiger-skin as before.
When the king, his attendants, and his disciples were seated, he offered them the customary guest-offerings, beginning with the *arghya*, in due order.

His heart captivated by the king’s sweetness, he spoke while displaying his shimmering rays of light from his teeth—pure as a mass of moonbeams—as if manifesting the devotion to Śiva itself: "Dear sir, your very humility proclaims the greatness of your virtues."
You are a vessel for all prosperity, yet your acts of charity are proportionate to your wealth;
from birth until now, I have never cast my eye upon riches.
For this reason, there is a body that has not been sold for wealth—which is but fuel for the fire of the entire multitude of defects;
there are vital breaths preserved by alms;
and there exist some syllables of knowledge, however imperfectly grasped.

May you accept whatever small particle of merit has been accumulated and brought near through service at the feet of the Blessed Lord Śiva-bhaṭṭāraka; for the minds of the virtuous are like flowers that can be grasped by those of modest virtues, as they are fit to be used here.
Moreover,
virtuous people, esteemed by the wise, bring delight even when merely heard, like well-chosen words;
for they create an opening even in a most steadfast mind, as fame does.

"O auspicious one, as if being carried away by the streams of my curiosity— which is entering me like frothy white waves— I have been brought here by my multitude of virtues," the king replied to him, "Venerable sir,
even toward their own bodies and such, the virtuous are devoted only to their masters."

"By the very sight of you, an immeasurable mass of merit has been acquired, and by this very visit, I have been raised to a desirable state"— having spoken thus and stayed for a long time with various conversations, he went home.
On another day, Bhairavācārya also went to see the king.
And to him to whom the king had offered himself, along with his harem, his retinue, and his treasury, he replied with a smile: "Father, where is wealth?
Where is this [man]?"
Where are we, raised in the forest?
Our high-mindedness withers completely under the heat of wealth like a creeper;
for us, who are like fireflies, this brilliance shines forth without causing distress to others.
"Only those like you are worthy vessels for prosperity," he said, and after remaining there for some time, the wandering mendicant departed;
yet, in that same manner, he presented five silver lotuses as an offering on each occasion.
On one occasion, however, he entered carrying something wrapped in a white cloth.
Having sat down and remained as before for a moment, he said:
"O illustrious one, the Blessed One says to you: 'A Brahmin named Pātālasvāmin, who was my disciple, has been snatched from the hand of a Brahmarākṣasa by a great sword named Aṭṭahāsa.'"

he who regarded enmity as a gift, war as a favor, the arrival of battle as a great festival, an enemy as a treasure-revealer, an abundance of foes as prosperity, the challenge to combat as the granting of a boon, a sudden assault as the increase of fortune, and the falling of a weapon’s blow as a shower of wealth.

She was like a personification of tranquility among her friends,
like a reed-plant among her elders,
and like the very increase of graceful charms.
Like the purification of womanhood through expiation,
like the fulfillment of the command of the god of love,
like the realization of the purpose of beauty;
Like the increase of destiny for pleasure, like the fulfillment of desire for loveliness, like the perfection of fate for beauty;
Like the origin of a lineage for affection,
like the attainment of a boon for loveliness,
like the conclusion of creation for beauty.
Like the future of youth,
like a cloudless rain of wit,
like the wiping away of Fortune's disgrace;
She was like the nourishment of fame for conduct,
like the satisfaction of the heart for dharma,
and like the creation of the atoms of good fortune by Prajāpati.
Like the tranquility of tranquility itself,
like the discipline of discipline itself,
like the nobility of nobility itself.
Like self-restraint itself personified,
like fortitude itself, and like the very confusion of delusion, the chief queen named Yaśomatī was the ground of his life-breaths, affection, confidence, dharma, and happiness;
she dwelt upon his chest like the Goddess Lakṣmī upon the breast of the Conqueror of Naraka.
By his very nature, that king was a devotee of the Sun;

every day at sunrise, having bathed, wearing white silk garments, and with his head covered by a white cloth, he knelt upon the ground facing the east and offered worship in a circle smeared with saffron paste, using a cluster of red lotuses placed in a pure ruby vessel—lotuses as red as his own heart, which was likewise devoted to the Sun.

And for the sake of offspring, Sucarita muttered his prayers at dawn, at noon, and at the close of day; with a mind intent on his purpose, he was constantly engaged in muttering the *Ādityahṛdaya* mantra. For the minds of the deities are subject to the entreaties of their devotees;
thus, once during the summer season, that king happened to sleep upon the roof of a palace white as plaster brightened by the rays of the moon.
And by his side, on a second bed, lay Queen Yaśomatī;
as the night was nearly spent,
the lord of stars, whose beauty was being eclipsed by the approaching hour of dawn, was about to set, his radiance fading away.
When the dewdrops, cool as if they were the perspiration of the moon, were trickling down— producing joy in the night-lotuses touched by the tips of fingers—

and when the lamps within the inner apartments were flickering as if intoxicated, having been struck by the breaths of women sleeping under the influence of wine and having thus transferred their intoxication;

And as the King was being fanned by the beauty of his face with breaths that were fragrant as honey—breaths which, reflected in his spotless nails, seemed to have his feet massaged by the stars; and whose limbs, stretched out in confidence, seemed to be offered by the celestial nymphs of the quarters; and which were cooled by the breezes from the lotus-fans of his own hands; and who was graced by the reflection of the moon’s orb upon the surface of his stainless cheeks, appearing like a white flower-crest hanging down from the seizing of hair during amorous play—the Queen Yaśomatī suddenly cried out, "O Noble Lord!"
"Save me! Save me! she cried out, as if calling to her attendants with the tinkling of her ornaments; trembling in every limb, she rose up.
Then, as if scorched in both ears by that cry of "Save me!"—a sound never before heard on the entire earth, let alone from the mouth of the Queen—the King abandoned his sleep in an instant.

With his right hand trembling in rage, he drew his polished sword from its sheath as if it were the blue lotus from his ear; with that blade, he seemed to part the night itself, while his upper garment fluttered like the sky that serves as a partition between them. Adorned by a golden bracelet on his sprout-like left wrist—which slipped down due to the force of his brandishing the sword and wandered through the quarters like a heart searching for the cause of his fear—he caused the palace to tremble as he swiftly lowered his left foot and stepped forward.

He was resplendent with a necklace that had fallen before him and been severed by the edge of a sword—as if it were a fragment of the moon’s rays—and he was reddening the horizons with his two eyes, which were as crimson as if stained by the juice of betel from Lakṣmī’s kisses, or else by sleep and anger;
and with his triple-furrowed brow, bound in darkness, he seemed once again to be turning back the night. "O Queen," he said.
Saying, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid," he sprang up with speed;
and when, casting his eyes in all directions, he saw nothing at all, he then asked her the cause of her fear.
Then, while the female watchmen rushed off as if to the household deities,
and when the attendants sleeping nearby had awakened,
and the heart-trembling terror had subsided, she spoke: "Noble Lord,..."

I know that in a dream two radiant youths emerged from the orb of the divine Sun, filling the quarters of the sky as if with the glow of early morning light and making the world of living beings appear as if made of lightning; they were adorned with crowns, earrings, armlets, and armor, and held weapons; they were bathed in blood as red as cochineal insects; the entire world bowed down to them with uplifted faces and hands joined in reverent salutation at their heads; and they were followed by a single maiden who seemed like the moon’s own form descended through the *suṣumṇā* ray, as they descended to the surface of the earth.
"And while I was lamenting, those two began to pierce my belly with a weapon and enter it;

then I woke up, trembling at heart and crying out for my noble husband. And at that very moment, the morning conch resounded at the gateway, proclaiming, as it were, the fruit of her dream—the first utterance of royal fortune.
The kettledrums resounded loudly as if proclaiming a future prosperity;
and the voices of those reciting auspicious awakenings were heard crying out "Victory! Victory! at the dawn's first song, as if struck by the joy of the drumstick.

And the man, having slowly awakened from sleep in the stable of his beloved horses, recited from the *Vaktrāparavaktra* meter before the steeds—which were emitting sweet neighs—as he scattered drops of melting frost-water over the emerald-green barley: "A treasure by the transformation of a tree; a fine gem by its shimmering luster."
In this world, the arrival of good fortune is clearly indicated by omens.
Like the dawn preceding the sun, like the exceedingly swift wind heralding the arrival of rain.
The arising of past omens foretells for men whether it be auspicious or even inauspicious.

But the king, hearing this, with a heart full of joy, said to her: "Queen, you are despondent at a time for rejoicing! The blessings of your elders have flourished; our desires are fulfilled; you have been favored by the family deities; the blessed Lord Sun has become gracious to you, and before long he will gladden you with the birth of three most virtuous children."
Having descended, she performed the rites as they were being carried out;
Yaśomatī was also gratified by that speech of her husband.
Then, after some time had passed, Prince Rājyavardhana was first conceived in the womb of Queen Yaśomatī.
Even while he was still in the womb, his mother— appearing pale as if from his glory alone,

her body weary as if from the weight of his virtues— was unable to bear the burden of her limbs; she turned away from food, as if satiated by the nectar-like essence of the spreading radiance of his beauty.
Gradually becoming languid from the weight of her growing womb, she was led with great difficulty by her friends for the sake of worship, even though she was held back by them;
resting like a stone statue, she appeared as if she were embraced by bees clinging to her out of greed for lotuses against the nearby pillars and walls, and she was unable to lift her feet.
Lured by the desire for lotus stalks, she wandered very slowly as if being led along by the palace swans clinging to the rays of her toenails;
she even extended her lotus-hand toward the reflections falling upon the jeweled walls out of a longing to grasp them,
let alone toward her friends.
She even desired to grasp the rays of light from the ruby pillars,
much less command the house-creepers; as for performing domestic duties, what need is there to mention them?
Let alone her pair of feet, which were distressed by the weight of her anklets—she could not even mentally endure ascending the palace;
she was unable to support her very limbs, let alone her ornaments.
Even when merely thinking of climbing the pleasure-mountain, she became pale and her breasts grew heavy.
Even when rising to greet others, though she placed her bud-like hands upon the peaks of both her knees, she seemed to carry the day within her womb out of pride;

and with her lotus-face turned downward— having entered within her as if out of eagerness to see her offspring, reflected upon the surface of her breasts— she, thus delighted, bore a beauty redoubled by the child dwelling in her belly and her husband dwelling in her heart.
Having been addressed by her friends, she placed her body in their laps, her feet upon the laps of her female attendants, and her head upon the heads of her co-wives.
And when the tenth month had arrived, she gave birth to one fashioned as if from the atoms of Indra’s thunderbolt for the sake of winning the favor of all the mountains,
capable of bearing the weight of the three worlds, and equipped as if with the ornaments of the circle of hoods of the serpent Śeṣa.
When Prince Rājyavardhana— who caused all the mountains to tremble and seemed as if fashioned from the limbs of the world-elephants—

was born, the subjects became as if composed of dance, filled with joy; and for one month, which the king made feel like a single day, he held a great festival that was resonant with the sound of countless blown conchs, sharp with the beating of hundreds of drums, filling the world with the deep roar of kettledrums, and enchanting the mortal realm with people intoxicated with delight.

Then, after some time had passed, when the sky was filled with budding *kandali* flowers, when the *kadamba* trees were covered in buds, when clumps of young *tokma* grass had sprouted, when the lotuses were still closed, and when the minds of the *cātaka* birds were yet unawakened—that month known as Māsa, the abode of silent swans—the joy arose simultaneously in the heart of Queen Yaśomatī and in her womb, like the discus-bearing Viṣṇu in the womb of Devakī;
and gradually, as if embraced by the merits of all living beings, her slender body once again assumed a pale hue.
At the commencement of her pregnancy, she bore two jar-like breasts that turned dark at the tips of their lovely nipples as if sealed for the sake of protecting the universal emperor;
her gaze, long, lustrous, and white, directed toward his face, possessed a sweetness like a river of milk;
and her gait became slow, as if from the weight of a body presided over by the entire host of auspicious deities.

As she moved very slowly, her reflection appeared as if submerged in the spotless jeweled pavement; thus, by means of that reflection grasping her tender feet, she seemed to begin an act of prior service toward the Earth.

And as she lay upon her couch during the day, the image of a decorative leaf-design on the headboard—resting against the surface of her stainless cheeks—resembled Lakṣmī herself, awaiting the time of her delivery.

On nights when she had ascended to the top of the palace roof, the orb of the moon was seen reflected upon her breast—its garment loosened by the pangs of pregnancy—as if some unseen hand were holding a white parasol over the womb.

Even the yak-tail fans held by the attendants painted on the walls of the bedchamber began to wave as she slept; and in her dreams, she was consecrated with water from lotus-leaf cups held in their trunks by the four elephants of the quarters.
And as she was awakening, even the attendants carved as statues upon the moon-chamber pillars repeatedly uttered cries of "Victory!";
during her summons to her followers, incorporeal voices issued forth saying, "Command!";
and even in play, she could not tolerate the violation of her commands.

Moreover, she desired to bathe in the waters of the four great oceans combined into one; her heart longed to wander among the bowers of forest creepers on the shore and the sandy banks of the coastal woods; and even in matters of urgent business, her creeper-like brows moved with graceful deliberation.
Even though jeweled mirrors were present, he had a longing to behold his face in the polished surface of a drawn sword;
the sounds of bows, which are contrary to the nature of women, caused discomfort to his ears once the lutes had been set aside,
while his eye found delight in the lions within their cages.
Even during the prostrations to her gurus, her head seemed as if paralyzed and could only with great effort bow down.

Her friends, their eyes wide with joy as if anticipating the great festival of her imminent delivery, brightened the palace with the corners of their glances; they never for a moment left her side, incessantly performing, as it were, a protective rite of offering by showering the quarters with rain-like petals from blossoming white, red, and blue lotuses.
And the eminent physicians, seated in their accustomed places, bearing various medicinal herbs like mountains supporting the earth, provided her with steadfast support.
Exquisite jewels were fastened upon the knots of the necklaces, as if they were the very hearts of the oceans arrived there along with Lakṣmī.

Then, when the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūlīya had arrived, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, after the time of evening had passed and while the night was just beginning to ascend like a maiden, a sudden clamor arose within the inner apartments from the womenfolk. Rushing out in great agitation, Suyātrā—the daughter of Yaśomatī’s own nurse and as dear to her as her own heart—fell at the king’s feet and cried, "O King!"
"Congratulations on your increase of fortune through the birth of a second son! saying this, she took up the vessel of fullness (*pūrṇapātra*).

At that very moment, a court astrologer named Tāraka—a man highly esteemed by the king, who had correctly predicted hundreds of matters beyond the senses, displayed great power, was a master of all astronomical compendiums, honored among all calculators, well-disposed, and possessed of knowledge of the three periods of time—approached and announced:
"Your Majesty, please listen."

"It is said that Māndhātṛ was born on such a day, free from all afflictions such as the *vyatīpāta* yoga, when all the planets were situated in their highest positions and at such a *lagna*. Since then, in this intervening period, no other person has been born in the world with such a conjunction for the birth of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

This son of Your Majesty has been born, the foremost of the seven universal monarchs, a vessel for the great jewels that are the marks of a universal monarch, the protector of the seven oceans, the initiator of all seven sacrificial threads (*saptatantu*), and equal to the sun (the possessor of seven horses)."
In the meantime, even without being blown, conchs resounded with a piercing sweetness;
even without being struck, the consecration drum rumbled with a sound as deep as the roar of the agitated ocean;
and even without being beaten, auspicious musical instruments rang out.
The resonance of the trumpets spread through the quarters of the sky like a drum proclaiming safety for all the worlds;
the joyful horses neighed loudly with mouths praised by the eager grasping of mouthfuls of green dūrvā grass-blades, their manes and crests tossed about;
and the elephants, as if dancing with playful upraised trunk-tendrils, trumpeted melodiously, pleasing to the ear.
And before long, a divine breeze blew, fragrant with the scent of wine like the breath of Lakṣmī as she released her discus-weapon;
in the dwellings of the sacrificers, the sacrificial fires blazed without fuel, their auspicious arrival announced by clusters of flames turning to the right;
and from the surface of the earth, great treasures emerged, their jars beautiful with handles fashioned like bands of golden chains.
With the resonance of the struck auspicious musical instruments echoing through the quarters, even the guardians of the directions seemed to raise a clamor of "Glory! out of joy;
and at that very moment, twice-born men dressed in white, like the lords of the Kṛta age for the increase of progeny, approached with Brahmā at their head;
and the family priest stood before him like Dharma incarnate, holding in his hand water for peace and the sacrificial fruit.
The departed elders of the kin appeared like ancient traditions;

crowds of prisoners, released and fleeing in confusion with faces matted by long networks of beards and bodies darkened by the stains of thick filth, ran about like the kinsmen of the waning Kali Age;
and the market streets, plundered by the people, looked like the rows of camps of Unrighteousness who had just departed at that moment.
Surrounded by throngs of dancing, expectant, dwarfed, and deaf children, the elderly nurses, as if they were the very deities of motherhood incarnate, danced in their agitation over so many infants.

And there commenced a great festival for the birth of a son, in which the established order of the royal court vanished; the presence of chamberlains was disregarded, the staffs of the cane-bearers were set aside, and entry into the inner apartments became free from restriction. There, master and servant were equal, the young and the old were indistinguishable, the learned and the unlearned were alike, and it was difficult to discern between the intoxicated and the sober. The dalliance of conversation between noble maidens and courtesans was the same, and the entire population of the camp broke into dance.
Beginning from the following day, [the women] arrived from all directions, like kingdoms of women brought forth,
like the caverns of the Asuras opened up,
or like the inner apartments of Nārāyaṇa set in motion.
Families descended to earth like celestial nymphs;
attendants carried flower garlands strewn with bathing powders held in broad baskets;
and vessels filled with pieces of camphor as white as fragments of crystal slabs.

There were vessels made of jewels, imbued with the fragrance of saffron; ivory caskets white as sandalwood, bristling with rows of betel-nut slabs and entangled in fine nets of khadira-wood filaments moistened by mango oil;
and *pāṭala* trees, their *pārijāta*-like fragrance being drunk by swarms of humming bees.

Thousands of the harems of the surrounding feudatories were seen approaching the royal palace from all sides, dancing with their jeweled anklets jingling as they stamped their feet; they were followed by attendants carrying vessels of vermilion and vessels of fragrant powders, as well as small betel trees laden with hanging clusters of betel leaves and rolls of betel nut.

Gradually, the festival unfolded: in one place, the king’s affection was celebrated by the dance of elderly sons of noble families who were otherwise unaccustomed to dancing; in another, the king’s favorites were being dragged away by intoxicated, low-born maidservants while the monarch looked on with an internal smile; elsewhere, the lord of men laughed heartily at the dance of an aged noble vassal clinging to the neck of a drunken courtesan from the royal camp; in another spot, the elaborate secret amours of a minister were being hinted at through songs sung by wicked camel-herders acting upon the king’s secret signals; in yet another, public laughter was provoked by an old female ascetic being embraced by a drunken female scavenger; in some places, there was a battle of foul words initiated by parasites and servants vying with one another in intense rivalry; and in other areas, the eunuchs of the harem—unskilled in dancing—were being forced to dance by the king’s women against their will.
It was like a mountain with heaps of flowers,
like a pleasure-house with taverns for liquor,
and like the Nandana grove with the fragrances of the Pārijātaka tree.
It was like a frosty mist with the pollen of camphor,
like a boisterous laughter with the sounds of drums,
and like the churning of the nectar of immortality with its tumultuous clamor.
He was as if possessed of whirlpools by the circles of his *rāsaka* dances,
as if covered in horripilation by the rays of the jewels in his ornaments, and as if adorned with a ceremonial turban-band by the sandalwood marks upon his forehead.

Like echoes accompanied by responses, like festivities filled with the joy of celebrations accompanied by the granting of favors, young men—numbering many thousands—played about: some, like Kamboja horses, galloped along with filigree garlands of manes hanging from their shoulders; some, like deer, flew up with flickering pupils; and others, like the sons of Sagara, tore up the earth with merciless kicks of their feet as if with spades.
In some way, the earth endured the agitation caused by the feet of the dancing and singing bards;
as the princes of the realm played, the pearls on their ornaments burst from being struck against one another,
and by the dust of vermilion, the shell of the cosmic egg became as if crimsoned with the blood of the newly born Hiranyagarbha.
The vault of the sky shone as if it were a thousand sandy banks of the Mandākinī revealed by the thick clouds of fragrant powder;
the days gleamed as if colored by the filaments of Brahmā’s lotus shattered by the upheaval of the world, their sunlight turned tawny by the rising dust of scattered perfumes;
and the people stumbled over the heaps of pearls fallen from necklaces snapped apart in the crush.

They were followed by musical instruments—some being very gently struck at various points on their frames, some with sweet-sounding flutes emitting tinkling notes, some with cymbals producing a *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound, some with stringed drums being beaten, some with upright lutes made of bottle-gourds, some with the resonant blaring of bronze trumpets, and others with deep-toned *tānaka* drums all struck in unison;
and at every step, they kept time and rhythm as if with sympathetic hearts, following along to the *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds of their own ornaments.
Like cuckoos warbling soft, sweet, and intoxicating notes, they sang indecent verses of *rāsaka* dances that were nectar to the ears of the libertines;
they wore garlands of skulls and possessed sprouts of leaves upon their ears.
With sandalwood tilakas upon their foreheads, they seemed to embrace the sun with their creeper-like arms raised high and made resonant by rows of bracelets;
with their bodies radiant from the smearing of saffron, they leaped about like young maidens of Kashmir.
With their crests of large kuraṭaka flowers hanging from the curves of their hips, they were as if ablaze with the fire of passion;
with the seals of their faces smeared with streaks of vermilion, they were like rows of edict-plates for Kandarpa, whose commands are unimpeded;

with the dust of camphor and fragrant powders scattered by their fists, they were like the carriage-roads for the wandering of the desires of youth; and with young men struck by their unrestrained garlands of flowers, they were like female doorkeepers for the great festival of youth.
With their earrings swaying like leaves, they were like the shimmering creepers of the sandalwood tree of Love;
resonant with the cries of swans from their graceful footsteps, they were like the surging waves of the ocean of the erotic sentiment;
and devoid of discrimination between what should and should not be said, they were like the childhood play of good fortune.
With their slender bodies bristling with horripilation from the sound of the deep drums, they were like *ketakī* flowers shedding their pollen;
like lotus-ponds with faces blooming throughout the day,
yet like night-lotuses that never succumb to sleep even at night.
As if possessed, they were surrounded by throngs of lords of men;
like affections, they captivated the heart;
like songs, they kindled passion.
Like nourishments, they produced bliss; like intoxicants, they seemed to intoxicate even passion;
and like dyes, they seemed to color even desire.
As if making even bliss itself blissful,
as if causing even the dance to dance,
and as if making even the festival itself yearn for more;
In their sidelong glances, they seemed to drink him in with the shells of their outer corners;
in their gestures of threat, they seemed to bind him with the nooses of their fingernail-rays;
and in their displays of anger, they seemed to strike him with the movements of their creeper-like eyebrows.

In the four pleasure-grounds, the courtesans of the marketplace danced as if scattering their charms, while elsewhere they were granted space by the people who had been terrified by the whips of the staff-bearers.
Some were like forest deities wandering beneath the shade of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), surrounded by groves of white umbrellas being held aloft;
some, with their hands resting on the hanging ends of their upper garments draped over both shoulders, swayed as if mounted upon pleasure swings;

and others, with the ripples of their silk scarves being parted by the tips of their golden armlets, resembled flowing rivers whose currents are divided by pairs of *cakravāka* birds swimming across them.

Some royal consorts, who had commenced their dance, shone like lakes where swans are drawn toward groves of blue lotuses; for their wide, sidelong glances were caught by the three-pronged tips of the white chowries being waved over them. Others, with palace swans drenched by droplets of perspiration reddened by the alaktaka dye falling from their moving feet, resembled moonlit nights when the lunar orb is tinged with the glow of twilight. Still others, with their eyebrows knitted at the gestures of the chamberlains as they leaned forward due to the golden girdles placed around their necks, appeared like the snares of Kama with the nooses of their outstretched arms spread wide.
As the throngs of women danced everywhere, the earth, reddened by the flowing lac from their feet, seemed to glow as if composed of passion;
with their shimmering orbs of breasts, the great festival became as if made of auspicious jars;
and with the tossing of their vine-like arms, the world of living beings shone as if filled with bracelets of lotus stalks.
Time was made as if composed of lightning by their shimmering, playful smiles;
the days became as if made of black antelope skins by the rays of their flickering eyes;
and the sunlight turned greenish in hue, as if made of parrot feathers, by the radiant ear-ornaments of *śirīṣa* flower clusters.
With their braided hair and tamāla sprouts falling loose, the sky appeared as if made of collyrium;
with their upraised, bud-like hands, the creations seemed as if composed of lotuses;
and by the luster of the rubies and rainbows, the rays of the sun shone as if they were made of the feathers of blue jays.
With the echoes of the clashing ornaments, the quarters of the sky tinkled as if they were made of tiny bells;
even the aged women became like madwomen,
and even the most venerable men, like those possessed by demons, felt no shame.
Even the learned forgot themselves as if intoxicated;
even the minds of the sages quivered with the desire to dance,
and the king gave away his entire possession.
In every direction, heaps of wealth were plundered by the people like the treasuries of Kubera;
and while that great festival was thus proceeding, as time gradually passed once more,
the King had protection-seeds of mustard placed upon his head.
His body was tawny with yellow orpiment like a spark from the fire of his burgeoning majesty;
his neck was adorned with a row of formidable tiger-claws set in gold as if to manifest his innate kṣatriya splendor;
and with his first indistinct babbling, he seemed to be slowly producing the syllable *oṃ* of Truth, like the sprout of pride breaking forth from his heart.
She attracts the hearts of her kinsmen like swarms of bees drawn by flowers with their innocent smiles;
her lotus-face is adorned with teeth that appear like sprouts of playful laughter born from being sprinkled by droplets of water from her mother’s jar-like breasts;
and she is guarded by the assembly of women in the inner apartments as if by her own character.

While he was being protected by the circle of ministers as if by a *mantra*, being never forsaken by the community of noble youths as if by his own conduct, and being nurtured by his own lineage as if by his own fame;
While Harṣa was taking five or six steps, held by the fingers of his nurse’s hand like a young lion within a cage of weapons wielded by his guards,
and while Rājyavardhana was entering his sixth year, Queen Yaśomatī conceived Queen Rājyaśrī, just as the earth, in the form of Nārāyaṇa, conceives the goddess Śrī.
And when the days of her delivery were complete, she was like a lotus pond with its long red stalks for eyes;
like the autumn following the rainy season, possessing the sweet voice of a swan;
and like the beauty of spring, a forest grove whose limbs are as delicate as flowers.
Like the sky pouring down Vasudhārā, pure as great gold;
like the shore raining down a multitude of jewels;
like the crescent moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, bringing joy to the eyes of all people.
She gave birth to a daughter who was like Śacī beholding Jayantī, worthy of being seen by the thousand-eyed Indra, and like Menā giving birth to Gaurī, who is sought after by all the mountain kings.
By her, she shone exceedingly over her two sons like a single-stringed pearl necklace upon two breasts;

at that very moment, however, Queen Yaśomatī’s brother brought forth a son about eight years of age, whose crest of curly black hair was being fanned, whose head was followed by a line of smoke from the fire of the *huṃkāra* of the wielder of the *khaṇḍaparaśu* (Śiva), appearing like a second-born Makaradhvaja (Kāmadeva).

With one half of his body darkened by the rays of an emerald earring and the other half whitened by the light of a three-pronged pearl ornament, he seemed to display a combined incarnation of Hari and Hara.

He presented to the two princes an attendant named Bhaṇḍi, who—wearing a ring of flower-metal upon his thick forearms, appearing like Paraśurāma returned to childhood marked by the scars of his axe that had once exhausted the race of Kṣatriyas;

with curved coral sprouts strung upon his neck-thread, resembling Hiraṇyakaśipu whose chest-hardness had shattered the claws of Narasiṃha; and even in his youth possessing such firmness as to be like the seed of the tree of valor having taken another birth.
The king’s gaze toward his third son was equal to that which the Lord casts upon the two eyes;

likewise, the two princes, bestowing joy upon the hearts of all living beings, shone intensely when joined by him who was naturally well-disposed toward them, like the months of Madhu and Mādhava accompanied by the Malaya breeze.

Gradually, growing up together with their other brother Prajānanda, they entered their youth; with firm thighs like pillars, broad forearms, long arms like bolts, and expansive chests like door-panels, they became as pleasing as tall *sāla* trees and like two great cities capable of providing refuge for all the world. Then, like the moon and the sun, they pervaded the world with their flashing moonlight of glory and their heat of majesty, being both beautiful to behold and difficult to gaze upon;
like fire and wind, they were united as one, manifesting both brilliance and power.
With bodies as firm as stone and bound with armor, they were like the immovable mountains Himavat and Vindhya;
like two great bulls fit for the Kṛta Yuga;
and like Aruṇa and Garuḍa, whose bodies were divided between the mounts of Hari.
They possessed the gait of the lordly elephants like Indra and Upendra; they wore earrings and crowns like Karṇa and Arjuna;
and like the eastern and western quarters of the sky, they were capable of bringing about the rise and setting of all luminaries.

As if their lives were at its end through excessive pride, they stood in the narrowness of the *kukuṭīraka*—a place where the obstruction of the tide’s barrier was imminent—despising even their own shadow as it turned away from the light;
feeling ashamed even by the reflection of their own bodies clinging to their toenails;
and remaining in pain even at the breaking of their hair.
They were ashamed even by the second parasol reflected in their crest-jewels; their ears pained at hearing the title "Lord" applied even to the Blessed Six-faced One (Kārttikeya);
and their eyes were tormented by the reflection of their own person seen in the mirror.
Even when joining their palms in twilight salutations, their heads felt as if pierced by a stake;
even at the sight of a rainbow held by a rain-cloud, their hearts were tormented with longing;
and even before painted kings who did not bow, their feet were consumed with burning resentment.
They held in low esteem even the splendor of the sun, which is content with its limited orb;
they mocked even the ocean, whose majesty had been seized by the mountain [Maināka];
and they censured even the mighty wind, who remains without a body.
Though fanned by the yak-tail whisks of even the Himavat mountains, they were scorched;
though pained by the conchs of even the oceans,
they could not endure even another Varuṇa, the lord of the four seas.
They caused even those kings whose umbrellas had not been taken away to lose their luster; they were gracious even toward the virtuous,
and they poured forth honey from their mouths.

Causing even those situated at a distance to wither under the heat of the lineage of wicked kings, they bore palms daily stained by the soot of their study of the scriptures, as if blackened by extinguishing the fires of the majesty of all other monarchs;
and at times of practice, they seemed to converse with the regions of the quarters— regarded as brides nearby— through the deep sounds of their bows.
The names Rājyavardhana and Harṣa became manifest throughout the entire earth; in a very short time, they attained renown even in other continents.
Once, having summoned them, their father, who had retired to his inner apartments, spoke to them affectionately: "My two sons,..."
The first limb of sovereignty is that good servants are difficult to find;
generally, like atoms in a composite whole, they contribute to the substance of the king by acting in concert.
The base, by making him dance with the passion for sport, lead the foolish man to the state of a peacock.
Like reflections entering a mirror, they transfer their own nature [to others];
like dreams, they produce false perceptions through illusory appearances; like morbid humors, they cause transformation;
and like *cātaka* birds, those of low birth cannot be captured.
Fishermen catch the very intention quivering in the mind like a fish;
bards paint pictures in the sky like a scroll of Yama;
and excessive seekers implant a thorn in the heart.

"Since they have been tested in many ways through various trials and found to be free from all attachment to vice, pure, disciplined, valiant, and handsome—these two brothers, sons of the King of Mālava named Kumāragupta and Mādhavagupta, who are as inseparable from my body as my own two arms—I have appointed them to be your attendants.
You both must treat them no differently than you would any other member of our household. Having said this, he commanded the doorkeeper to summon the two of them.
Before long, Rājyavardhana and Harṣa, their eyes fixed upon the entrance, saw him entering with the chamberlain;
the elder brother was foremost, eighteen years of age, neither too tall nor too short, appearing to steady the earth—shaken by the constant passage of many kings—with his exceedingly heavy footsteps;
he shone with a pair of very slender lower legs that emerged from thighs thick and firm with flesh, hardened by the constant practice of leaping, as if produced from the prominent knots of the knees.

He was distinguished by a waist that revealed its slenderness through the contours of his flanks, appearing like Mount Mandara, which was worn thin by the friction of Vasuki as he was violently whirled around by the gods and demons;
with his exceedingly broad chest, he seemed to provide space for the boundless honors bestowed upon him by his master;
and with the quiet, graceful movements of his long, hanging arms, he appeared to be crossing the ocean of youth, which is otherwise so difficult to traverse.

His thick forearm was marked by the scar of the bowstring, which appeared like a sprout from the flames of his blazing majesty, veiled by the mass of rays from the rubies on his left wrist’s bracelet;
he bore the lustrous glow of the gem in his ear-ornament, hanging down to the slope of his high shoulder like the reddish-brown skin of a deer worn as a vow for the mastery of weapons;
and he possessed a face that, with its cheeks filled with the reflections of the filigree figures on his high-set armlets, resembled the moon with Rohiṇī dwelling within its heart.
With his eyes cast downward, their pupils steady and unflinching, he seemed to be instructing the clusters of lotuses—whose faces were upturned in their longing for Lakṣmī—in the virtue of modesty;
he bore upon his head an *amlātaka* flower as a crest-ornament, as if it were his own devotion to his master;
and he manifested a humility that appeared as if it had been bestowed by all the bows, terrified of having their bracelets broken, who surrendered it out of compassion.
Even in his childhood, he was resplendent with his senses subdued like conquered enemies;
he followed the path of noble birth, which is the ground of trust for those who love him;
and though possessed of fiery energy, he shone with a pleasing disposition, like the sun graced by the moon within it.
He saw Kumāragupta behind him, who, by the very firmness of his body, seemed to be emitting a fragrance even from those who were immovable;

he appeared to be selling to the hands of joy the people purchased merely by the sight of him through his good fortune; and following him was his younger brother, who, owing to his extreme height and fair complexion, resembled a moving mountain of red arsenic.
He was as if kissed on the head by his heavy fame, which, desiring to emerge, took the form of a crest of unobtrusive *mālatī* flowers;
he seemed to announce, through the meeting of his eyebrows, the first sign of the long-awaited union between modesty and youth— two qualities that are mutually opposed—
and he maintained a steady gaze, as if it were the very devotion to his master fixed within his heart due to his extreme composure.

They beheld Mādhavagupta, whose chest—cooled by the application of the purest sandalwood paste and adorned with a necklace as its pillow—bore the likeness of a vast bed of moonstone for the Goddess Śrī, who was weary from her wanderings among endless vassals; he appeared to display a tribute paid by the terrified remnants of those exhausted by the hunt: his eyes by deer, his bridge of the nose by boars, the seat of his shoulders by buffaloes, the joints of his forearms by tigers, his prowess by lions, and his gait by elephants.

Having entered, they paid homage from a distance, touching the earth with their four limbs and their heads; then, directed by the affectionate gaze of the king, they took their appropriate places and, after standing for a moment, the monarch commanded them: "From this day forward, you two must attend upon the princes."
"Whether you are moving or standing still, sleeping or waking, you must never leave the presence of these two for even a moment;

in this way, before long, all your desires will become like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*), bestowing upon you the excellence of an abundance of desired fruits. Having heard this, the two replied simultaneously with their heads swaying like the earth, "As the King commands. Rising up, Rājyavardhana and Harṣa paid obeisance to their father, and taking them both, they departed.

From that time forth, they remained for both princes like the opening and closing of their eyes, never departing from the range of their vision for even a moment; like inhalation and exhalation, they stood facing them day and night; and like their arms, they were constantly by their sides.

Then Rājyaśrī also, her familiarity increasing day by day with all the arts and with companions skilled in dance, song, and other pursuits, gradually grew up and, in but a few days, attained the bloom of youth.
The glances of all the kings fell upon her alone, like arrows upon a single target;
and by means of sending messengers and other such methods, the kings sought her hand.

Once, however, while the king was staying in the palace of the inner apartments, he heard an *āryā* verse being sung by a man stationed in the outer courtyard, which had come up in his turn: "At the time when the clouds rise, she casts one into the great whirlpool of agitation."
Like a river that increases its banks year after year, a daughter causes her father to swell with emotion.
Having heard this, he dismissed his attendants and said to the Great Queen standing by his side: "O Queen, our daughter Rājyaśrī has reached the bloom of youth;
like her own excellence of virtue, my anxiety does not depart from my heart for even a moment."
At the very onset of youth, fathers become fuel for the fire of grief regarding their daughters;
the swelling of her breasts darkens my heart as the rising of clouds darkens the day.

This lawful custom established by someone—that children born of one’s own body, cherished on one’s lap, and not to be abandoned, are taken away unexpectedly by strangers who arrive out of season—is not approved by me.
These indeed are the vulnerable points of saṃsāra;

this is that all-conquering power of the burning heat of the fire of grief, such that even though the state of being born is the same for both [sons and daughters], the virtuous suffer when a daughter is born—
for this reason, at the very time of birth, the righteous offer water to their daughters with their tears.
Out of fear of this, sages who have not taken wives and have abandoned living in households dwell in empty forests;
for what conscious person indeed could endure the separation from their children?
Just as messengers with excellent news arrive, so does my wretched anxiety enter my heart ever more deeply, as if feeling ashamed.
What can be done?
Nevertheless, those who have entered the householder's life must indeed conform to worldly customs;
for generally, even when other excellent qualities are present, the wise take primary regard for noble lineage alone.

"The Maukhari dynasty—worshipped by the entire world like the footprint of Maheśvara standing upon the heads of the upholders of the earth—is like that. Among them, the eldest son of Avantivarman, who was the very ornament of that line, named Grahavarman, has come to earth like the planet Jupiter; he, not inferior to his father in virtues, seeks her hand. If your ladyship’s mind also gives its consent, then I wish to bestow her upon him. When her husband had spoken thus, the Queen, her heart distressed with affection for her daughter and her eyes filled with tears, replied: "Noble Lord,"
Indeed, mothers are no different from nurses in their mere utility for rearing daughters;
however, in the matter of giving them away in marriage, the fathers alone are the authority. Furthermore, the affection for a daughter, born of compassion, far exceeds the affection for a son.
"The noble son alone knows how this state of distress may be brought to an end for us both as long as we live.
The king, having reached a firm decision regarding the giving away of his daughter, summoned his two sons and made them aware of the matter;

then, on an auspicious day, in the presence of the entire royal court, he poured the water of the gift of his daughter into the hand of that same principal messenger who had arrived previously, sent by Grahavarman to request her hand.

When he had departed with his purpose accomplished and filled with joy, and as the days of the wedding drew near, the entire populace was adorned with profuse offerings of betel, aromatic powders, and flowers; merchants of artisans from every land were arriving,
and a multitude of implements and materials was being brought in by the king’s men from all the villages.
There, the royal gatekeepers were bringing various gifts for the king;
the king’s favorites were preoccupied with entertaining the circles of kinsmen who had arrived by invitation;
and auspicious drums were resounding with sharp strikes from the tips of sticks wielded by leather-workers fierce with the intoxication of wine.

The mortars, pestles, and stone slabs were being adorned with flour-paste figures of the five fingers; the forecourts were filled by successions of wandering bards appearing from every direction; the image of Indrāṇī was being consecrated as the presiding deity;
and the master masons, honored with white flowers, unguents, and garments, were taking up the measuring lines for the wedding altar.
The city was being whitened by workmen mounted on ladders, who carried baskets of lime in their hands and jars of plaster upon their shoulders;
the tips of the palace gateways, ramparts, and walls were being colored by floods of water from heaps of safflower being crushed and washed, which reddened the hands and feet of the people;
and the courtyards were made to ripple with the waves of elephants and horses being inspected as dowry for the bridegroom.

The courtyard was made resonant by the rhythmic clanging of hammers as circles of goldsmiths began their work on molten gold, while plasterers busied themselves applying thick coatings of sand and lime to newly erected walls; meanwhile, the auspicious moment for the commencement of the construction was being determined by a group of astrologers intent on calculation.
Auspicious paintings were being drawn by a circle of clever artists;
a group of plasterers was fashioning clay models of fish, tortoises, sea-monsters, coconut trees, banana trees, and betel-nut trees;

and kings themselves, having girded their loins and being intent on achieving excellence in the work entrusted to them by their master, were smoothing floors with lime-plaster while erecting the pillars for the wedding dais—pillars whose tops were marked with sprouts of mango and Ashoka, reddened with lac-dye, and before which were placed jars filled with refreshing water. Thus, various activities were commenced.
