And from sunrise onwards, the place was filled on all sides by auspicious women—fortunate, beautiful, well-attired, and not widowed—their foreheads adorned with streaks of vermilion powder, singing auspicious songs pleasing to the ear that contained the names of the bride and groom's lineages; coloring neck-threads with fingers smeared with various pigments; skillfully painting decorative leaf-patterns; whitening water-jars and adorning rows of cool, white sandalwood floors; dyeing wedding bracelets and silk-thread bindings with cotton-petal buds whose petals were still joined; preparing body-unguents mixed with a paste of saffron thickened with milk and ghee, as well as face-pastes that heightened the excellence of their beauty; and fashioning garlands of cloves interspersed with *kakkola* and nutmeg, their interiors studded with shimmering, abundant fragments of crystal-like camphor—all these noble ladies of the surrounding vassals.

It was covered on all sides by garments shimmering like thousands of rainbows—clothes being woven by elderly city matrons skilled in the creation of various types of cloth; those already woven being dyed by washermen who were radiant with the honor bestowed upon them by the elderly women of the inner apartments, who were themselves adept in etiquette; some being dried in the shade while held and swayed by attendants clinging to the ends of the fabric; others, once dry, having their fringes fashioned into curved patterns; others being smeared with thick pastes of saffron; others having their fragile upper cloths bent and folded by female slaves with uplifted arms; and consisting of silks, woolens, fine linens, spider-silk fabrics, and silks resembling snake-sloughs, which were as soft as the core of a tender plantain tree, so light they could be carried away by a breath, and so delicate they could only be inferred by touch.

The royal palace became radiant, delightful, anxiety-inducing, and auspicious, with couches being draped in swans’ feathers from brilliant cases; with bodices being adorned with star-shaped pearls; with countless thousands of silk cloths being cut for various uses; with canopies shining with delicate *dukūla* silks of fresh dye; with pavilions whose entire floors were covered without gaps by heaps of fine fabrics; and with pillars being wrapped in strips of fine cloth.

Queen Yaśomatī, however, her heart agitated by the festival of the wedding, was as if divided into many parts though she was but one: with her heart toward her husband, with curiosity toward her son-in-law, with affection toward her daughter, with courtesy toward the invited women, with instructions toward the servants, with her body in constant movement, with her eyes inspecting what was done and left undone, and with her joy in the great celebration.

The king also, his delight in his son-in-law increased by the camels and mares presented one after another, and though he had attendants skilled in executing his commands who were intent on looking to his every wish, performed everything himself, overwhelmed as he was by affection for his daughter;
and thus, while that royal household became as if free from widowhood and the world of living beings seemed to be filled with auspiciousness, [the prince] was born.
As the quarters of the sky appeared as if composed of wandering minstrels,
the atmosphere was made as if of drums,
and the retinue moved about as if composed of ornaments.
When the world appeared as if composed of kinsmen,
when time was perceived as if consisting of bliss,
and when the great festival was unfolding as if composed of the goddess Lakṣmī;

While [the festival] was proceeding— like a treasure-trove of happiness, like the fruit of birth, like the fruition of merit, like the youth of prosperity, like the state of crown prince of joy, and like the moment of fulfillment for a desire—
it was, as it were, being counted by the fingers of the people and gazed upon by the banners along the road.
As if being welcomed by the echoes of auspicious musical instruments,
as if being summoned by astrologers,
and as if being drawn forward by his own desires;

The wedding day arrived at dawn as if being embraced by the hearts of the bride’s female companions; the royal palace was cleared of all common folk by the doorkeepers and made secluded. Then, the chief chamberlain, having entered the presence of the king, said: "O King,"
"A betel-bearer named Pārijātaka has arrived from the presence of my son-in-law," said the king,
and pointing out a young man of handsome appearance, he asked, "My boy, is Grahavarman well? showing great respect for his son-in-law even from a distance.

Hearing the sound of the king, he ran forward a few paces, extended his arms, and, being skilled in service, placed his head upon the ground for a long time; then rising, he announced, "O King, [the groom] is well; as you command, he honors Your Majesty with salutation. Recognizing him as one who had come to announce the arrival of the son-in-law, the king, having shown him hospitality, dispatched him back with this message: "Ensure that no fault arises from the passing of the marriage hour during the first watch of the night."
Then, when the day had come to a close, having transferred the splendor of the entire lotus forest to the face of the bride as it were,
while the sun was glowing like a sprout at the foot of the beauty of the wedding day,
and while the pairs of cakravāka birds were parting as if their love and shame had been lightened by the mutual affection of the bride and groom;
When the twilight glow was shimmering in the sky like the auspicious banner of Saubhāgya, its body delicate with crimson silk;
when the darkness, mottled like the neck of a pigeon, was clouding the faces of the quarters as if it were the dust raised by a bridal procession;
and when the host of stars was rising as if ready to perform the auspicious conjunction of the planets.

As the orb of the moon, the lord of stars, was being lifted by the mountain of sunrise like a marriage-auspicious jar, its white radiance increasing; as the darkness at nightfall was swallowed by the moonlight of the bride’s face; and as the beds of lilies, with their faces upturned, seemed to mock the moon for rising in vain, Grhavarma arrived. He came preceded by foot-soldiers running before him like longings personified, with uplifted red sprouts of passion and broad, quivering scarlet chowries repeatedly brandished; by throngs of horses filling the quarters of space, their neighing offering a welcome to the ears of the soldiers; and by herds of mighty elephants, adorned with moving ear-chowries and golden trappings, their bells ringing *ṭāṅkāra*, as if reconstituting the darkness dissolved by the moonrise with the help of female elephants whose faces were garlanded with constellations, just as the moon ascends the eastern quarter. A clamor was raised before him by dancers and bards accompanied by the cries of various birds, like the spring season with its young cuckoos. He turned the entire world yellowish-gold with the light of a circle of lamps scented with fragrant oil, as if with a mass of saffron-powder dust; his head, resting upon a flower-crown placed amidst a wreath of full-blown jasmine, seemed to laugh at the moonlit night with its halo. Adorned with a floral garland across his chest that surpassed the bow of the god of love—himself conquered by his own beauty—he was as charming as the Pārijāta tree with the sweet warbling of swarms of bees wandering in pride over his floral fragrance. With his heart drawn away as if by curiosity to behold the face of his new bride, as if falling forward with his mouth, Grhavarma drew near and stopped.
But the king, followed by his circle of royal counselors, went out on foot to meet him as he arrived at the palace gate along with his son.
Having descended from his vehicle and offered his salutations, the king—like Mādhava embracing Manmatha—embraced him firmly with outstretched arms;
then, having likewise embraced Rājyavardhana and Harṣa in due order, he took them by the hand and led them into the interior.
He attended upon him with services such as providing a seat that were indistinguishable from his own;
and before long, a learned Brahmin named Gambhīra, a dear friend of the king, said to Grahavarman:

"My son, having obtained you, the two lineages of Puṣpabhūti and Mukhara—possessing masses of virtues celebrated throughout the entire world that bring joy to the ears of the wise—have finally been united with royal fortune, like the solar and lunar dynasties."
"From the very beginning, you have stood in the heart of the Lord by virtue of your qualities like the Kaustubha gem;
but now, you have become one who must be borne upon the head by the Supreme Lord, like the moon.
Even as he was speaking thus, the astrologers approached the king and said, "O King,"
"The auspicious hour for the union has arrived; let the son-in-law enter the chamber of ceremony," they said.

Then, addressed by the king with the words, "Rise, go," Grahavarman entered the inner apartments and reached the door of the ceremonial hall, passing through the thousands of eyes of the women eager to behold their son-in-law—eyes that fell upon him like groves of blooming blue water-lilies.
Having dismissed his attendants, he entered.

Then, there she was, surrounded by a retinue consisting mostly of a few trusted dear friends, kinswomen, and women; her face veiled with a crimson silken cloth like the dawn twilight, making the lamps lose their luster by her own radiance; and embraced not too tightly by youth, as if that youth were apprehensive of her extreme delicacy.
She was as if mourning her departing childhood, through long, silent sighs released with difficulty from a heart constricted by trepidation;
trembling violently, she was held motionless by shame as if in fear of falling;
and with a mind quivering with terror, she gazed upon his hand—which rivaled the lotus—as Rohiṇī gazes upon the moon when its eclipse is imminent.
Her slender body was as white as sandalwood, appearing as if born from the heart of a night-blooming lily whose loveliness had been gathered by the gift of moonlight;
she wafted the fragrance of flowers as if emerged from the very heart of spring;
and she drew swarms of bees with the perfume of her breath as if produced from the Malaya breeze.
She was like Rati reborn after following Kāmadeva;

she was like another Śrī fashioned by the ocean out of wrath toward the gods and demons, created from all the qualities of jewels—splendor, loveliness, intoxication, fragrance, and sweetness—which originate from the Kaustubha gem, the moon, wine, the Pārijāta tree, and nectar;
and she wore ear-ornaments made of the luster of pearls, which, with their glossy appearance as young girls, resembled clusters of white Sindhuvara blossoms.

As he entered, Cupid seized that thief of her heart who had been offered by the bride; she was as if diverting the deer-like reflection of her eyes upon the surface of her cheeks, which were like a green meadow with the emerald luster of her ear-ornaments; with her face cast down, she repeatedly made efforts to lift it up, agitated by the sight of the bridegroom’s auspicious marriage-thread, while she rebuked both her friends and her own heart.
Whatever was performed by the women in the hall of curiosity— with faces smiling in jest— the son-in-law executed it all with exquisite grace;
then, taking the bride by the hand as she appeared in attire suited to her marriage, he went forth and proceeded to the palace,
which was white as fresh plaster and surrounded by invited kings who had arrived like the mountains surrounding the slopes of the Snowy Mountain (Himalaya) for the wedding of Tryambaka and Ambikā.

Its perimeter was illuminated by five water-pots made of young barley-sprouts, tender and bristling with fresh shoots, variegated with delicate colors, as well as by the faces of enemies and by female attendants holding auspicious fruits in their hands with palms joined in reverence; there, Brahmins were momentarily distracted from their observation as they watched the fire being kindled with fuel supplied by the preceptors, while unblemished green *kuśa* grass was laid down near the fire.
And he ascended that altar— which was strewn with heaps of stones, antelope skins,
clarified butter, sacrificial ladles, fuel, and bundles of grass, and which was radiant with parched grains mixed with dark śamī leaves placed in a new winnowing basket—
just as the moon, accompanied by its light, ascends the heavens.

And he crept toward the fire, which had waving, reddish shoots for its flames, like the flower-armed god of love approaching a red *aśoka* tree with Rati as his companion; and when the oblation was offered into the consumer of the burnt offering, he circumambulated it clockwise along with the flames that turned to the right, as if curious to behold the face of the bride;

and as the handful of parched grain was being scattered, the fire appeared with its body whitened by the rays from [the bride's] nails, smiling as if in wonder at the unprecedented beauty of the bride and groom.

In the meantime, the bride wept without any facial contortion, appearing like a mass of dark clouds formed by a multitude of large, clear pearl-like teardrops that extinguished the reflection of fire as it fell upon the surface of her own translucent cheeks.
A great cry of lamentation arose from the female relatives whose eyes were filled with tears.
Once the entire cycle of marriage rites was completed, the son-in-law bowed down before his parents-in-law along with his bride.
And he entered [the chamber], which had the deities Rati and Prīti painted upon its door-panels; which was filled with the humming of swarms of bees that had first entered as if out of affection;

which was illuminated by auspicious lamps that were flickering in the breeze from the wings of the bee-swarms, as if trembling for fear of being struck by the lotuses at their ears; and which was presided over by the God of Love (Kāmadeva), who stood beneath a painted red Aśoka tree in full bloom in one corner, holding his strung bow and straightening an arrow with his three-quarters of an eye squinted sideways.

The bedchamber shone with a couch that was well-spread, provided with pillows, and accompanied by a golden statuette holding an ivory fish-case on one side, and a golden fly-whisk resting against it on the other—resembling the goddess Lakṣmī herself with a full-blown white lotus in her hand;

and it was further resplendent with a silver sleep-vase placed at the head of the bed, which possessed the beauty of a night-lotus and appeared like the moon arrived to assist the flower-armed god of love.

And there, as the newlywed bride lay sleeping with her face turned away in modesty, he spent the night gazing at the reflections of her face in the jeweled walls and mirrors—reflections that seemed like the faces of the household deities who had come out of curiosity to overhear her first conversation, appearing through the jeweled lattice windows.

Having stayed in his father-in-law’s household, raining, as it were, nectar into his mother-in-law’s heart with his virtuous conduct, he remained for ten days—days filled with unprecedented joy through ever-new attentions that were never repetitive. Then, having caused a longing like that of a royal gatekeeper in the king's palace, and taking with him the hearts of all the people as if they were travel-provisions (śambala) presented as part of her dowry, he was finally dismissed by the king with great difficulty and went to his own country together with his bride.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Universal Monarch," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by Śrī Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
Fifth Chapter: Destiny first ordains happiness for men, followed by terrible suffering.
Having cast forth light like a flickering flash of lightning, she strikes down the thunderbolt.
It casts down many great beings simultaneously, with utter disregard.
As it revolves, time is but one, like an infinite mountain range.

Then once, having summoned Rājyavardhana, who was clad in armor, the King sent him to the North with a large escort to slay the Hūṇas, as a lion goes to hunt deer; he was accompanied by an immeasurable force and supported by ancient ministers and loyal great feudatories. And as he was departing, King Harṣa followed him for several stages on horseback.

And when his brother had entered the quarter resplendent with the luster of Kailāsa, the deer-eyed prince, being in the bloom of youth and impelled by the passion for valor, spent several days roaming abroad on hunts near the foothills of the snowy mountains— regions teeming with lions, śarabhas, tigers, and boars, where the beauty of his body was touched by the rays of the longing glances of forest deities—
and he made the forests devoid of wild beasts in a very few days, raining down brilliant crescent-headed arrows discharged from a bow drawn back to his ear.

Once, however, during the fourth watch of the night at the very break of dawn, he saw in a dream a lion being consumed by an irresistible forest fire that turned all the quarters of the sky tawny with its flickering mass of flames;
and in that very conflagration, he beheld a lioness who, having abandoned her cubs, was leaping up and throwing herself into the fire.
And the thought occurred to him: "In this world, the bonds of affection are indeed harder than iron."
When he realized that even animals act in such a manner when drawn [by fate],
his right eye throbbed again and again,
and a trembling suddenly spread through his limbs.
Without any apparent cause, his heart seemed to tremble within its very bonds, and a profound sense of unease arose for no reason at all.

His mind was agitated by various conjectures as he wondered, "What is this? Deprived of his fortitude, with a face bowed down by anxiety and eyes whose pupils were motionless, the partridge-eyed prince for a moment made the earth appear like a forest of land-lotuses blossoming, as he gazed with eyes fixed in stillness.
And on that day, with a vacant mind, he amused himself with hunting as the sun ascended;

then, at midday, returning to his palace, he remained full of apprehension while two slender palm-leaf fans were being moved very gently on either side of him, as he lay upon a cane mat spread upon the ground, its surface anointed with drops of exceedingly cool sandalwood paste and supported by moon-white pillows. Then, from afar, he beheld a person whose shaven head was adorned with a cloth turban of a dark hue like the dye of indigo, and who carried a letter-case.
With the darkness of his body being imposed upon it by fatigue and the heat of the sun, he was as if being reduced to charcoal by the fire of grief within;
he was followed, as it were, by the Earth herself, who, curious to hear news of the king, pursued him under the guise of a column of dust raised by his exceedingly rapid strides;
fanned on both sides by the edges of his wide upper garment fluttering in the headwind, he seemed to have grown wings through his great haste and was flying swiftly toward his destination.
He seemed to be driven from behind by his master’s command,
dragged forward by his long-drawn sighs of exertion,
and as if being snatched away from his eagerness for the task by the sun, whose reflection formed upon the surface of his perspiring forehead.
His body was rendered vacant by his senses, as if they had been cast away in a sudden flurry;
he stumbled even on level ground due to the emptiness of his heart, as if out of respect for the gravity of the matter inscribed upon his brow;
he was like a fragment of a dark cloud from which the thunderbolt of an evil report was about to fall.
He saw approaching a deer named Kuraṅgaka, who was like a wisp of smoke from the fire of grief about to blaze forth, and like the seed of a crop of evil deeds about to bear fruit; seeing him,
his heart broke, its fear having been aroused by a succession of preceding omens.
Kuraṅgaka, having offered his salutation, approached and first presented the dejection reflected upon his face,
and afterwards the letter; and King Harṣa himself took it and read it.
Taking the very meaning of the letter to heart, he was overcome with grief and, appearing as if struck by a stroke, said, "Kuraṅgaka,
what is the illness of my father?
Simultaneously, with eyes shedding drops of tears and a mouth from which faltering syllables issued forth, he replied, "My Lord, there is a great fever of burning."
Upon hearing that, his heart suddenly split as if into a thousand pieces;

and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), desiring long life for his father, he bestowed his entire personal wealth—consisting of immeasurable heaps of gems, gold, and silver—upon the Brahmins.
Then, addressing a young man standing before him who was bearing a sword at his head, he said, "Have the horses saddled."

With a trembling heart, he mounted a horse brought by a groom who had rushed forward in agitation and set out all alone. However, as he departed, a troop of horses began to gallop toward him from every direction, stirred by the sound of conchs signaling an untimely march; they arrived one after another in a state of alarm, filling the hollows of the entire world with the loud, rising din of their hooves.
Furthermore, as he set forth, deer passed on his left, manifesting the imminent destruction of that lion among kings.
Facing the orb of the hot-rayed sun, as if tearing his own heart apart, a crow cawed harshly upon the dry wood of a forest fire;

then a naked mendicant, whose body was soiled by a thick layer of grime accumulated over many days—appearing like a mass of soot—and who bore the mark of a peacock feather on his head, approached him.

His departure being greeted by ill omens, he felt profound apprehension; yet, with a heart softened by paternal affection, he disregarded them one by one. Keeping his eyes fixed unwaveringly upon the neck of his horse, with laughter and conversation silenced, he was followed by the silent retinue of the king’s court, and traversed in a single day a road that would otherwise have required many yojanas.

As the divine sun, its brilliance vanished, turned its face downward as if despondent at the news of the king’s illness it had perceived, the prince—though repeatedly entreated by his circle of affectionate kinsmen headed by Bhaṇḍi—refused all food.
With the path made clear by a succession of villagers being led along by the porters stationed ahead, he was carried away while still moving until night fell;
and on the following day, at midday, he heard no shouts of victory.
The sound of musical instruments had ceased, singing had been brought to an end,
and the festival had been dispersed.
There was no movement of wandering bards, nor were the wares in the market stalls spread out;

in various places, the sky was being scraped as it were by the tips of the horns of Yama’s buffalo, in the form of rising streaks of smoke from the *koṭihoma* sacrifice, curling with the force of the wind.
It was as if being ensnared by the nooses and nets of the God of Death;
its approaching misfortune was being signaled by flocks of crows circling overhead all day long, shrieking harshly like the iron bells adorning the buffalo of Time;
and in some places, the serpent Ahibudhnya was being propitiated by grieving relatives who lay down beside it.
In one place, the circle of Mothers was being propitiated by noble youths burning lamps;

in another, the Amardaka shrine was being beseeched by Dravidians intent on bringing offerings of human heads; and in yet another, Caṇḍikā was being entreated by Andhras who were carrying away the ramparts of their arms.
In one place, Mahākāla was being entreated by dejected new servants who were melting guggulu resin held over his head;
in another, a circle of trusted followers was intent on a fire-oblation of their own flesh, which they had cut off with sharp knives;
and in yet another, the process of selling human flesh was being carried out by the princes of the king.
As if defiled by the ashes of a cremation ground, as if seized by inauspicious omens,
as if devastated by *yātudhāna* demons,
and as if swallowed by the age of strife (*kalikāla*).
It was as if covered by layers of evil,
plundered by the distractions of unrighteousness,
and assailed by the reproaches of impermanence.

He reached the royal camp, which seemed as if it had been made its own by the playful whims of Destiny—appearing empty, as if asleep, as if robbed, as if embarrassed, as if deceived, and as if swooning.

Even as he entered, on the path of the marketplace, he beheld a picture-board of Yama; it was surrounded by a dense throng of children agitated by curiosity, and upon it was depicted the transition to the other world by a painter, who, holding a reed in one hand, displayed the scene with a terrifying buffalo-riding Lord of the Dead (Yama) supported by an upright staff and crossbar held in his left hand.
And he heard a verse being sung by that very person: "Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives..."
In age after age, who have passed away; to whom do you belong, or who are you?
Thus, with his heart being torn even more deeply by this, he proceeded in due course toward the palace gate, which was now forbidden to the entry of all people.

Having dismounted from his horse, he beheld a young physician named Suṣeṇa emerging from within; the physician’s facial expression was devoid of cheer, as if his very senses had been released from him. The prince offered his salutation and asked, "Suṣeṇa,"
"Is there any special favor for my father, or not?"— thus he asked,
being saluted very gently by the doorkeepers, while all his possessions were being presented to him and his family deity was being worshipped.
The rite of cooking the sacrificial pap of nectar had been commenced; the sixfold oblation was being performed;
and the trembling blades of dūrvā grass were being smeared with drops of speckled clarified butter as they were offered into the fire.

The Great Peacock Spell (*Mahāmāyūrī*) was being recited, domestic rites for pacification were being performed, and offerings for the protection against spirits were being prepared; diligent Brahmins were engaged in the chanting of the *Saṃhitā*, and the temple of Śiva resounded with the sound of the eleven-fold Rudra-mantra being muttered.
There was the ritual bathing of Virūpākṣa with a thousand jars of milk performed by exceedingly pure Śaiva ascetics;

and there were the kings, seated in the courtyard, their minds tormented by the failure to obtain a sight of their lord, receiving news from the attendants emerging from within, who had abandoned bathing, eating, and sleeping, whose bodies were left in a state of neglect and soiled dress, motionless as if painted, passing day and night with faces dejected by sorrow; and in the courtyards, a circle of people bound together, whispering to one another, while someone there was exposing the faults of the physicians.
One was reciting the symptoms of incurable diseases, another was reporting bad dreams,
and another was describing reports of malevolent spirits.
One was proclaiming the predictions of astrologers;

another was singing auspicious signs; another was contemplating impermanence and disparaging cyclic existence; another was censuring the manifestations of the Kali age and reproaching fate; yet another was angry with Dharma and reviling the tutelary deities of the royal family.

Accompanied by another external attendant who censured the ill fortune of his wretched state as a son of noble birth, he entered the royal palace where the king’s condition was being described as miserable. While being watched by his father’s attendants whose eyes were flooded with incessant tears of water, he reached the third courtyard, smelling the fragrance of various medicinal substances and liquids, and of boiling decoctions, clarified butters, and oils being cooked.
And there, in that place which was exceedingly silent, where many cane-bearers held the door-frames, where the paths of the side-alleys were concealed by triple-layered curtains,
and where the side-doors were closed;
The sound of door-bolts had ceased, the wind was kept out by the closed windows,
and the attendants were filled with distress.
The doorkeeper was provoked by the sound of footsteps striking the stairs; all activities were being directed by silent gestures;
and the armor-bearer sat not too close by.
In the corner stood a woman carrying water for rinsing the mouth, startled by the summons;
in the moon-chamber, the circle of silent women had gathered on the roof-terrace; and the group of female relatives, distressed by great grief, held their necks out from behind a curtain.
In that place, where the attendants were distressed by the heaped-up funeral pyre,
where a few intimate friends had entered,
and where the physicians were terrified by the onset of a deep-seated fever;
while the minister was becoming despondent, the family priest was faltering, and the friends were sinking in spirit;
When the learned were dispirited, when the neighboring vassals were deeply distressed,
and when the fly-whisk bearers lost their composure;

In him, whose head and eyes were withered by suffering; whose wealth of grace, his riches, and his desires were wasting away; and whose beloved sovereign was rendered powerless as his strength failed due to the lack of food he had renounced out of devotion to his master.

While the young princes, having remained awake throughout the entire night, had fallen upon the surface of the earth; while the assembly of noble sons, descended through generations of lineage, were carrying away the pure [bodies], and the chamberlains were shrinking with grief;
and while the panegyrists were offering their praises without any joy.
While his servant sat sighing in despair,
while the women of the harem had their lips grey with the remains of chewed betel, and while the chief steward was intent on procuring the medicinal diet prescribed by the embarrassed physician;
The pain of dryness in his mouth was relieved by streams of water from goblets being drunk by his dependents;
many gluttons were fed according to the king’s desire;
and all the merchants were busily engaged in procuring a full assortment of medicinal ingredients.
In which [palace], the servants in charge of water-rites were inferred to be suffering from terrible thirst by their being summoned again and again;
in which the water for rinsing the mouth was being cooled by being placed in jars surrounded with ice; and in which the cooling rods were made chilly by camphor powder applied to white, moist cloths.
In a place where the liquid was being taken up in mouthfuls from new vessels smeared with drying mud;
where soft lotus stalks were covered by the tender leaves of a wilting lotus pond;
and where the ground for drinking water-vessels was occupied by clusters of blue lotuses still attached to their stems.
In which the boiling water was being cooled by the falling of streams,
which emitted the sharp fragrance of pale-red sugar,
and in which the inner eyes of the jars resting on sand upon the couches were at rest;
In that place, where Golayantra vessels with necks encircled by fresh water-moss were present;
where coarse sugar was held in water-jars whose impurities had been drunk up by parched grain flour and parched rice flour shimmering within bowls of Galvarka stone;
and where there was a collection of crystal, oyster shells, and conch shells strewn with the powdered juice of cooling medicinal herbs.

He stood in a white mansion where there were abundant, gathered fruits such as *āmala* and *mātuluṅga*, grapes, pomegranates, and others; where drops of propitiatory water (*śāntyudaka*) were being scattered by Brahmins who had been made to receive them; and where a stone slab for applying forehead-pastes was being pounded by female servants.

As if being consecrated with the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) by the feverish flame for victory over the next world; tossing restlessly upon his wavy bed as if Śeṣa struggling in the Ocean of Milk under the heat of the poison;
white with the dust of pearl-sand like the ocean drying up at the end of an aeon;
and being lifted up by Time as Kailāsa was once raised by the Ten-faced Rāvaṇa.

He was being touched by the white hands of attendants— who were intent on incessantly anointing him with sandalwood paste— hands that seemed to have been reduced to ash by the touch of his exceedingly hot limbs; he appeared as one already departed for another world,
being bid farewell by his own enduring fame under the guise of sandalwood ointment,
and bearing a body variegated by the continuous falling of lotus, water-lily, and blue-lily petals, as if mottled by the glances of the Goddess of Death.
He bore a head whose hair was being painfully compressed by a thick silk cloth, causing a continuous succession of agonizing pain;

and with his forehead—terrible with its network of blue veins rising from unbearable agony, as if marked by the lines drawn by the fingers of Death—he inspired fear, as if counting the days until the limit of his death;
and he fixed his gaze with pupils slightly withdrawn inward, as if in agitation at the imminent sight of Yama.

He was exhaling a succession of hot sighs that resembled a shimmering mirage, rippling with the grey luster emitted by his rows of parched teeth; through this darkened tongue, as if scorched by his excessively hot breath, he manifested the onset of a dreadful derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*);
and by placing upon his chest necklaces of gems and pearls, sandalwood paste, and moonstones, he made himself appear as if ready for the sight of the messengers of Death (*kṛtānta*).
With his pair of arms raised as he shifted his limbs and shook his body,
he seemed to be constructing a shower-house for the sake of cooling his fever with the rays from his outstretched fingers;
even by means of his reflections falling upon the surfaces of the nearby jeweled pavements and mirrors, he appeared to be proclaiming the intensity of his torment.
He esteemed even fainting as a place of rest, like a loving mistress;
he was possessed by ill omens—the very syllables of Death’s summons—as perceived with trepidation by the physicians;
and at the time of his great departure, he was transferring the succession of his own torments into the hearts of his kinsmen.
Seized by discontent as if by the shadow of envy,
it was like the onset of calamities,
like the discharge of every weapon by emaciation.
It was made into an elephant by its own helplessness, made into an object by its unevenness,
and made into a field by its destruction.
Made the object of his gaze by sickness,
marked as the goal by his southern course,
and as if drunk up by agonies;
As if devoured by wakefulness,
as if swallowed by pallor, as if made into a morsel by the breaking of his limbs;
As if being carried away by calamities,
as if being divided by agonies,
as if being plundered by sufferings.
Desired by destiny,
determined by necessity,
and smelled by impermanence.
Overpowered by non-existence,
rendered lifeless by conceptual construction,
and given free rein to the afflictions.
It is the dwelling place of despondency,
in the vicinity of death,
and close to the final exhalation.
It dwells in the mouth of the Great Departure,
at the threshold of Long Sleep,
and upon the tongue-flame of the Lord of Life.
Speech was sparse,
the mind was wavering, and the body was agitated.
Life is exhausted,
idle chatter is abundant, and labored breathing is constant.
It is conquered by yawns,
dependent on mental afflictions,
and bound by recurring conditions.

He beheld his father being touched on the head and chest by Queen Yaśomatī, who sat at his side with eyes swollen from incessant weeping; though she held a fly-whisk, she fanned him only with her sighs; her body was greyed by the dust of various medicinal herbs, and she repeatedly cried out, "Noble Lord, are you sleeping?
Upon seeing this, his mind was churned by the sudden onset of grief, and he became as if apprehensive toward his fortunes, perceiving his father as one already dwelling in the city of Death.
For a moment he was as if rejected by his inner sense and cast off by his fortitude,
made a field for agitation.
Emptied by passion,
made the object of despair,
he carried his heart like a blazing fire.
Bearing senses that were as if deluded by poison tainted with venom,
surpassing even the netherworld (rasātala) in its darkness and excelling even the sky in its emptiness, he found nothing left to be done.

And the king, having seen his most beloved son from afar, though in such a state, was overcome by intense affection; rushing forward in spirit, stretching out his arms and calling out, "Come! Come!", he rose from his bed with half his body and hurriedly approached him.
Lifting up the prince who was bowed low in humility, he forcibly drew him to his chest and, as if entering the very center of the lunar orb out of love, embraced him.
As if bathing in a great lake filled with nectar,
as if being bathed in a vast cascade of yellow sandalwood juice,
and as if being consecrated by the melting waters of the snowy mountain;

Pressing limb against limb, rubbing cheek against cheek, and closing his eyes which were dripping with incessant tears clinging to the tips of his lashes, he embraced him for a long time as if forgetting the feverish torment. Having at last released him with great difficulty, the prince watched him as he withdrew, offered salutations, bowed to his mother, and sat down near the bed; he gazed at him as if drinking him in with an unblinking, motionless eye.
And again and again he touched [him] with his trembling palm; and with a throat wasted by exhaustion, as if with great difficulty, he said, "Child, you are emaciated.
Bhaṇḍi, however, replied, "Your Majesty," and so on.
"Today is the third day since he has taken food," she said;
hearing this, his voice choked with a surge of tears, he sighed deeply and spoke with great effort: "Child, I know you to be dear to your father and possessed of an exceedingly tender heart."

In such matters, the exceedingly difficult-to-restrain affection for kinsmen agitates the mind even of the wise, for it is all-destroying; therefore, you ought not to give yourself over to excessive grief.
Though I am indeed burning with the fever of an intense internal heat, I am burned even more by this affliction of yours, O long-lived one;
your emaciation cuts me like a sharpened weapon.
My happiness, my kingdom, my lineage, my life, and my afterlife all depend upon you;
as they are for me, so they are for all subjects.
The afflictions of those like you cause suffering to the entire surface of the world.
For those like you do not grace the lineage of those who possess little merit;
these marks of yours declare that sovereignty over even the four oceans is as if held in the palm of your hand— the fruit of stainless karma accumulated over many previous births.
By your very birth, I have achieved my life's purpose; I am now free from all desire for continued existence. It is only out of deference to the physician that he makes me drink this medicine.

Moreover, for those like you who are destined to take birth through the merits of all living beings for the sake of protecting the entire surface of the earth, parents are merely the means for assuming a body;
kings, however, possess true kinship through their subjects,
not through blood relations.
"Therefore, arise and perform all your duties once more;

when you have finished eating, I too shall myself take the prescribed medicine. As he was addressed in this manner, the fire of grief, as if wishing to burn his very heart, blazed up even more intensely within him.

Having stood for only a moment, and being again directed by his father to take food, he descended from the white palace and reflected in his mind: "Truly, this great dissolution has arrived unexpectedly, like a thunderbolt falling from a cloudless sky; even ordinary grief is a death with breath still remaining."
A great disease for which no medicine has been prescribed;
entering the fire without being reduced to ashes;
dwelling in hell even while one has not yet ceased [from worldly existence].
A rain of embers without light,
a sawing that does not cause fragmentation,
and the falling of a diamond needle without causing a wound.
"How much more so when relying on specific details;
what can I do in this matter? Thus addressed by the royal officer, he went to his own abode, which seemed as if made of smoke due to the falling of tears.
They were like fire, producing a burning in the heart; like poison, inducing a surge of fainting;
and like great sins, engendering loathing.
He took several mouthfuls that were like alkaline water and caused excruciating pain; then, rinsing his mouth, he commanded the fly-whisk bearer, "Go and find out how my father is."

Having gone and returned, he reported, "Your Majesty, it is exactly so. With his mind distressed because he had not yet received the betel and with his heart longing for her, while the sun was still high, he summoned all the physicians in private and, with a dejected heart, asked, "What should be done now in such a situation? They, however, replied, "Your Majesty, maintain your fortitude."
"In just a few days, you shall hear again that your father has returned to his natural state.

Among those physicians, however, was a young man about eighteen years of age named Rasāyana—a physician who had attained mastery over the eight branches of Ayurveda through hereditary lineage in that very royal household, who was cherished by the king no differently than his own son, and who, by virtue of his naturally acute intellect, understood the true nature of diseases as they are; this youth stood silent with tears, head bowed, when he was addressed by the prince: "Friend Rasāyana,"
"Tell me the truth, if you see it as something improper," he said;
and he replied, "Your Majesty,
tomorrow at dawn I shall report the matter exactly as it stands."

And in this very interval, the keeper of the palace lotus-pond, consoling a ruddy goose (*kokila*), recited aloud an *aparavaktra* verse: "O bird, make your mind firm; abandon grief yourself and abide on the path of discernment."
The sun now takes refuge upon the summit of Mount Sumeru together with the splendor of the lotus-lake.
Having heard that,
he who understood the significance of words further slackened his hope for his father's life;
and when the physicians had departed, his fortitude shattered, he ascended once more toward the presence of the king at the onset of night.
And there [she cried]: "There is a great burning; bring necklaces, O deer-eyed one! Give me jeweled mirrors upon my body, O Vaidehī!"
"O Līlāvatī, smear your forehead with Himalayan clay;
O Dhavalākṣī, apply the powder of camphor;
O Kāntimatī, place a moonstone upon your eye."
Place a blue lotus upon your cheek, O Kalāvati; apply sandalwood paste, O Cārumati;
fan away the breeze from your garment, O Pāṭalika!
"O Indumati, allay the burning heat;
O Madirāvati, produce joy with lotuses moistened by water; O Mālati, bring forth lotus stalks."
O Āvantikā, fan the palm-leaf whisk;
O Bandhumatī, bind the head that is running away;
O Dhāraṇikā, support the neck!
Place your hand with its spray of water upon my chest, O Kuraṅgavatī; massage my arms, O Balāhikā;
and press my feet, O Padmāvatī.
"Take me firmly, Anaṅgasenā!

O Vilāsavatī, what time is it? Sleep does not come! O Kumudvatī, tell me stories!"—hearing such words from his father incessantly, with a grieving heart, he passed the night awake, made long by sorrow.

At dawn, having descended and approached the gateway of the palace, although a groom presented him with a horse, he returned to his own quarters on foot. There, hurrying for the sake of his brother's arrival, he dispatched swift-coursing, long-distance camel-herders one after another;
and having washed his face, he did not accept the personal adornments brought by his attendants.
He heard the indistinct murmuring, "Rasāyana! Rasāyana! uttered by the princes standing before him in dejection;
and he questioned them, "Sirs, tell me, what is this Rasāyana?
When thus asked, they all remained silent at once, but being pressed again and again, they finally spoke with great difficulty: "O King..."

Having heard that he had entered the fire, he became as if scorched within by heat and instantly turned pale; and this thought arose in his mind: "Granted that he does not do it himself, yet like any other noble person, he would not cause such unpleasant and distressing news to be heard."

And he thought again: "Just as this [asceticism] was practiced by him, it has been made even more radiant by his entry into the fire; like a son of good family, he is like refined gold. Or rather, this is entirely appropriate for his affection—how could his father not be his father?"
Or rather, is Ambā not my mother, and are we not her brothers?

Even when another master becomes difficult to find, life itself, while it is still sustained, is a cause for shame in the world; how much more so in the case of our father—whose name is auspiciously invoked, who is composed of nectar, our sincere kinsman, and whose favor toward his dependents is never in vain?
What is this present act he has performed while burning himself? For what of his—standing firm for an eon, consisting of glory—is being burnt?
He has merely fallen into the fire; we alone are the ones consumed by it.
"Blessed indeed is that leader among the meritorious;
yet this royal house is devoid of merit, since it is separated from such a noble son.
Moreover, what burden of duty or what remainder of work could there possibly be for me with these lives?"
"What is this preoccupation that my cruel life-breaths have not yet departed, or what obstacle is there for my heart that it does not shatter into a thousand pieces?"
Afflicted by grief, he did not go to the royal palace; he abandoned all his duties and,
having fallen upon his bed, remained there with his head covered by his upper garment.
While the king was in such a state of joy and the god [Viṣṇu] remained as he was, the hands of all the people seemed nailed to their cheeks,
streams of tears appeared as if molded from plaster upon their eyes,
and their gazes were as if knotted at the tips of their noses.
The sounds of weeping were as if engraved upon their ears; cries of "Alas, what misery! were as if innate to their tongues;
and sighs were as if sprouted from their mouths.
The words of lamentation became as if inscribed upon their lower lips,
and the sorrows became as if stored within their hearts;
sleep, fearing the burning heat of hot tears, did not enter the hollows of their eyes.
Her smiles vanished as if shaken by the wind of her sighs;
her speech did not flow, as if utterly consumed by the fire of her torment,
and even in conversation, no jests were heard.
It was no longer known where the musical assemblies had gone;
the dance performances were not remembered, as if they belonged to another lifetime;
and even in dreams, the ornaments were no longer grasped.
Even talk of enjoyments could not be found,
nor was even the name of food mentioned; the circles of drinking fountains were like flowers in the sky.
The words of the bards seemed to be brought from another world; joys seemed to belong to another age;
and the god of love was once again consumed by the fire of grief.
Even by day, their couches were not released from sleep;
and portending the downfall of the Great Man, numerous great omens arose simultaneously on all sides throughout the world, instilling fear in living beings for the sake of the king’s non-existence.
For instance:
The entire circle of the great boundary mountains trembled as if the earth itself were first moving, desiring to depart along with its Lord;
the atoms of water, their waves noisy from mutual clashing, swirled about as if remembering Dhanvantari who had vanished within it;
and comets rose up in all directions like masses of hair, long, fierce, and curled, belonging to those terrified by the state of the mountain.

The world became as if grey with the smoke from the life-terminating *homa* sacrifices commenced by the guardians of the quarters, while the faces of the directions were made terrifying by comets; and within the solar disc, which had lost its luster and was tawny like a heated vessel of black iron, some seeker of the king’s life offered himself as a human sacrifice under the guise of a fearsome headless trunk (*kabandha*). Then the moon appeared, radiant with the expansive circumference of its blazing halo, looking like a rampart of fire constructed out of fear of Rāhu, who was yawning in his desire to seize it.

The quarters of the sky, devoted to the king, were consumed as if they had already entered the fire before him; stained by the spray of flowing blood, the Earth, the bride, appeared as if she had donned a garment of pale-red silk to follow her husband in death. The gates of the directions were blocked by masses of untimely dark clouds, like iron door-panels, as if the world-protectors were terrified by the sudden calamity of the king’s destruction.
The terrible roars of thunderbolts swelled forth, sounding like the sharp blasts of war-drums beaten for the departure of the Lord of the Dead, tearing at the heart;
showers of dust, tawny as the hair of a camel, turned the light of the sun grey as if stirred up by the hooves of Yama’s approaching buffalo;
and rows of jackals, howling discordantly with upturned faces, wailed as if catching the flames of meteors falling from the sky.

In the royal capital, the images of the family deities near the lion-throne appeared as if manifesting grief through their disheveled tresses, with the transformations of their hair-crests discernible as they smoked; a swarm of bees, bearing the likeness of the tangled, dark-braided locks of the Night of Doom, wandered in agitation above the inner apartments and did not cease its flight for even a moment; meanwhile, the cawing of ravens cried out incessantly.

From the center of the white parasol’s circle, an old, cawing vulture—like life itself to the kingdom—tore out with its darting beak a fragment of ruby, red as a lump of fresh flesh; and, tormented by great portents, he somehow passed the night. On another day, he approached the royal palace, where the tinkling of ornaments falling apart due to his swift pace sounded like a proclamation of victory for Despair; even from afar, the palace swans, with their jeweled anklets jingling as they moved restlessly on their feet, craned their necks and seemed to ask, "What? What? as if being questioned.
Blinded by tears, she was as if being shown the way by the female house-pheasants crying out in response to the tinkling of their waist-bands as they stumbled over her broad hips;
covering her face with the mass of blood from her forehead, which had split open upon striking the surface of an unseen door-panel— like a fringe of her own red silk garment— she wept aloud,
dropping her cane-staff which resembled a stream of liquid gold melted away by the force of her grief.
She was pulling back her upper garment, which was rippled by the breath from her mouth and fluttering like a female serpent drawing in its sloughing skin;

her breasts were covered by a mass of hair that hung down from her bent shoulders, disheveled by grief and devoid of any braided arrangement, tossing about like a garment of dark-blue *tamāla* shoots woven together and stirred by the wind;

and she was repeatedly shaking her sprout-like hand, whose palm had become swollen and coppery-dark from the pain of striking her breast, appearing as if scorched by the constant wiping away of her scalding tears.
At the waterfall of her eyes, she seemed to bathe the people standing nearby—reflected in the surface of her own cheeks—in order to plunge them into the fire of grief;
with the trembling rays of her pupils darting from her restless eyes, she seemed to burn even the day itself, which was turning dark with her own sorrow. "Where is the prince?
Where is the prince? she asked every person as she approached, accompanied by the female door-keeper of Yashovati named Vela.

Meeting him as his despondent eyes looked up toward her, she approached and placed both hands upon the inlaid floor; with her face cast downward, she seemed to sprinkle her withering, dust-covered lower lip with the streaming rays of her teeth, and thus entreated him:
"My Lord, save me, save me!
While my husband still lives, what desperate act has the Queen resolved to do?"
Then, having heard that further news, he was as if fallen from his fortitude,
as if melted by grief, and as if swallowed up by anxiety.

As if weighed down by heat, as if embraced by anguish, he was rendered motionless; and this thought arose in his mind: "Though the assault of sorrow falls repeatedly upon the heart of one whose consciousness is lost, like a blow from an iron mace striking a stone, it kindles the fire within my pitiless body but does not reduce it to ashes."
Rising up in haste, he went to the inner apartments;
and from afar, he heard the queens who were preparing for death saying, "O dear mango tree, take care of yourself; your mother is departing on a journey."
Dear Jātīguccha, I am going; take leave of me.
Without me, you will today become protectorless, O sister, O pomegranate-creeper of the palace.
"O red Aśoka tree,

my son, you must forgive the kicks from feet and the offenses of breaking off sprouts for ear-ornaments; O young Bakula tree of the inner apartments, you who have become spoiled by receiving mouthfuls of wine!"
I see you, dear Priyaṅgulatikā! Embrace me tightly; I shall become difficult for you to attain.
O auspicious mango-tree at the door of my residence,
a handful of water as an offering must be given; you are my child,
O brother parrot-cage.
So that you do not forget me, what are you saying? "I have become distant from you,
O Śārikā!"
O Mother, may our meeting take place again in a dream;
I shall return home at dawn with the domestic peacock that followed me on the road.

Mother, this pair of swans, who ought to be cherished like a son, has not been honored by me, a woman of little merit, with the marriage festival of this pair of *cakravāka* birds, O you who are so affectionate toward your children!
Turn back, O doe of the house;
O favorite of the chamberlains, bring the lute; let me embrace her for a moment, O Candrasenā.
O Bindumatī, let this person be looked upon with favor;
this is your final salutation.
"O maidservant, release my feet,
noble Kātyāyanikā!"
Why do you weep, O nurse? Compose yourself; why do you fall at my feet?
Sister,
take me by the neck for the last time;
alas, my dear friend Malayavatī has not been seen.
O Kuraṅgavatī,
this is a salutation with joined palms;
may you grant your consent.
This is the final salutation,
Kuvalayavatī;
this is your last embrace.

"Friends, these lovers' quarrels must be forgiven"— hearing such conversations as these, his ears burning with pain even as he entered, he saw her coming out, having given away all her possessions and having taken up the ornaments for death.
Like Jānakī about to enter the presence of her husband before the fire,
she was like the divine Śrī herself just risen from the ocean, her body still moist from a recent bath;
wearing two garments tawny with saffron, she resembled the sky bearing the two splendors of twilight.
She wore a silk garment clinging to her body like the auspicious sign of a widow’s death—a garment made rosy by the mass of luster from her lower lip, which was darkened by the stain of betel-juice;
with a red thread around her neck hanging between her breasts, she created the illusion of a stream of blood trickling from a heart that had burst open;
and with a necklace whose threads were caught on the thorns of her askew, crooked earrings, she seemed to be strangling her own throat with a noose of white silk.
With her body anointed with fresh saffron paste, she seemed as if swallowed by the flaming funeral pyre that desired to consume her;
she filled the lap of her garment with exceedingly white teardrops, as if they were flowers for the worship of the funeral fire;
and at every step, she scattered her slipping bracelets like an offering to invoke the household deities.
Around his neck was a garland of flowers and strings reaching down to his feet, making him appear as if mounted upon a swing;
he seemed to be addressed by the blue lotuses of his eyes, which were resonant with the humming of bees within,
while he was being circumambulated by the palace swans, who moved in circles bound together by their jeweled anklets that acted as companions to his own.
She held motionless a picture-board as if it were her own mind intent on death, with her life-breath closely bound to it;
she embraced her beloved husband’s spear-shaft like a banner of a devoted wife, upon which white flower-garlands were tied and swaying.
She was shedding tears before the royal parasol— which, like a kinsman, was as white as her own virtuous conduct—

and she was with great difficulty instructing the ministers who had received her command after she had somehow regained her sight, which had been obstructed by the excessive flow of tears welling up as they prostrated at her husband’s feet;
meanwhile, her ears were being drawn toward the wailing of the household, whose cries grew louder as the circle of distressed elderly kinsmen was turned back by her entreaties.
Her heart was being carried away by the roars of the lions in their cages, which resembled the speech of her husband;
she was adorned by her nurse out of devotion to her husband, while she was being restrained by an old woman through a fainting fit that seemed like a familiar friend.
She was embraced by her friend with both physical pressure and the weight of shared calamity;
she was surrounded by her attendants who were gripped by grief as if it had seized every limb of their bodies; and she was presided over by noble youths and great elders who were gasping for breath.
She was followed by chamberlains and aged attendants in distress;
she gazed tearfully even at the royal hounds, the favorites of the king,
and fell at the feet of her co-wives as well.
She was being addressed even by painted figurines; she was having her hands folded in salutation before her even by the house sparrows; and she was taking leave even of the domestic animals.
He saw his mother embracing even the trees of the palace grounds, and from afar, with eyes welling with tears, he said, "Mother,
do you too abandon me, one of such meager merit?"
"Be gracious,
turn back!"— even as he spoke thus, his crest kissed, as it were, with affection by the rays of the jewels in his anklets, he fell at her feet;
but Queen Yaśomatī, while her youngest and most beloved son lay thus with his head at her feet, despondent and overwhelmed by a surge of agitation as if seized by a heavy mountain, remained silent.
As if entering the netherworld of blinding darkness and fainting,
she was overwhelmed by a mass of affection that had long been pent up and now burst forth with a torrent of tears;
though she made every effort to restrain it, she was unable to stop the flow of her tears.

With the unbearable surge of grief made manifest by the violent throbbing of her full breasts, her throat faltering as it was seized by a stammering sob, the region of her lower lip made tremulous by extraordinary anguish, her nostrils tightened by the repeated quivering of her lips, she closed her eyes and flooded her stainless cheeks with a deluge of tears. Covering her slightly upturned moon-like face with the edge of her silken garment—which was inlaid with the rays of her fingernails and seemed like a stream of clear tears emerging from within—she, with a pained heart and flowing milk, O Mother, remembered his entire childhood as he lay in her lap, beginning from the day of his birth, while her own heart remained fixed upon the house of her kin.
"Father,
do you not see me, a sinner who has set out for the next world and am thus exceedingly distressed?"— thus she cried out again and again to her parents,
"Alas, my child!"
"By ill fortune, you were not seen," she cried out as she lamented for her beloved son who was absent;
"I have become protectorless," she mourned for her daughter staying with her father-in-law’s family; "O merciless one! [she continued].
"What offense has this person committed against you? she reproached fate;
"There is no woman equal to me in the sharing of sorrow," she censured herself in many ways;
"I have been robbed by you, O cruel one! she reviled Death (Kṛtānta) out of season, and wept for a very long time with a loud cry, like an ordinary woman.
When the force of his anger had subsided, he affectionately raised up his son;

and with his hand, he wiped away the tears from the weeping boy's eyes—tears that flowed more copiously like liquid, while the mass of rays from his fingernails clustered upon the lashes of his eyelids.

Her own eyes, too, being drenched by a whiteness that was itself being swallowed up by intense passion, their inner depths released and their edges swollen with boiling tears, were distressed by the continuous falling of a succession of extremely fine teardrops; their lashes were starred with bright white spray. Having wiped them again and again, she drew back to her ear-tip the lock of hair hanging from grief, which had seized her tear-moistened cheek; she pushed aside the mass of hair that lay askew, disordered by locks slipping down; and lifting with her hand her breast-veil—which was wet, filled with streams of tears, slightly displaced, and rippled like a submerged garment—she washed her lotus-face with water poured forth from the mouth of a silver royal swan, its beauty marked by a thin copper line at the edge of the cloth. Then, having wiped her hands on two clean pieces of cloth held by the mute and simple folk, and having stood for a long time with her pair of eyes fixed steadily upon her son’s face, she sighed deeply again and again and said: "My child,"
You are not unloved, nor are you devoid of merit, nor are you worthy of abandonment;
for with your very milk, my heart was nourished.
And yet, at this moment, my vision, obstructed by the abundant favor of my lord, does not behold you.
Moreover, my son,

I am neither Lakṣmī, who is addicted to gazing upon other men, nor am I the Earth, the instrument of kingship and devoid of compassion; I am the wife of the royal house, born into a lineage pure through righteousness, possessing only the wealth of virtuous conduct.
Have you forgotten me—the wife of a preeminent man who is a veteran of a hundred battles, like a lioness to a lion;

a woman born of heroes, the wife of a hero, and the mother of a hero? For how else could one such as I, purchased by your prowess, act otherwise when my hand was taken by such a father of yours—one who resembles Bharata, Bhagīratha, and Nābhāga, and who is a bull among kings?

Attended by the constant service of endless vassals who were not distracted from their duties, he received upon his head the consecration with jars of Jāmbūnada gold offered by the wives of his neighboring kings;
with his forehead, he obtained the honor of the binding of the Great Queen’s diadem, a prize difficult even for one's heart's desire to attain;
and his breasts were suckled by sons such as yourselves, while they wore Chinese silks fluttering in the breeze of the yak-tail whisks waved by throngs of captive wives of his enemies.
With my pair of feet honored by the rows of rubies in the crowns of all the wives of the entire circle of vassal kings bowing down upon their heads,
and with every limb thus rendered fulfilled, what else do I require? My merit being exhausted, I desire to die while still a widow.
And I am unable, now that my husband is burnt and I am separated from my noble son, to utter useless lamentations like a woman deprived of her lover;

rather, by first announcing his departure to the sky—like the dust of your father's feet—I shall be highly esteemed by the celestial nymphs who are devoted to heroes. And as for me, consumed by the fresh sight of such terrible suffering, what will the fire have left to burn?
At this moment, for me, life itself is more reckless than death;

for while my lord— resembling Mount Kailāsa— dwells abroad, what logic is there in a craving for a life that is as insignificant as a blade of withered grass, when compared to this fire of grief for my husband, which is fueled by inexhaustible affection and is far cooler than the flames of death?

Moreover, my son, even while I am alive, the pleasures of your kingdom shall not touch you, for I am a great sinner by having disregarded the death of the king; and for those consumed by sorrow, prosperity becomes inauspicious, ill-omened, and useless, my child.
"I wish to abide in this world through the fame of those who trust me, not through my physical form;
therefore, father, I entreat you first of all, lest I be tormented by the frustration of my desires.
Having said this, she fell at his feet.

He, however, hurriedly drawing back his feet and bowing his body, raised his mother— who held her form with both hands and had her head touching the ground— perceiving the inevitability of her grief and considering that very action to be more meritorious as it was appropriate for a woman of noble family; and knowing her to be firm in her resolve, he remained silent with his face cast down,
for even noble birth, though distressed by affection, welcomes what is suited to the time and place.

Queen Yaśomatī, having embraced him and smelled his head, departed from the inner apartments on foot; as if obstructed by the quarters of the sky filled with the echoing cries of the citizens, she went to the bank of the Sarasvatī.
There, with glances timid by the nature of women, as if worshipping the sun with clusters of blooming red lotuses, she entered the fire like the lunar form entering the solar orb.
The other [the prince], overwhelmed by his mother’s death and surrounded by his circle of kinsmen, went to his father’s side.

And he beheld his father, whose vital functions were reduced to a mere remnant and whose pupils were rolling, as if the king of stars were longing for the setting; and, overwhelmed by the surge of unbearable grief, he was robbed of his fortitude by his affection.

Embracing his lotus-feet—which were caressed by the garlands of crowns of all the haughty kings—he wept for a long time, letting out cries like anyone else, yet shedding a continuous stream of clear tears as if pouring from eyes made of great clouds; a stream that seemed to melt away his inner anguish, turning into water like the network of moonlight from his teeth, dissolving like the beauty of his eyes, and flowing forth like the nectar of his face.

The king, his gaze fixed upon him and his ears attuned to the sound of incessant weeping, recognized him and spoke very softly: "My son, you ought not to be thus; for those such as you are not lacking in great courage."

For the state of being a great being is first the support of the world, and subsequently the mark of royal lineage; one who is the leader of those possessed of courage relies upon all excellence— where are you,
and where is this despondency?
To you, whose splendor is like that of the sun, the address "you are the lamp of your lineage" is like a slighting;
to you, whose prowess is augmented by valor and sharp wisdom, the address "you are a lion among men" is like an insult;
and to you, for whom the status of a universal monarch has been proclaimed by your very marks, the address "this earth is yours" is like a tautology.
The words "Let Fortune be accepted" were like a contradiction to one who had already been grasped by Fortune herself;
"Let this world be occupied" was insufficient for one who desired to conquer both worlds;
and "Let the treasury be taken possession of" was useless for one whose sole devotion was toward the accumulation of fame as pure as a cluster of moonbeams.
"Let the kingdom be made your own"—this was like a redundant statement for one who had already won over the world by means of his multitude of virtues;
"let the burden of sovereignty be borne"—this was like an inappropriate command for one who was worthy of bearing the weight of the three worlds;
"let the subjects be protected"—this was like a mere restatement for one whose long, staff-like arms had already seized the quarters of the horizon.
"Let the attendants be protected"—this was merely incidental to him who resembles a world-guardian;

"the practice of weapons must be performed"—what more could be commanded of him whose forearms are blackened by the calluses of the bowstring? "Restlessness must be restrained"—for one who has already subdued his senses at such a youthful age, my speech finds no occasion.
"The thought that 'the enemies must be brought to total destruction' belongs to innate splendor alone"—
even as he spoke these words, the lion among kings closed his eyes so as never to open them again;
and at this very moment, the sun too was deprived of its light, as if by its own life-span.
Thereupon, as if feeling ashamed of his own offense born from taking away the life of the king, he became downcast;
and as if being consumed within by the fire of grief for the king’s absence, he turned a coppery hue.
Following the worldly custom with a very slow gait, as if to inquire after the unpleasant news, he descended from heaven.
As if wishing to offer a handful of water to the lord of men, he approached the shore of the western ocean;
and having just offered that handful of water for the king, his thousand rays turned crimson as if scorched by the fire of grief.

And as the sun, whose body was now tranquil, entered the depths of a mountain cave as if entering a vast treasury of world-weariness produced by the death of the great sovereign, [the world] grew dark.
The sunlight faded as if moistened by the storm of tears shed by the great multitude gathered together;
the world turned crimson as if from the glow of the eyes of all people reddened by weeping; and the day grew dark blue as if scorched by the heat of the continuous, burning sighs of many men.
As the lotus-beds were being abandoned by Fortune, as if she had set out to follow the king; as the earth grew dark, its luster withdrawn as if in grief for her husband;
and as the distressed ruddy geese, having deserted their mates like virtuous sons who have left their wives behind, took refuge at the edge of the forest while uttering piteous cries.
When the lotuses had closed their buds as if terrified by the loss of the sun’s parasol;
when the crimson glow had faded like a flood of blood from the bursting hearts of the women of the quarters;
and when the lord of lights had gradually departed for the other world, leaving behind only his affection;
When twilight had set in, pale-red with a thick hue spreading across the expanse of the sky like a funeral banner unfurled;
when streaks of darkness, repulsive to the sight, flickered like rows of black yak-tail whisks adorning a bier for the dead;
and when the night, dark as black aloe-wood, was fashioned by someone like a funeral pyre.

While the fortunes of the night-lotuses, with their ear-lobes adorned by ivory-white petals and their crowns fashioned from garlands of filaments, seemed to rise up as if intent on following him in death with smiling faces;
while the warbling of flocks of birds settling in their nests upon the treetops was heard like the tinkling of the bells of the celestial chariots of the gods descending;
and while the moon was seen in the eastern quarter like the parasol of Indra rising to meet a king who has set out upon the path to heaven.

Like Śibi himself, the king personally took up the bier of the corpse with his own shoulders; then, accompanied by his vassals and citizens led by the family priest, he carried it to the river Sarasvatī and, upon a funeral pyre befitting a monarch, reduced him to a state where only his fame remained through the rites of the sacrificial fire.

King Harṣa too, surrounded by the entire circle of the royal family—now gathered together like the whole world of living beings, yet all rendered speechless by grief—remained as if drenched from the outside by the liquid of affection melting within him, though scorched by the internal fire of sorrow. Seated upon the bare ground, he stayed awake throughout that entire night, as terrible as the river Bhīmarathī, along with his kinsmen;
and this thought arose in his mind:
"Now that my father has passed away, this world of the living is indeed reduced to such a state."
The paths of the world have been broken;
the grounds for prosperity have become barren for all desires;
and the gates of bliss have been closed.
Truthfulness has fallen asleep;
the conduct of worldly life has been lost;
and the strength of the mighty arm has melted away.
Sweet speech has vanished;
the various displays of manly prowess and pastimes have departed; and the pride of being skilled in battle has come to an end.
Delight in the virtues of others has been destroyed, the grounds of trust have come to rest, and noble deeds have become mere footprints.
The scriptures have become useless;
the singular passion for valor has become supportless;
and the state of being a connoisseur has become a mere subject of stories.
Let the people offer handfuls of water to valor;
let them enter the life of renunciation for the sake of protecting their subjects; and let them bind the widow’s braid upon their excellence as men.
May the Fortune of Kings take refuge in this hermitage;
may the Earth don two white garments;
and may Elegance wear bark-cloth.
Let his brilliance perform austerities in the forests of penance,
and let his heroism clothe itself in rags;
where else can gratitude go for his sake?
Where, moreover, will the Supreme Lord find such atoms of the emanations of Great Beings?
The ten directions have become empty of virtues;
the world has become shrouded in darkness regarding the Dharma.

Now life is fruitless for those who subsist by the sword without my father; from where could such heroic assemblies come—those gatherings that prick the cheeks of brave warriors with the talk of strife initiated by the passion of unequalled battle throughout the day?
Would that his lotus-face, with its long red eyes, might be seen once more even in a dream!
"May I embrace again even in another birth those two arms, which possess a weightiness exceeding that of iron pillars;
may I hear even in another world her voice, which, as she calls out 'O son!', pours forth nectar and is as deep as the roar of the churning Ocean of Milk"—
as he was thus reflecting on these and other such thoughts, the night somehow came to an end.
Then, while the flocks of cocks were crying out with open throats as if in grief;

while the palace peacocks were throwing themselves down from the roofs of houses, mountains, and tree-tops; and while the winged creatures, having abandoned their dwellings, were setting out for the forest;
and while the darkness, suddenly thinned, was fading away.
While the lamps, their self-affection having diminished, were longing for non-existence;
while the sky, its body clothed in bark-garments of shimmering crimson rays, had as it were entered the life of a wandering mendicant;
and while the stars, grey as the necks of sparrows, were being swept away by the hour of dawn like fragments of a king’s bones.
While the famous herds of wild elephants were carrying jars filled with the essence of mountain minerals and were heading toward various lakes, rivers, and sacred bathing places;
and while the moon—pale as a mass of fresh, pure honeycomb—was being set down like a sacrificial cake upon the shore of the western ocean.

Gradually, as the moon set— its brilliance seemingly turned ashen by the spreading smoke from the king’s funeral pyre, its heart darkened by the scar of the burn from the fire of grief for the monarch, its form withered by the distress caused by the multitude of moon-like faces of all the women of the harem who had departed, and its spirit despondent like Rohiṇī after her first disappearance—
the sun ascended to heaven as if it were the King himself,
and the continuity of night seemed to have been replaced by the kingdom.
Then King Harṣa set out for his morning ablutions, like a lotus pond being awakened by a circle of roused royal swans; meanwhile,
in the inner apartments, the few remaining chamberlains were overwhelmed with grief, and the palace swans were silent and motionless, their tinkling anklets having ceased their sound.
While the father’s retinue stood in the inner courtyard like a herd of wild elephants whose leader had fallen,
and while the royal elephant— despondent, weeping aloud, and seated upon its post— stood motionless and sluggish;
and while the royal horses, having taken to the courtyard, were announced by the wailing of the stable-keepers;
When the clamor of the shouts of victory had subsided and the great assembly hall was empty, he departed from the royal palace with a burning gaze,
went to the bank of the Sarasvatī, bathed in it, and offered water for his father.

Having performed his ritual bath without wringing out his hair, he put on two fresh white silk garments (*udgamanīya-dukūla*) and returned to the palace. Intent on sighing, without a sunshade and without attendants to clear the way, even when a horse was brought before him, he proceeded on foot alone. With his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose—eyes as red as blood-stained lotuses—he seemed to vomit forth the fire of grief for his father, who now remained only as a memory in his heart, fearing that he too might be cremated. Even though he had not taken betel, the natural crimson glow of his sprout-like lower lip, which had been washed clean long ago and resembled a fresh leaf of the *kalpavṛkṣa*, appeared like mouthfuls of flesh and blood being ejected from his heart due to its violent impact; thus, with the release of hot sighs, he entered the palace.

But the king’s favorites— his servants, friends, and ministers— departed on that very day; abandoning their beloved children and wives, though restrained by their weeping kinsmen, their hearts were so captivated by the multitude of the king’s virtues that some bound themselves to the Bhṛgu rocks,
some remained at those very sacred fords, and others, with their minds distressed, spread out grass and kuśa and allayed their incomparable grief through fasts.

Some, helpless under the impulse of grief, entered the fire like moths; some, their hearts being scorched by the flames of terrible sorrow, went for refuge to the snowy mountain while restraining their speech;
and some, lying on beds of young leaves in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains with their bodies sprinkled by the showers of spray from the trunks of herds of wild elephants, allayed their fever.
Some, having abandoned even the objects of sense present before them, turned away from service and took possession of empty forest lands with limited alms-food;
some became wind-eating sages, whose wealth was their dharma, and who practiced the regulation of breath;
and some, having donned saffron robes, studied the doctrine of Kapila on the mountains.
