Some, draped in garments of shimmering, dangling robes, displayed their radiant devotion to their Master;
others grew old with their bodies being licked by the tips of the tongues of the deer in the penance groves;
while still others, having taken their vows, wandered about shaven-headed, carrying water in water-pots whose mouths were wiped by sprout-like hands and whose lids were of a deep coppery hue.
King Harṣa, too, remained in that same state, overwhelmed by grief for his father;

he regarded prosperity as a curse, the earth as a great sin, sovereignty as a disease, enjoyments as serpents, his home as hell, his kinsmen as fetters, life as infamy, his body as treachery, health as a stain, longevity as the fruit of demerit, food as poison, poison as nectar, sandalwood as fire, desire as a saw, and even worldly success as the bursting of his own heart—
thus he was averse to all activities.

Ancient noble sons who had come down through the inheritance of their fathers and grandfathers, teachers whose words were to be accepted because of the reverence established by their lineage, aged members of twice-born castes learned in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Itihāsa*, consecrated ministers and kings distinguished for learning, noble birth, and character, well-known wandering mendicants who had correctly realized the true nature of the self, kinsmen who shared equally in joy and sorrow, chief counselors who understood the minds [of others], sages who were friends without motive, exponents of the Veda skilled in explaining the worthlessness of worldly existence, and experts in the *Purāṇas* adept at dispelling grief—all these surrounded him.

Rendered dependent by them, he was unable even in his mind to indulge in the flow of grief; yet, being entreated, he with great difficulty turned his attention toward such activities as eating. With his heart fixed on his brother, he thought: "Perhaps, having heard of my father’s death—which is like the great dissolution of the world—the noble one, bathed in tears, might not don the bark garments."
Either the royal sage would not resort to a hermitage,
or that lion among men would not enter a mountain cave;
or else, with his pair of lotus-eyes overflowing and filled with the water of tears, he would behold the earth left without a protector.
Whether the Supreme Person, overwhelmed by the poison of the calamities of his first misfortune, should remember his true self;
or whether, having generated detachment through the realization of impermanence, he should not reject the approaching Fortune of Sovereignty;
or whether, with his body ablaze from the fire of terrible suffering, he should undergo the consecration.
Or, having come here, even when addressed by kings, he would not act with discourtesy;
for the noble one is indeed excessively partial toward his father, as he always addresses me with praise, saying, "O dear Harṣa!"
Has there ever been, or will there ever be again, anyone whose bodily stature was as tall as a golden palm tree,
whose great lotus-face remained upturned and blossomed throughout the day out of love for the sun,
and whose two arms were as radiant as pillars of diamond?

Reflecting on these and other such things— such as "Who else possesses such graceful movements, languid with laughter and intoxication like the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), or who else is so proud,
valiant, and generous?"— he remained there with a heart eager for the sight [of his brother], waiting for his arrival, somehow or other enduring the time.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Death of the Great King," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
The sixth chapter begins: Of those who had been dispatched as secret emissaries and brought back after being repeatedly selected from the earth...
Like one desiring victory, Death gathers together the brave.
The fault of betraying one who has placed trust in him leads to the destruction of the villain and provokes the wrath of the hero.
Like the sound of a young tree being snapped, it steals away the sleep of the elephant.
Then, when the twice-born man who had partaken of the first funeral rice-ball (pretapiṇḍa) had eaten,
and the distressing days of impurity (aśaucadivasa) had passed,

and when the collection of royal paraphernalia— consisting of beds, seats, chowries, parasols, vessels, vehicles, weapons, and so forth— was being bestowed upon the twice-born, causing a burning sensation to their eyes;

When the bones had been carried away along with the hearts of the people to sacred pilgrimage sites; when the funeral monument, piled with heaps of plaster and serving as a thorn of fashioned grief, stood as a mark of the pyre; and when the great lordly elephant, victorious in great battles, had been sent forth to the forest; [The king] was overcome by a fever born of the sorrow for his son. His body was parched by the fire of grief, and he was tormented by the heat of the sun. He was unable to bear even the touch of the breeze from a fan, much less the touch of water. He did not find rest even upon a bed of lotus petals, nor did he find pleasure in the shade of sandalwood trees. He was like one who has lost his way in a vast wilderness, wandering aimlessly. He was like a bird whose wings have been clipped, unable to fly. He was like a tree whose roots have been severed, trembling in every limb. He was like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted, flickering at the end. He was like a river whose waters have dried up, reduced to a mere mirage. He was like a mountain whose summit has been shattered, crumbling away. He was like a cloud whose rain has ceased, hanging heavy and empty. And from him he heard that his brother—though he had already defeated the Mālava army with ease—had been treacherously slain by the Lord of Gauḍa while alone and unsuspecting in his own palace, having laid down his weapons because his trust had been fostered by false pretenses.
Upon hearing this, the prince of great majesty suddenly blazed up, as the force of his grief was fanned by the spreading fire of his fierce anger.
Then, shaking his head in indignation, he seemed to vomit forth the fire of his wrath, which was made to appear like glowing coals by the fragments of crest-jewels shattered upon his head.
With his lip curled back in rage, he seemed to be drinking up the lifespans of all the powerful ones with its incessant quivering;
displaying, as it were, conflagrations of the quarters with the darting glances of his blood-red eyes;
and creating a gloomy downpour of a shower of sweat-drops spread forth by the fire of his wrath, which was itself being consumed by the heat of his own unbearable, innate heroism.
Like Hara, he had assumed a terrifying form;
like Hari, he had manifested the body of Narasiṃha;
and like a sun-stone mountain, he blazed upon seeing the expansion of another's splendor.
His form was as difficult to behold as the twelve suns that rise on the day of universal destruction;
he caused all the mountains to tremble like a great cataclysmic wind;
and his towering body grew ever larger like the Vindhya mountain.
Like a great venomous serpent enraged by the assault of a wicked king, like the son of Parikṣit intent on burning all serpents,
and like Vṛkodara thirsting for the blood of his enemies;
Like a celestial elephant rushing toward a rival tusker,
like the ancestral tradition of manliness,
and like the intoxication of pride.
Like the onset of arrogance,
like the descent of youth upon splendor,
like the total exertion of pride.
It was like the arrival of a new age for the heat of youth,
like a royal consecration for the passion for battle,
and like a day of lustration for impatience.
He fell into a state of extreme agitation and said:

"Who, setting aside that vile lord of Gauḍa, could so quickly bring such a great man— who had just then conquered the entire circle of kings through the sincere prowess of his arms— to such a death, shorn of weapons and despised by all the world of heroes, as if the offspring of Fire (Agni) were to extinguish the noble one who resembles the Pot-born (Agastya)?"

Who would not feel partiality in their hearts toward the noble qualities of valor—qualities that remind one of Paraśurāma’s prowess, like royal swans drawn to the white mass of foam on the Bhāgīrathī—were it not for that ignoble act?

How indeed will he fare, his rays having spread forth without regard for affection, like those of the summer sun at the time of draining the waters from a bed of lotuses, in order to take the life of this noble man, so fierce as he was?
To what destiny shall he go?
Into what womb will he enter, or in which hell will he fall?
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste)— who indeed would do such a thing?

Even as I utter the name of this evildoer, my tongue seems as if stained by the impurity of his sin. What business could the Noble One have had with that wretch, that he should enter him—who was like a pillar of sandalwood, skilled in delighting the whole world—and, devoid of compassion, bring him to ruin like a wood-worm? Surely this fool, greedy for the taste of sweetness and drawing out the Noble One’s life as if it were honey, did not foresee the calamity of the falling of the shafts of misery.

The vile Gauda has accumulated nothing but a mass of exceedingly dark infamy, like soot used as a lamp in the path of a net that defiles its own home; for even though the sun—the crest-jewel of the three worlds—has already set, the Creator has ordained the moon, the sole lord of the deer sporting in the circle of planets, to suppress the darkness that is the enemy of the path of righteousness. Furthermore, even when the goad that enforces discipline is broken, the sharp claws of the lion remain effective for subduing a rogue elephant, being capable of cleaving the firm frontal globes of all intoxicated tuskers.
"Who would not put such men to death, who, like base jewelers, destroy radiant gems?
Where will this evil-minded man go now?

Even as his father was speaking these words, the commander-in-chief—who was a friend of his father and the foremost in all military engagements—arrived, his body as bright as a mountain of yellow orpiment.

Resembling the trunk of a mature and straight *sāla* tree, tall and having reached full maturity as if through the heat of extreme valor, he stood in the final stage of his life; though he had risen from many beds of arrows, he seemed to laugh at Śantanu for his exceedingly long lifespan.

Touched by old age, which—as if terrified even of his body’s invincibility—manifested a trembling, he somehow clung to his hair that was as firm as steel; with a mane of straight locks white as a mass of moonbeams, he seemed to have transferred even while living to the lionine state, a condition fashioned from the essence of guileless valor. With his vision obscured by a pair of eyebrows whose skin was wrinkled, slack, and hanging down, as if wishing to avoid the great sin of beholding the faces of other masters, he remained there.

With his formidable face, radiant with the region of his cheeks covered by a thick, white tuft of whiskers, he seemed to be vomiting forth the onset of autumn—even out of season—with its vast expanse of blooming kāśa groves, as if signaling the time for valor;
with his long, hanging mane of beard, he fanned his deceased master, who remained as if present in his heart, with a white chowrie;
and his broad chest was made uneven by large, gaping wounds that appeared like mouths opened wide, as if parched from drinking the water of the whetted edges of swords even in old age.

With the continuous rows of letters formed by the deep scars of many great wounds carved by the tips of sharp weapons and axes, he seemed to be counting the successive victories in every battle; like the eastern mountain walking on foot,
he seemed to surpass even the *Mahābhārata* in the loveliness of his various heroic exploits,
and through his relentless persistence in crushing adversaries, he seemed to be instructing even Paraśurāma.

By his wandering abroad, which was a graceful display of attracting the splendor of honor while remaining indifferent [to worldly ties], he seemed to instruct even Mount Mandara; by his adherence to the discipline of a military commander, he seemed to surpass even the ocean;
and by his steadfastness, firmness, and loftiness, he seemed to put even the mountains to shame.
By the throbbing radiance of his innate and fierce splendor, he seemed to treat even the sun as a blade of grass;
by the fact that his back was chafed by bearing the burden of the Lord, he seemed to mock even the bull of Hara; and he was the friction-stick for the fire of indignation.
Arrogance is the offspring of heroism;
intoxication is the offspring of pride; and dissipation is the offspring of insolence.
The heart of *haṭha* (forceful effort),
the life-breath of the desire for victory, and the very respiration of enthusiasm.
He is a goad for the intoxicated, a subduer of serpents for wicked beings,
and the cessation of the state of non-humanity.
He was the family preceptor of heroic assemblies,
the standard for those possessed of valor, and one who had seen the very limits of the entire range of weapons.
He was the fulfiller of bold declarations,
the restorer of those who had been broken,
and one who reached the further shore of his promises.

An expert in the vital points of great conflicts, a drum for the proclamation of those seeking battle, Siṃhanāda sat right nearby; with a voice as deep as the resonance of a kettledrum, he roused the martial spirit of the brave warriors and announced: "O King!"
Like crows deceived by a soiled cuckoo that has taken refuge nowhere, base men, deceived by a Fortune who is herself most defiled, do not perceive their own ruin;
for the defects of Fortune, such as blindness, are like the jaundice of a disease—

what indeed can that wretch do, he who, out of extreme cowardice, is perpetually turned away and has never beheld the faces of the enraged and majestic, whose fires of wrath blossom with the bristling hair on cheeks tawny with the swelling pride of a valor that surpasses all?
That ascetic does not know this: that high-minded men, when provoked, bring about the immediate destruction of their entire lineage just like malevolent spells;
for spirited men burn even in water when struck. This deed, which is skilled at hurling one into a bottomless hell, is indeed worthy of him who is excluded from the assembly of all heroes.

For when the bow—foremost wealth in the great struggle of the high-minded—is held aloft, and when the sword—a forest of blue lilies for the playful sport of Lakṣmī’s swan—is grasped, even such desperate expedients as the churning of the ocean and the like are of no avail for the attainment of fortune; how much less so those such as these?

And how could those who possess mighty arms and whose kinsmen are pure fame—even mountains, which, being themselves unable to protect the earth as appointed by the Creator, vomit forth iron for the sake of striking with their thunderbolt-hard, club-like arms—ever contemplate an unworthy deed even in their minds?
For before the rays from the hands of noble warriors, which outshine all planets, the rays of the sun are rendered lame when attempting to seize the quarters of the sky.

The intermediate space between the waves breaking against the horns of great buffaloes is terrifying; the southern quarter is merely a worldly convention, whereas in reality it is the frown of the warrior—the dwelling place of Yama.
And it is a marvel that, when heroes let out lion-like roars in battle, their manes do not suddenly fly out along with the bristling horripilation born of the thrill of daring.
Indeed, only two things are capable of containing the mass of splendor produced by the four oceans: the fierce submarine fire that consumes its opposite, or the heart of a great man.
For how could there be an extinction of the innate heat of a radiant being before it has reached all the oceans?
The Lord of Serpents, who carries a vast burden of expanded hoods in vain, supports with his own body nothing but a lump of clay.
Only the arms of heroes—whose forearms shine with the weight of elephant trunks and whose commands march forth unimpeded—know the essence of the pleasure of enjoyment;
like the sun, they pass their days in comfort with undiminished splendor, grasping the shoots of their feet as upward-facing lotus-beds.
But for the coward, whose heart is like the deer-marked moon and whose back is pale, how could fortune remain steady for even two nights?
The heroic sentiment, expanding and raining down a multitude of immeasurable glories,
stands before us; the paths of manly prowess have been cleared by advancing majesty,
and the enemies, scattered by the mere sound [of his name], become the very gateways to one's pride.
The empty quarters of the sky, illuminated by the light of his weapons, appear as if colored red like the earth by the spray of his enemies' blood; even royal fortune becomes enamored of him;
and even his kingly majesty becomes radiant, as if the row of his toenails were being polished on the whetstone edges of the jeweled crowns of many kings.
Through incessant practice with weapons, the faces of enemies become darkened as if they were the palms of one's own hands;

while the body becomes white with hundreds of bandages bound over various wounds, so too does fame become white. The cruel blows of the sword, when hurled against the door-like chests of armored enemies, vomit forth prosperity as if it were a flame of fire.
He who, having lost his own kin through the enemy, proclaims the grief of his heart by striking the breasts of the wives of his foes;

he who sighs with the wind from the falling of harsh sword-blades and weeps with the downpour of tears from the bodies of his breathless enemies; he who offers water with the eyes of the women of the opposing side—he is superior, not the other. For the awakened heroes do not fix their sense of kinship upon momentary bodies that vanish like those seen in a dream; rather, the perception of the body of heroes is fixed upon enduring fame.

And just as soot and grime do not touch a jewel-lamp—which is radiant by nature with a continuous, blazing expansion of light—so too does grief never touch a man of spirit. You are the foremost among the courageous, the preeminent among the wise, the first among the capable, the leader among the noble-born, the precursor among the spirited, and the originator among the intolerant.

Moreover, these breast-panels of the great warriors—which are ever-present with the smoke of their smoldering anger; which find satisfaction in the water of the sword-edge; which are embraced by the shadow of their formidable forest-like arms; which serve as cool retreats for fortitude; and which are under their own control—are at hand.
Therefore, what is the use of this one wretched lord of Gauḍa?
Act in such a way that no other person shall ever again behave in this manner.

Distribute fly-whisks among those who lust after the faith of the entire earth and who falsely desire victory; dispel their addiction to the shade of royal umbrellas with the sighs of the women of the inner apartments; and cure the eye-diseases of passion caused by the sidelong glances of the unfaithful Fortune of noble lineages with the sweat from lukewarm waters of blood.

Allay the swellings of unrighteous heroism with the piercing wounds of sharp arrow-heads; uproot the foul impurities of iron shackles and chains with great medicines; destroy the foot-soreness caused by the indulgence of footstools with the application of the caustic lye of harsh commands;
and cure the itching in the ears caused by hearing the word "victory" with the bitter draught of stern decrees.

Remove the distortions of stiff, unbending necks with forehead-pastes of sandalwood in the form of the rays from your toenails; uproot the thorns of ill-conduct, which fester with the heat of pride in wealth, using the pincers of commands for the payment of tribute;
and shatter the darkness of the knitted brows of haughty warriors with the lamps of light from the radiance of your jeweled footstools.

O Victorious One, soften the great fevers of false pride with the health of your head, freed from the heaviness caused by the agility of treading upon the feet [of others]; soften the callousness of scars from bowstrings with the warmth of hands folded in salutation through constant service. Do not abandon that very path, desirable to the three worlds, by which your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have gone.
Abandoning this grief befitting only a base man, assume the royal fortune that has descended through the lineage of your house, O Lord, like a lion seizing a doe.

Since the king has departed for the state of the gods and Rājyavardhana’s life has been consumed by the serpent-like wicked Gauḍas, you alone are now the Śeṣa, the world-supporter, for the upholding of the earth in this great dissolution.

Console the subjects who are without refuge; like the autumn sun scorching the foreheads of kings, set down your footsteps upon the heads of your enemies. Return to the state of Kalmāṣapāda by means of your toe-nails that burn like fire, which are like circles of smoke from the sighs of those tormented by the pain of initiation into new service, and by the youthful glow of the crest-jewels of your trembling foes.

Moreover, when his father was slain, the ascetic Paraśurāma—reared alone among deer, his mind naturally tender and delicate due to his Brahminhood—having made his resolve, uprooted the entire host of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times; he cut down their lineage with a raised sword that silenced the trumpeting of the world-elephants with the roar of his fierce bow drawn in the forest and produced a fever for the world with the twanging of his vibrating bowstring.
How much more so, then, can our Lord, the crest-jewel of the proud, whose mind is like a thunderbolt of natural physical hardness?
Therefore, having now made this vow, take up your bow—the banner of a sudden expedition marked by the gathering of your life-force for the destruction of the wretched Gauḍa’s existence.

For the most terrible fever of suffering burning the body of your Majesty, who is already scorched by the fire of humiliation, cannot be quenched except by the cooling treatment of anointing it with the red sandalwood paste of the enemy's blood.

Indeed, when all other means for pacifying the heat of insult had been exhausted, the Son of the Wind (Bhīma) drank the nectar of the enemy's blood—which he had tasted while kissing Hiḍimbā—as a remedy no less effective than Mount Mandara.

"And by the son of Jamadagni, he bathed in the lakes formed from the blood of the Kṣatriyas— lakes whose waters were cool to the touch, providing a soothing relief to the feverish flames of his wrath," he said, and then ceased speaking.
But King Harṣa replied to him, "What has been stated by my venerable lord is indeed a duty that must be performed."
Otherwise, even though the Lord of Serpents has taken possession of my domain, the jealous arm of this man still regards him as a rival;
his creeper-like brow moves toward seizing the host of planets to subdue them,
and his hand desires to seize the hair of the mountains even as they bow down before him.
His heart desires to make even the sunbeams, scorched by their own heat, serve as chowries;
his foot seeks to turn even the heads of the lions, enraged by the title of "King," into footstools;
and his lower lip quivers to issue commands for the seizure of even the quarters of the sky, which have been taken at will by the self-willed world-protectors.
Furthermore, when such a wretched birth has occurred and my mind is overflowing with indignation, there is simply no room for performing acts of mourning.

Moreover, while that vile wretch— the pestilence to my heart, the executioner with the mace, the scoundrel despised by the world, the lowest outcaste among the lords of Gauḍa— still lives, I am ashamed to heave a mere sigh of grief with parched lips like a child,
and to offer a handful of water from my two hands, which have not yet brought about a deluge of tears from the restless eyes of the enemy's women.
Or rather, let my eyes behold the circle of smoke from the funeral pyres of the lowest Gaudas, or let my two hands offer handfuls of water to them;

hear my vow, I swear by touching the very dust of your noble feet: if within a counted number of days I do not cause the earth to resound with the rattling of fetters upon the feet of all those men who are arrogant with the fickleness of their bows, then, like a moth in a fire fed with clarified butter, I shall cast myself, a sinner, into the flames.
Having said this, he commanded Avantī, the chief minister of peace and war who was standing nearby: "Let it be written:
from the mountain of sunrise, whose peaks are abandoned by pairs of *cāraṇa* singers startled by the rattling of the sun's chariot wheels;
up to Suvela, where the details of the plundering of Laṅkā by Kākutstha are inscribed upon the slopes of Mount Trikūṭa."
From the western mountain, whose hollows resound with the tinkling of the anklets of the excellent wives of Varuṇa intoxicated by wine,
to Mount Gandhamādana, whose cave-dwellings are scented by the fragrance of musk-stone perfumed by the wives of the Guhyakas—
let the hands of all kings be prepared, either for the payment of tribute or for the taking up of arms.
Let the quarters of the sky or fly-whisks be grasped; let heads or bows be bowed down;
let commands or bowstrings be made into ear-ornaments.
Let the dust of his feet become a crest-ornament or a helmet;
let the joined palms form a barrier against elephant herds;
let the ground be released from arrows.
Let cane-sticks or spear-staffs be grasped;

let yourself be well-observed either in my toe-nails or in the mirrors of my swords, for I have arrived. Like a cripple, how can there be any turning back for me until a foot-ointment has been prepared—one that travels across all continents and consists of the light from the jewel-stones in the crowns of every king?
Having thus made his resolve, he left the assembly hall—having abandoned his seat and dismissed the circle of courtiers—in anticipation of beginning his bath;
and rising as if composed, he performed his entire daily routine.
And for him who had heard the vow, the heat of the day subsided like the spreading of his own pride, as the three worlds grew calm.

Then, when even the Blessed One had departed as if fearing the loss of his own domain, and the sun had lost its luster; when the groves of day-lotuses, though their filaments were hidden within, seemed to contract as if out of fear;

when the flocks of birds remained motionless with their wings withdrawn and did not manifest themselves as if out of dread; and when the entire populace, with bowed heads and joined palms, honored the world-pervading twilight as if it were a solemn vow— [The original text continues here.]

When the quarters of the sky were being obscured by dense garlands of darkness—as if they were encircled by rings of iron ramparts reaching the clouds, offered by the world-protectors who trembled at the fear of falling from their own positions—he did not remain long in the hall of the evening twilight.

As if being saluted even by the circles of lamps whose flames flickered in the wind from the moving earrings of the bowing assembly of kings, he dismissed his people; and having forbidden the entrance of his attendants, he entered his bedchamber.
There, lying on his back, he relaxed his limbs upon the surface of the couch.
And as if pursued by a shadow, the grief for his brother seized him with force while he was alone with a lamp;
with eyes closed, he saw his elder brother as if still living within his heart,
while sighs issued forth one after another like those seeking his brother’s life.
Covering her face with a flood of tears as if with the hem of a white silk garment, she wept silently for a very long time and reflected in her mind:
"How indeed can such a transformation as this befit a form so beautiful?"
The noble one was harder than iron ore extracted from a mountain, for his bodily frame was as firm as a massive stone slab;
and how could this wretched heart of mine even once breathe again in the absence of the noble one? Was it love, devotion, or perhaps mere obedience?
What fool would have imagined that my life would survive the death of the Noble One? That such a union has vanished in an instant; by the effortless hand of cruel fate, I have been separated from it.
My grief was stifled by suppressed rage, and though I wept for a long time, I did not do so with a broken voice;

for, devoid of compassion, I have regarded the trivial affections of living beings—which are as fragile as a web of spider-silk and serve merely as the bond for worldly existence—as mere kinship. Thus, even though my noble brother has ascended to heaven, I remain as if unconcerned, as if he were a stranger to me.

Furthermore, what fruit has been obtained by that wretched fate, now that this pair of brothers—who once shared a heart contented by the bonds of mutual affection and partook in happiness—have been thus torn asunder?
And those very virtues of my noble brother, which once gladdened the world like the moon, now burn me as if he had entered another realm and his funeral pyre were already lit;
with such thoughts and others, he lamented in his heart.

When the night had turned to dawn, at the very break of day, he commanded his doorkeeper: "I wish to see Skandagupta, the superintendent of the entire elephant corps. Thereupon, being summoned by a succession of many men running simultaneously, he departed from his own palace on foot—without even waiting for his elephant—greatly agitated.
The common folk were being cleared away by staff-bearers acting with great haste.

At every step, he bowed to the preeminent elephant-physicians in every direction and inquired after the news of the night; meanwhile, ahead of him, there were throngs of mahouts moving in long, non-circular formations—like the Vindhya forests with their dense thickets of bamboo canes marked by the plumage of tall peacocks, as if those forests had come forth for the effort of crushing the elephant enclosures—and these men were showing handfuls of emerald-green fodder, entreating newly captured lordly elephants, rejoicing in their hearts at having obtained the intoxicated tuskers they desired, approaching from afar to pay homage, and reporting the onset of rut in their own elephants.
with those petitioning for admission to the drum;
with those walking in front, their long beards grown out of grief for the elephant lost through the fault of negligence;
and with newly arrived mendicants running about in the hope of the joy of obtaining an elephant.
There were groups of courtesans' overseers who, having long awaited their opportunity, stood with uplifted hands;

there were rows of forest guards, busy conversing with their serviceable female elephants and displaying banners of fluttering leaves; and there were throngs of mahouts, raising high the forests of their sharp goads and manifesting the leather bags used for elephant training, intent on reporting the arrival of new herds of wild tuskers.
And by throngs of messengers from the elephant-forest ranges, who had been dispatched to report news of the movements of the newly captured elephants;
who inspected the heaps of elephant fodder at every moment;
and who announced the collection of forest produce in the villages, cities, and market towns.
Creating a tumultuous clamor with his clusters of bracelets,
he— through the manifestation of his great authority acquired by his master’s favor and through his natural exercise of majesty— seemed to issue commands even while remaining indifferent,
as if ordering the oceans to provide him with an inexhaustible abundance of conch-shells from the ears of elephants.
As if plundering the mountains to collect the red mineral paste for his erotic body-unguents;

as if stripping away the sovereignty of the world-quarters from the elephants of the quarters by means of his strides, which were heavy enough to bend Mount Kailāsa under the weight of Śiva’s feet, thus seemingly destroying the earth’s pride in bearing such a burden;
and as if driving in a row of tethering-stone pillars on both sides with the thrusts of his two long, staff-like arms that hung down to his knees and swayed with the force of his gait.

With his lower lip— slightly raised and hanging down, tasting like the flavor of nectar, and as tender as a fresh sprout— he seemed to entice the noble female elephant with a morsel; bearing a nose-bridge as long as his own royal lineage,
he seemed to drink up the expanse of the quarters with the stretch of his pair of eyes, which were exceedingly glossy, sweet, white, and wide, as if they had drunk the Milky Ocean.

With his topknot, which was beautiful with its exceedingly long, dark, and soft luster as if it had grown under the constant shade of an unbroken parasol, and which was naturally fragile yet charmingly swaying like a young creeper, he seemed to cut down the sun’s rays that deprived him of light; though he had abandoned the use of the bow since the destruction of his enemies’ factions, the sound of his great virtues was heard throughout the ends of all directions; and though he possessed the entire host of rutting elephants under his command, he remained untouched by pride.
Though possessed of prosperity, he was full of affection;
though made of earth, he was full of virtue; and like elephants, he stood above those who were prone to giving (or, bestowing gifts).

Bearing a servitude that was as desirable as lordship and yet remained beyond reproach, he had ascended to a state of being a favored recipient of his master’s grace— unapproachable by others like a noblewoman steadfast in devotion to a single husband;
he was a friend without cause to the wise and an unpaid servant to those who serve him.
Skandagupta, a slave not purchased by the learned, entered the royal palace and,
from afar, performed a salutation, touching the ground with his head while supported by the lotuses of both his hands.
When he had sat down very near him, King Harṣa then said to him: "The details of this noble undertaking and of what we intend to do have already been heard by you;
therefore, let the elephant forces stationed in the outposts be brought in quickly.

The fire of pain caused by the insult to my noble brother does not tolerate even a slight delay in the march. Thus addressed, [Rājyavardhana] bowed and replied: "May my lord take note of what has been commanded; however, there is a small matter to be reported out of devotion to my master."
May Your Majesty listen to this:

for everything undertaken by Your Majesty is worthy of you—worthy of a lineage born of the Puṣpabhūti dynasty, worthy of your noble birth, worthy of your innate splendor, worthy of your pair of arms that extend like the trunks of world-elephants, and worthy of your extraordinary brotherly affection.
Even the wretched worms called *kākodara* do not tolerate an insult, much less those masses of splendor such as yourself.
"By the mere account of the increase of the kingdom of the gods, Your Majesty has already seen a small measure of the wickedness of the evil;

indeed, such is the nature of the world. For in every village, every city, every district, every country, every island, and every direction, the dress, appearance, diet, speech, and conduct of the people differ. Therefore, let this total trustfulness—born of a naturally simple heart and accustomed to the customs of your own land—be abandoned."

Daily, through the onset of the fault of negligence, Your Majesty, as was the case with Nāgasena— who was born into a family of *nāgas*— his destruction occurred when his mantras were overheard by a *sārikā* bird in Padmāvatī;
and likewise, the ruin of Śrutavarman’s fortune occurred in Śrāvastī when his secret counsel was overheard by a parrot.
The disclosure of his secret counsel while he was dreaming led to the death of Suvarṇacūḍa in Mṛttikāvatī;

and a beautiful attendant holding a golden chowrie, having read the letters from the reflection of a line imprinted on the crest-jewel of the Yavana king, met her fate at the hands of Yama; furthermore, the army of Vidūratha, with swords drawn, crushed Bṛhadratha of Mathurā, who was greedily digging up a treasure trove in the dead of night.

The soldiers of Mahāsena, emerging from the limbs of illusory elephants, overthrew the Lord of Vatsa who was habituated to dwelling in the Nāgavana grove; and Mitradeva, having approached the head of Sumitra—the son of Agnimitra—who was exceedingly fond of dance while seated in the midst of actors, severed it with his sword like a lotus stalk. Furthermore, enemies of Śarabha, the Lord of Aśmaka, disguised as students of music with sharp swords hidden within the hollows of bottle-gourd lutes, cut off his head, for he was one who held dear the playing of stringed instruments.
The ignoble Puṇyamiśra crushed King Bṛhadratha of the Maurya dynasty—who was weak in wisdom—by displaying his entire army under the pretext of a mere show of force;

and the wondrously curious Caṇḍīpati led away his master Kākavarṇa somewhere by means of a sky-faring mechanical vehicle constructed by a Yavana who had been brought under subjection by force; and the Śaiśunāri king was seized by the throat and slain with a sword on the outskirts of the city.

Vasudeva, the minister, caused the Śuṅga king—who was excessively devoted to the company of women and entirely under the sway of the bodiless god of love—to lose his life through the daughter of a maidservant, Devabhūti, who acted as a queen in disguise.

And the ministers of Mekala, by means of a tunnel from Mount Godhana, led away the King of Magadha—who was addicted to the caverns of the Asuras—into their own territory, using a path made delightful by the jingling sound of the countless jewels and anklets of beautiful women.
Furthermore, at the festival of Mahākāla, Tālajaṅgha, the Vetāla, killed Kumārasena, the youngest son of Pauṇaka and the son of Pradyota, who was frantic with talk of selling human flesh.

And physicians in disguise, who were intent on the efficacy of elixirs and had demonstrated the virtues of their medicines before many people, brought about consumption in Gaṇapati, the son of the King of Videha; and a brother who gained the confidence of women became the cause of death for Vīrasena, the King of Kaliṅga, by means of a secret wall in the chamber of the chief queen;
and a son seated beneath the mattress of his mother’s bedchamber became the cause of death for Dadhra, the lord of Karūṣa, who was desirous of consecrating another son as his successor.

The messenger of Śūdraka, in secret, caused the moon-like Cakoranātha—who took pleasure in eclipsing the moon—to be removed from life along with his ministers; and the soldiers of the Lord of Campā, who were hidden in the thickets of tall reeds while he was hunting and slaughtering the Gaṇḍakas, snatched away the lives of Cāmuṇḍīpati’s troops; and the Maṅkhas, whose mouths were loud with shouts of "Victory! and who were incited by others, dug up the foolish Kṣatravarman, the Maukhari, who was excessively devoted to the praise of Puṣkara.

And it has come to the ears of Your Majesty that in the city of Ariṇa, Candragupta—who was disguised in the dress of a woman—destroyed the lord of the Śakas because he was lustful for another's wife; thus, the negligence of the heedless caused by women is well known.
For example, Suprabhā, intoxicated by wine, killed Mahāsena, the King of Kāśi, with parched grain smeared with honey for the sake of her son’s kingdom.

And Ratnavatī, her pride of love aroused by a pretext, struck the enemy of Ayodhyā, Jarūtha, with a mirror whose edge was as sharp as a razor; and Devakī, infatuated with Devarāta, struck the Souhmian Devasena with an ear-lotus whose nectar was sprinkled with powdered poison; and the beloved wife, enraged at her co-wife, struck Rantideva of Vairantya with a jeweled anklet that showered a rain of the dust of yoga.
"Bindumatī shall kill Vṛṣṇi Vidūratha with a weapon hidden in her braid;
Haṃsavatī shall kill Sauvīra Vīrasena with a jewel from her girdle smeared with poison;

and Pauravī, her face anointed with invisible ointment, shall kill Somaka, the lord of the Pauravas, by making him swallow a mouthful of poisoned wine. Having said this, she ceased speaking and departed to carry out her master's command.
King Harṣa also established all the administrative arrangements of the kingdom;
and when King Harṣa, having made his vow, ordered the march for the conquest of the quarters, various omens appeared in the dwellings of the neighboring vassals whose lives were spent.
For indeed, herds of restless black antelopes roamed here and there like the glances of the messengers of Death approaching from no great distance.

In the courtyard, swarms of honey-bees, whose humming resembled the tinkling of the anklets of the fickle Goddess of Fortune, emitted a harsh sound even during the day; meanwhile, inauspicious jackals, with flames issuing from the cavities of their gaping, distorted mouths, howled for a long time with a dreadful cry for ill omen; and forest pigeons, their wings tawny like the cheeks of young monkeys, fell down as if their flight were rooted in the flesh of corpses.
The trees in the groves simultaneously bore out-of-season blossoms as if addressing him;
the statues in the assembly hall wept violently, their breasts struck by the blows of trembling palms;
and the warriors saw their own headless trunks in the surfaces of their mirrors, with their heads whirling in fear of being seized by the hair.
Upon the crest-jewels of the royal consorts, footprints marked with the signs of the wheel, conch, and lotus appeared;
the chowries suddenly slipped from the bud-like hands of their maidservants;
and even when turned away in a lover’s quarrel, the soldiers remained for a long time with their backs to the proud women.

The honey-drinking bees ceased their festive gatherings for drinking sweet wine upon the cheeks of the female elephants; the lions, as if fainting from having smelled the scent of Yama’s buffalo, did not graze even the green fresh grass, though it was as soft as a pillar; and the palace peacocks, though coaxed by the musical clapping of girls whose hands were eloquent with moving bracelets, remained sluggish and did not dance.
Night after night, the pack of dogs howled loudly at the gateway, their faces upturned as if their eyes were fixed upon the deer-mark on the moon;
the female jackal wandered through the courtyards all day long, her forefinger twitching in a threatening gesture as if counting those whose lives had come to an end;
and upon the paved floors, rows of young grass sprouted, rippling like the curved lines of a deer’s hooves.
The reflections of the lotus-faces of the warriors' wives were seen in the wine of their goblets—faces with braids tied up and radiant with the luster of unapplied yellow pigment (rocanā).
The earth trembled as if terrified by the imminent seizure of its own self.
Showers of blood, glowing red like blooming bandhūka flowers, appeared upon the bodies of the fallen heroes like splashes of red sandalwood juice used for the decoration of those condemned to death.

As if performing the ritual of circumambulation with fire around the perishing royal fortune, masses of blazing meteor-staffs fell in succession, burning clusters of stars with their outbursts of charcoal-like sparks from incessantly flickering embers;
and even before that, a harsh whirlwind wandered about, carrying away fly-whisks, umbrellas, and fans from every palace like a female door-keeper.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Vow," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
The seventh chapter of the *Harṣacarita*: The earth became a courtyard for women; the ocean was a mere canal, and the netherworld was dry land.
And for a hero who has made his vow, even Mount Sumeru is like an anthill.
That the mountains do not bow before this mighty-armed one who holds his bow is indeed a marvel.
What need is there even to mention the counting of those wretched crows who are known as enemies?

Then, after some days had passed, on a most auspicious day calculated by hundreds of astrologers, at a moment for an expedition favorable for the conquest of all four quarters, the king bathed with jars of polished steel and refined gold—like autumnal clouds skilled in shedding water—and performed with supreme devotion the worship of the Lord Nīlalohita. Having offered oblations into the fire whose mass of flames turned clockwise, he gave to the twice-born thousands of silver and golden vessels filled with sesame seeds adorned with golden leaf-patterns, and tens of millions of cows whose hooves and horn-tips were decorated with creepers of gold leaf. Seated upon a throne covered with a spread tiger-skin, he first smeared his body with sandalwood paste white as his own fame, starting from his feet, and then donned two silken garments marked with pairs of royal swans. He fashioned upon his head a wreath of white flowers like the crescent moon, the emblem of the Supreme Lord; he placed upon his ear a fresh sprout of *dūrvā* grass sprinkled with yellow pigment, appearing like the emerald ray of his ear-ornament. Upon his forearm he fastened the auspicious travel-bracelet along with his seal-ring. His head was sprinkled with a shower of peace-water scattered by the hands of the honored and delighted domestic priest. Having dispatched costly vehicles and distributed to the kings ornaments anointed with the light of abundant gems, having released the prisoners and the distressed paupers and sons of noble families with gifts of grace, and having appointed his right arm—the pillar of his conquest over the eighteen islands—as if it were his own self made manifest through its throbbing at that moment to oversee the campaign—he set forth from his palace. Surrounded by all the auspicious omens acting as if they were servants competing with one another to be first, amidst the tumultuous roar of "Victory! raised by the joyful subjects, he emerged like Hiraṇyagarbha from the cosmic egg to bring about the Kṛta Yuga.
And not far from the city, on the banks of the Sarasvatī, a great hut made of grass had been constructed,
with a lofty archway erected and a golden pitcher adorned with sprouts placed upon an altar.
Upon one wearing a bound garland of forest flowers, a row of white banners,
and wandering white garments;
When the second watch had passed,
he set out from his residence;

and there, the village accountant (grāmākṣapaṭalika), accompanied by his entire staff of scribes, approached him and, saying, "May Your Majesty, whose commands are never in vain, deign to receive the daily revenue today," presented a newly fashioned golden seal bearing the bull-emblem.
The king took it;
and as soon as the clay ball had first been set down, the seal slipped from his lotus-like hand and fell face-down upon the ground.
On the soft earth of the bank of the Sarasvatī, where the layer of mud was slightly dried, the lines of the letters shone forth clearly.
While his attendants were despondent, fearing an ill omen, the king thought to himself: "The intellects of the undiscerning are indeed incapable of perceiving reality;
for even when it has been announced by a portent that the earth shall become marked by the seal of your sole sovereignty, the vulgar interpret it otherwise.
Having thus mentally rejoiced at that great omen, he bestowed upon the twice-born a hundred villages whose boundaries were measured by a thousand ploughs.
He spent that day there, and when night had fallen, having honored all the assembled kings, he went to sleep. Then,
as the third watch was passing away, while all living beings slept in silence, the drum of departure was struck with a sound as deep as the trumpeting of the elephants of the quarters.
Having stood before him for a moment, eight sharp strokes were again clearly struck upon the drum to signal the number of *krośas* for the journey;
then followed the sounding of the *paṭaha*, and the joyful proclamation of the *nāndī*.
In the humming groves,
where the kāhala drums resound and the conch shells blare,

The quarters of the sky were filled with the clamor of the *koṇikā* pegs being struck by swift and heavy blows, while attendants were busily engaged in the activity of rousing the household staff, and the sound of the gradually increasing jingling of anklets grew louder.
In that place where groups of guards and executioners were being bound by the officers of force;
where the darkness of the night was dispelled by the light of thousands of torches kindled by the people;
and where pairs of lovers were awakened by the footsteps of the female wardens of the watch.
In the place where those who were falling asleep or waking up sat groaning with harsh cries; where the sleeping quarters were being vacated by elephants that had awakened;
and where the horses, rising from sleep, were shaking their manes.
The earth was being dug by spades noisy with the clanging of their handles;
the wooden stakes were being driven in with a jingling sound;
and the hooves of the horses were being tossed about as they pranced, loud with the tinkling of the fetters and chains being fastened.
The ten directions were filled to overflowing with the clanging sounds of iron chains used to bind rutting elephants as they were being tethered;
the elephant-riders’ backs, dusty from the blows of their whips, were being rubbed and stretched out as they cleaned and smoothed their leather armor;
and the tent-carpenters’ servants were busily wrapping up tents, canvas screens, pavilions, curtains, and canopies.
In which the flattened leather bags were being filled with bundles of stakes;
where the storekeepers were carrying their wares about like beasts of burden; and where many pack-animals were being driven along, laden with the transport of goods from the storehouse.
In the royal camp, where the houses of the vassal lords were crowded with the pressure of the treasury-jars being placed upon them by many motionless Niṣāda soldiers;
where wicked elephants were being loaded with heaps of equipment hurled swiftly by clever Dāseraka servants stationed at a distance;

and where the people were provoked to laughter by the sight of pot-bellied *cuṇḍī* women, who, being dependent on others, were being dragged along with difficulty by the hands of their husbands as they bent their hips sideways.
In that place where large, rutting elephants moved with bodies constrained by the cords of excellent leather thongs that were being tightened;
where a fever was produced in the ears by the ringing of bells being struck upon the herds of elephants;
and where young camels, distressed by the neck-rings being fastened upon their backs, were crying out.
In which noble sons of kings were being sent out as messengers; in which the vehicles of well-born young men of good family were being driven by ill-trained attendants;
in which the elephant-keepers, deceived at the hour of departure, were searching for new servants;
and in which the king’s favorite horses were being led away by troops carrying royal gifts.
The grandeur of the circles of the vanguard was being established by the troops of handsome *cārabhaṭa* warriors;
the saddle-saddles were equipped with rows of small bells and salted peas hanging from the saddles of the station-keepers,
while the troop of beloved guards, their earrings turned into protective amulets and their bodies entwined with nets, were settling the monkeys upon them.
In the morning, while the sprouts of fodder for the morning training were being dragged away by grooms and half-eaten,
while the cries of the grass-cutters were spreading abroad,
and while a great commotion was being stirred up in the various stables by young horses snorting and stumbling in their haste to depart;
While beautiful women, hastening at the call of their riders, were applying facial ointments to those mounted on ready elephants;
while stores of fodder and grain were being plundered by common neighbors running after the moving elephants and horses;
and while wagons were being overrun by wandering herds of oxen.
On the road, which was being struck by throngs of carts making a creaking sound as they turned their wheels; where oxen were being yoked at an untimely hour, laden with heaps of goods;
and where the first bulls of the Surabhi breed, greedy for the nearby fodder, were hanging down and stretching out their necks.
In which the kitchens of the chief great feudatories were being set in motion;
where processions of banners ran ahead;
and where the exit from the narrow interior of huts was found with difficulty by hundreds of beloved ones.
In that place where the attendants were being struck with clods of earth by the people rising from the huts shaken by the trampling feet of elephants,

where the small families of the tiger-settlements were fleeing amidst the crashing and clashing sounds, and where the merchants were despondent as their draft-oxen bolted away, harassed by the clamor and the loss of their wealth;

The interior of the city was filled with a multitude of female elephants from the harem setting out, their progress slowed by the crowding of people who thinned out as they were illuminated by the light of the torches carried before them;
horsemen called out to dogs that trailed behind them;
and the quality of the tall, lofty *tuṅgaṇa* trees was being praised by the creaking sound of those who, falling at their feet with impetuosity, found pleasure in the immobility of their gait.
At the time of the departure, when the world was swallowed by dust and the southern cavalrymen were sinking,
exhausted and failing to keep pace with their horses, elephant-drivers arrived from every direction mounted upon female elephants, holding aloft bows variegated with golden leaf-patterns.

By those seated on the inner seats with swords grasped by their intimate attendants; by those waving chowrie-petals as betel-bearers; and by those stationed at the rear seats carrying quivers, ornaments, and bundles of slings.
With saddle-cloths made to look like budding sprouts by means of curved golden rods shaped like leafy creepers;
with their steady placement ensured by silk pillows fixed to the binding straps of the saddle-flaps;
and with the sounds of jeweled stones in their foot-guards resonating as they struck against the moving heel-protrusions.
With their shanks covered by soft, well-fitting garments of variegated eyes, and with reddish-brown complexions mottled by saffron-colored cloths;

and with their bodies shining with a fair complexion, adorned with *rājāvarta* and *mecaka* gems whose superior luster was produced by the contrast of their white hue against the smooth, bee-black surfaces of their scales.

[He was accompanied by] attendants wearing *kañcuka* robes and short *cīna* tunics; clad in quilted armor (*vārabāṇa*) adorned with clusters of large pearls; dressed in bodices variegated with various dyes; wearing garments with the luster of parrot feathers; carrying beautiful weapons tucked into the sides of their bodies which had been worn away by physical exercise; followed by servants running to untie the curling locks of their hair as their pearl necklaces swayed and slipped from their throats due to the force of their movement; with the young tails of their peacock-feather ear-ornaments jingling as they struck against golden leaf-sprouts; with the stalks of their ear-lotuses held fast by the bands of their turbans; with their heads covered by soft saffron-dyed upper garments; wearing linen caps inlaid with fragments of crest-jewels; with swarms of bees hovering over their crests as if they were peacock-feather umbrellas; and carrying swift staffs for warding off *śārika* and *śārivā* birds encountered on the road.

In front were [the elephants], whose world-enclosures were filled with fierce and agile warriors leaping about as they adorned themselves with circles of variegated, blood-stained elephant-hide shields and waving fly-whisks;

who made the quarters of the sky resonant with the jingling of golden ornaments on hundreds of charging Kamboja horses; and whose ears were deafened by the sharp sound of hundreds of mercilessly beaten lambā-drums, while their names were being proclaimed aloud.
The palace gate was filled with kings whose commands were being awaited by their attendants standing with faces turned upward;
and when the blessed Maker of Day had risen, the signal conch blew repeatedly, proclaiming the time for the king to enter the assembly hall.

Then, after no long time—as if on his very first expedition for world conquest—he was borne upon a female elephant named Siddhayātrā, who, with the playful swaying of her ears tossed about in her movement, seemed to be bringing about a gathering of the elephants of the quarters.

He was held over him by an auspicious parasol with a formidable staff of beryl, its surface inlaid with pieces of ruby and its color deepening red as if out of indignation at the sight of the rising sun;
he wore a bodice clinging to his limbs, softer than the core of a plantain tree and fashioned as if by the Creator himself, appearing like a second lord of serpents;
and he bore a garment white as a mass of foam from the Ocean of Milk, like the very day of the churning for nectar.

Even as a child, he ascended to the station of Indra like the *pārijāta* tree; fanning the quarters with the pollen from the clusters of flowers in his ear-ornaments— shaken by the wind of the waving yak-tail fans— as if with a powder for subjugating the entire world,
he seemed even to drink up the rising sun with his splendor, its pale-red reflection merging with the crest-jewel upon his head.

With his lip-mark, smeared with thick betel and vermilion, as if bestowing upon other islands the very seal of his passion; with the circles of light from his great pearl necklace shimmering, as if making even the quarters of the sky accept fly-whisks; with his creeper-like brow, gracefully raised at its third part by the glance of the king, as if commanding even the three worlds to pay tribute;
and with his exceedingly long arm-walls, as if desiring to enclose even the seven great ocean-trenches out of a wish to protect them.
He was embraced by Lakṣmī, who had emerged as if having taken up the entirety of the sweetness of the Ocean of Milk;
he was being drunk in deeply, as if composed of nectar, by the thousands of eyes of the citizens of the capital who were upturned with curiosity;

and he seemed to sink into the hearts of the kings, which were moist with affection through the weight of his virtues, while anointing even the very marrow of the spectators with the liquid of his good fortune.
Like the Lord of the Immortals, he was distressed by the desire to wash away the stain of having slain his elder brother;
like Pṛthu, he drove away all the mountain-like kings gathered for the purpose of purifying the earth.

The king went forth, preceded by thousands of torch-bearers acting as forerunners—men who were as swift in their movements as the rays of the sun through their cleverness in office, yet stern in the enforcement of order; who seemed to seize the ten directions themselves, which were obscured by the throngs of people fleeing in fear; who seemed to bring even the wind—which had swallowed the movement of the streets with the falling of its moving palm-flags—under discipline; who seemed to drive away even the rays of the sun, which were being shaken off by the masses of dust raised by their rapid footsteps; and who seemed to cast away even the day itself, which was being dispersed by the light of their golden cane-staffs, as the crowds of men were being cleared away from here and there by these staff-bearers.

And as the circle of kings bowed— their bodies bent in humility, their minds trembling with fear, their heads beautiful with the mass of rays from their crowns of gems and gold loosened by the movement, and the dust of the flower-garlands upon their crests scattered—
the rays of their crest-jewels, emitting light, darted downward, sideways, and upward, moving like flocks of blue jays to bring about a favorable omen.

Making the sky thick with dust that resembled clouds, they were like temple peacocks flying upward; meanwhile, garlands of tender sprouts from the Kalpa-trees were being fastened at the gates of the quarters by the world-protectors. And as he was being saluted, the hero distributed among the princes—each according to his merit—a portion of his own honor through gifts of affection, as if purchasing their lives consisting of pride with these offerings: with side-long glances from the corners of their eyes, with full stares, with arched brows, with half-smiles, with jests, with clever conversation, with inquiries after their welfare, with returns of salutation, with the wild glances of his eyebrows, and with the issuing of commands.
Then, as the king set forth, the exceedingly loud resonance of musical instruments spread here and there across the horizons like the trumpeting of the world-elephants terrified by the clamor;

and from the elephants of the quarters, who were provoked to anger, thousands of streams of ichor flowed like the dark currents of the Yamunā, black as swarms of bees, while the paths of their rutting-fluids mingled with masses of vermilion dust so that the birds, seeing the solar disc turning crimson, suspected it was the hour of sunset.
And as it shook the world of moving and unmoving beings, the multitude of yak-tail whisks (cāmarasaṅghāta) licked the entire universe.
The sky was filled without interval by masses of foam, white as Sindhuvara garlands, discharged from the nostrils of the cavalry horses;

these masses seemed to drink up the day, which—its eight directions lost in their mutual collision—was as pale as clusters of tagara flowers, while the forests of sunshades with their high golden handles appeared to fill the firmament.
Though obscured by the dust of the night, the day shone forth by means of the morning sunlight from the rows of gems upon their crowns;
the quarters of the sky, turned green by the tinkling jeweled ornaments of silver and gold, rendered the horizons deaf with their resonance;
and the elephants sprinkled the circle of the directions with droplets from the heat of their rut, as if to extinguish the fire of their enemies' prowess.

The king, whose eyes were robbed of their power to open by the flashes of the crest-jewels as flickering as lightning, was himself struck with wonder; casting his gaze in every direction, he beheld the royal camp departing from its quarters like the world of living beings emerging from the belly of Vishnu at the beginning of a cosmic age.
"Flow forth, my child! Like the ocean rising from the mouth of the Pot-born Sage (Agastya) and flooding the world,
or like the current of the Narmadā issuing in a thousand streams after being compressed and released by the thousand staff-like arms of Arjuna."
Sir, why do you delay?
Your horse is galloping away.
"My good man,
you move as if with broken legs; why do you drive the camel while these attendants are rushing forward and about to fall upon it?"
O pitiless one, do you not see the child Vatsarāmila lying there, devoid of all feeling?
Stay close by him so that you do not perish in this dust.
Do you not see that the bag of barley-meal is leaking? Why do you hasten so,
O clever woman, abandoning the path of the oxen and running toward the midst of the horses?
O dear one, you enter the path of the elephant desiring to go;
the bag of chickpeas spills sideways, yet you do not heed me as I cry out.
"You are descending into a pit by means of a pit;
sit comfortably, you wanton woman! The jar of sauvīraka has been broken, Mantharaka!"
"You will have a good taste when you have gone; stretch out your ox toward the sugarcane!
Servant, how much longer do you gather jujubes? We must go far."
Why do you flee this very day, O Droṇaka? A very long military expedition awaits us; without Niṣṭhuraka, our path ahead is impassable and full of obstacles.
Sthāvaraka,
since you have not broken the pot of molasses,
a heavy load of *gaṇḍaka* rice will suffice; the ox is now ready for training.
"Servant, quickly cut a mouthful of fodder with the sickle from that bean field;
who knows what has become of the grass for those who have gone there?"
Dhava,
drive back the oxen;
this field is protected by the Vāhīkas.
The cart is hanging down;
Yakṣapālita, yoke the white bull Śākvara, who bears the burden, to the pole.
"You are rubbing your eyes, O woman; why are they swollen?
You wretched elephant-driver!"
You play in the trunk-staff of the elephant in rut;
you stumble in the mire of the crush.
O brother, friend separated from his state, rescue the ox from this mud; come here, young man!

In some places, it was being praised by a circle of bold men—grooms, guards, blockheads, porters, thieves, servants, flatterers, and outcastes—who were shouting "kilakila" with playful clamor, nourished by the remnants of food consisting of abundant crops crushed at their own will; while in other places, there was no path of escape amidst the narrow crush of dense herds of elephants, as they engaged in such various conversations as these.

In some places, there were those who, lacking companions, had acquired miserable villages through the toil of their afflictions; they had formed unions out of the exhaustion and agitation caused by the labor of transporting the meager provisions for their oxen, which were barely maintaining their strength; they themselves had taken up household utensils, saying, "Let this single expedition proceed somehow, let it go to the depths of Pātāla;
may there be well-being for the home of Gṛṣṇabhūti."
"Let him perform service for this camp, which is a heap of all sufferings!"— thus was he being reviled by sons of noble families who were destitute.

In some places, the way was cleared by royal hirelings and porters who were driving everyone before them: men moving with extreme speed as if they had been sewn together or strung in rows by falling into the currents of an exceedingly sharp torrent; carrying heavy clubs upon their dark and thick shoulders, holding golden footstools, couches, bowls, jars, and spittoons; irresistible in their pride of grasping the royal requisites that were near at hand; and bearing the implements of the kitchen. They were accompanied by those carrying the equipment for the great kitchen—those with hogs tied by leather thongs, their hair matted with clusters of hanging deer-flesh and sparrows, clutching young rabbits, vegetable leaves, and tips of cane; those with portions of their faces covered by white rags and sealed with wet clay to protect the vessels of milk; and those carrying a clutter of trays, warming-plates, ladles, copper cooking-pots, cauldrons, and baskets.

In some places, the sons of noble families were being distressed by wicked servants appointed to guide weak oxen that stumbled at every step, while the oxen themselves cried out, "At the time of the harvest, our affliction will be entirely different, for other rakes will come forward!
Elsewhere, the rural folk were running and galloping on both sides out of curiosity to catch a glimpse of the king.

The dust-cloud was raised by those who had emerged from the villages along the road—village headmen and scoundrels with elderly elders leading the way, supporting jars of water; carrying baskets of curd, molasses, sugar-candy, and flowers as offerings; moving forward with haste in wealth-laden carts; fleeing in terror at the sight of enraged and fierce staff-bearers; stumbling, falling, and yet casting their eyes upon the king even from afar; proclaiming the faults of former governors though they were non-existent, recounting hundreds of past officials who had overstepped their bounds, and declaring the offenses of long-standing sycophants.
In some places, the protection of the standing crops—being sought by those from Gauḍa who were pursued by the cavalry of horsemen engaged in a singular pursuit—was being observed;

while others, satisfied by the guards appointed by them, were offering praises, saying, "The King is Dharma incarnate," whereas others, manifesting despair at the crops already harvested, had fled with their entire families out of grief for the fields, their vital breaths nearly severed, their fear dispelled by agony, and had begun to revile the lord of men, crying, "Where is the king? Whence is the king? Or what kind of king is he?"

And with rabbits fleeing here and there, pursued at every step by packs of swift and fierce men with clubs in hand and struck like mountain-balls; with others being devoured all at once by the great crowds that had descended upon them and torn to pieces like sesame seeds; and with those skilled in escaping through the gaps between the legs of many creatures, who, having deceived their riders with deceptive maneuvers, were emerging by the force of life even as they were struck by falling clods of earth, clubs, sticks, axes, stakes, spades, hoes, sickles, and staffs—there arose a tumultuous clamor.

Elsewhere, a cloud of dust was being raised by those running in groups of monks, their hips covered with nets of fodder grey with the dust of chaff, their bits dangling from the edges of old saddle-cloths, their dirty saddle-blankets loosened by worn-out wool fragments, and wearing tattered rags and loose cloaks granted as favors by their lords; in some places, the future conflict with Gauḍa was being devoured by circles of cavalrymen moving in seclusion, while in others, disputing Brahmins were shouting from the tops of trees as they were being driven away by the canes of staff-bearers stationed at the base.
In some places, village dogs were drawn toward the villagers who were being entangled in the snares of the *kuluṇṭhaka* trap;
in other places, it was adorned by the jostling of horses being ridden by princes arrogant in their mutual rivalry for power; thus, through its manifold occurrences, it gave rise to wonder.
It was like the ocean of dissolution set in motion to swallow up the world,
like the netherworld created for the concealment of great serpents,
and like Mount Kailāsa fashioned as a dwelling place for the Supreme Lord.
Beholding the entire succession of living beings as it appeared before him— like a treasury of the four ages for the Lords of Creatures,
and like the practice of austerity which, though fraught with hardship, is the cause of successive blessings—
he proceeded toward the camp while observing it in this manner.
And to those venerable ones standing nearby, he said:
"The paths for world conquest were set in motion by Māndhātṛ; yet by Raghu, with the irresistible speed of his chariot, the quarters of the earth were brought under subjection in a very short time."
With his bow as his only companion, Pāṇḍu’s son Savyasācī, the Pāṇḍava, brought under tribute those kings who were arrogant with the pride of their hereditary strength of arm, lineage,

and wealth; having crossed the territory of Cīna for the sake of the Rājasūya sacrifice, he conquered Mount Hemakūṭa, whose groves resounded with the twanging of the tips of the bows of enraged Gandharvas—
for among the swift, victory is often delayed only by one's resolve.
Though separated by the Himavat and Mahāhimavat mountains, the tree-like Druma—timid at the clash of arms and lacking true form—carried the hand of the Kaurava lord like a servant.

Indeed, the kings of old were not overly ambitious for conquest, since on such a small portion of the earth there existed many monarchs, such as Bhagadatta, Dantavakra, Krātha, Karṇa, the Kaurava, Śiśupāla, Sālva, Jarāsandha, and the King of Sindhu.
King Yudhiṣṭhira was contented, for he tolerated the kingdom of the Kiṃpuruṣas right in his own vicinity, even though it caused the world to tremble from the victory of Dhanañjaya.

The realm of the Turushkas was but a cubit’s length for those full of zeal; the land of the Pārasīkas was but a span, though it was a mere trifle compared to the distance between the Snowy Mountains and Mount Gandhamādana— a distance that the indolent Caṇḍakośa failed to traverse even after conquering the earth and establishing a kingdom ruled by women.
Śakasthāna is like a hare’s footprint;
on Mount Pāriyātra, even an expedition is rendered futile when no counter-attack is visible;
the Deccan is easily won, having valor as its price.

From Mount Dardura—which possesses cave-dwellings made beautiful by the fragrance of sandalwood creepers shaken by the breezes from the waves of the southern ocean—to the nearby Malaya mountain, and even Mahendra which is attached to Malaya;
hearing such conversations from the powerful-armed princes that manifested their resolve, he reached his residence.

At the palace gate, having had the royal assembly respectfully dismissed on both sides with the movement of his creeper-like brows, he entered and sat upon a seat placed in the outer audience hall. He then proceeded further.
Having concluded his discourse, he sat for a moment;
then the doorkeeper, placing his sprout-like palms upon the surface of the earth, announced:
"Your Majesty, a messenger named Haṃsavega, dispatched by the Prince, the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, stands at the inner gateway."
The king, however, respectfully commanded, "Let him be ushered in at once. Then, due to his own skill and the king's favor, the doorkeeper himself went out.

Immediately thereafter, Haṃsavega entered the royal palace with humility; he was beautiful in appearance, bringing delight to the eyes, and possessed a noble majesty that surpassed all others, followed by a great multitude of men carrying abundant gifts.

From afar, with his body embraced by his five limbs [in prostration], he performed a salutation. Called out with great respect, "Come, come!", he ran forward and then withdrew, touching his forehead to the ground at the king's footstool. With the king placing his hand upon his back, he approached and bowed again; then, directed by the king’s affectionate gaze, he took his place in a spot not far away.
Then the king, assuming a slightly stooping posture and dismissing the female fly-whisk bearer standing between them, turned toward him and asked with courtesy, "Haṃsavega,
is the illustrious prince well?
He replied to him, "He is well today, since Your Majesty asks with words bathed in affection, moist with the fluid of friendship, and full of respect."

Having stood there for a moment, he said: "O Lord, who are the vessel for the splendor and enjoyments of the four oceans, it is difficult to find in this world any other gift worthy of you that is filled with true devotion, aside from your own heart. Nevertheless, our master—desiring to ensure that his message was not left empty—has made this ancestral *vāruṇa* umbrella named Ābhoga meaningful by placing it in its proper setting.
And many wonders, which cut through curiosity, are seen in it."
For indeed, every day, for the sake of cooling, one ray of Soma enters this [crystal] from among its thousand rays;

and once it has entered, during the course of meditation, sweet streams of lunar light flow at will from the jeweled rods— acting as teachers who instruct the lute-like teeth— as clear as the waters of the four oceans, which Varuṇa alone, whether past or future, is able to bestow through his shadow, and no other.
And this is not burned by the seven-flamed fire, nor carried away by the swift-flowing waters, nor moistened by water.
Dust does not soil it, nor does old age cause it to decay;
may Your Majesty first favor this with a glance, for he will also listen with confidence to my message.
Having spoken thus, he turned toward his own attendant and said, "Rise and show it to His Majesty.

Immediately upon these words, the man rose and held it aloft; and from its casing made of washed silk, he drew forth that which, as soon as it was being extracted, seemed to laugh impetuously at the exceedingly white radiance [of the moon], as if by Hara.
It was as if the circle of the hood-slates of the serpent Śeṣa had emerged from the netherworld;
it was as if the Milky Ocean had taken its stand in the sky, having become a wheel;
and it was as if an assembly had been formed in the courtyard of the firmament by a mass of autumnal clouds.
It was as if a flock of swans from the celestial chariot of Brahmā had spread their broad wings and come to rest in the sky;
it was like the birth-day of the moon, seen by the people as enchanting with its orb of white radiance emerging from the eye of Atri;
it was as if the very moment of the emergence of the lotus from Nārāyaṇa’s navel had been made manifest before one's eyes.

It was as if the eyes were filled with the satiated joy of beholding the full-moon night of the Kaumudī festival; it was as if a vast expanse of the Mandākinī’s sandy banks had been cast into the belly of the sky;
and it was as if the day had been transformed into a night of the full moon.

The night was slowly broken by pairs of cakravāka birds near the lotus ponds, their minds distressed by the suspicion that the moon had risen, as they parted and dropped the tips of lotus stalks from their opening beaks;
it was turned away from by circles of domestic peacocks who became silent, their cries of *kekā* stilled as they shrank back in fear of a mass of autumn clouds;
and it was awakened by clusters of night-lotuses, white with the loud laughter of their unfolding petals, swelling with the intense joy of the risen moon.
And the king, together with his court, his mind filled with wonder, gazed respectfully at that mark with a gaze that followed its every contour— a mark that was like a tilaka of the three worlds,
like the childhood of the White Island,
and like an incarnation of the autumnal moon.
Like the very heart of Dharma,
like the dwelling place of the lunar world,
and like the face of universal sovereignty, white with the luster of a circle of ivory teeth;
Whitened by its fringe of pearl-strings, it was like the halo of the sky;
with its belly bright with thick moonlight, it was like the lunar halo;
and with its whiteness mocking the beauty of the conch, it was like the motionless ear-tuft of Airāvata.
It was as white as a footprint of Trivikrama in the whirlpool of the White Ganges, worthy of the salutation of the three worlds;
its circumference was formed by rows of fly-whisks made of the fibers of the Mānasa lotus-stalk, appearing as if they were the rays from the crest-jewels of Varuṇa clinging to it;
and its summit was graced by a swan with outspread wings, rendered motionless by the longing to hear the sound of the anklets of the Fortune of the Universal Emperor above.
It shone brilliantly, held as a staff by a touch-sensitive lotus stalk from the Mandākinī that had been paralyzed by his supernatural power— resembling Vāsuki with its hood folded—
and it seemed to wash away the path of the stars with its whiteness,
while covering the day with the vast expanse of its radiance.
In its height, it seemed to dwarf the heavens;
it stood as if presiding over all auspicious things,
like a white pavilion of Śrī.
Like a cluster of blossoms from the cosmic tree,
like the central orb of the moonlight,
