like the pure smile of glory;
Like a mass of foam from the waters of sword-blades,
like a canopy of fame for his possession of valor,
it was a great umbrella, a marvel of the three worlds.
And when that [first gift] had been seen by the king, the officials gradually displayed the remainder of the tribute as follows:

ornaments marked with the royal insignia, which had passed through the hands of famous monarchs beginning with Bhagadatta, and which reddened the quarters of the sky with the rays of their most precious gems.

He saw heaps of crest-jewels that spread their luster, like necklaces that served as the very cause for the whiteness of the Ocean of Milk; he saw silken garments, beautiful with many colors, coiled within cane baskets, radiant as the rays of the autumn moon and fit for purification; and he saw collections of drinking vessels made from pearl-oyster shells, conch shells, coral, and other materials, carved by skilled artisans.

He saw collections of Kārdaraṅga skins, which were protected by covers and possessed the luster of beautiful golden leaf-patterns, with most elegant borders; soft Jātī-ribbons as delicate as birch bark to the touch;
and various products of very fine variegated cloth, such as cushions for the thighs and so forth.
There were cane seats with surfaces as tawny as the blossoms of the *priyaṅgu* plant; books containing elegant sayings, their bindings fashioned from *aguru* bark;

and juicy betel-nut fruits hanging from their sprouts—possessing the hue of ripe, pale-red *paṭola* gourds, the green of young *hārīta* birds, and the whiteness of milk—along with thick bamboo tubes filled with the juice of mango creepers and black aloe-wood oil, their bodies wrapped in sheaths made of the leaves of the *kāpotikā* plant, which are as brown as the temples of an enraged monkey.

He saw heaps of black agallochum, as dark as crushed collyrium, placed in pouches of fine silk thread which dispels great heat; heaps of gośīrṣa sandalwood, cool as clear white fragments of ice-stone; heaps of camphor, bright white and cool; heaps of musk-pouches; heaps of *kakkola* sprouts matted with clusters of ripe fruit; heaps of clove-blossom clusters and *jātī* fruit bunches; jars of *ullaka* perfumes exuding the fragrance of exceedingly sweet honey; and collections of white and black yak-tail whisks.
There were pairs of *kiṃnaras* with necks bound by golden chains, forest-dwelling women (*vanamānuṣīs*), *jīvañjīvakas*, and water-nymphs (*jalamānuṣīs*), who all curiously tore at [the air];
there were musk deer whose fragrance perfumed the quarters,
and yak-cows (*camarīs*) familiar from wandering about the precincts of the house.

He saw parrots, mynas, and other such birds with tongues eloquent in many well-spoken words, confined within cages of cane variegated with liquid gold; he saw chakoras in coral cages; and he saw ivory tusks, curved like earrings, bristling with strings of pearls from the lofty frontal globes of water-elephants.
At the sight of the parasol, the king’s heart was gladdened, and he mentally took note of it as an auspicious omen for his first journey.
And being pleased, he said to Haṃsavega, "My good man,

that the Great Lord obtained this great parasol— which is the abode of all jewels and worthy of being borne upon the head of the Supreme Lord— from the Prince, as if from the great ocean obtaining the friend of the night-lotuses (the moon), is no cause for wonder; for indeed, the childhood learning of the great is their very service."
When the collection of gifts had been removed from that place, Haṃsavega, having stood there for a mere moment,
dismissed the chamberlain with the words, "Rest now.
He himself also rose, bathed, and, desiring auspiciousness, entered the shade of the Ābhoga tree facing the east.

Then, as he entered, a chill born of his shadow was led, as it were, to the status of a crest-jewel; moonstones on his forehead seemed to kiss him, shedding drops of water; camphor dust seemed to dissolve into his pair of eyes; necklaces, made misty by the falling spray of frozen dew-drops, seemed to be bound upon him; a continuous stream of yellow sandalwood juice seemed to fall upon his chest; his heart became as cool as if made of white lotuses; and a melting slab of hidden ice seemed to smear his limbs.
Filled with wonder, he reflected in his mind: "Aside from this one undying friendship, what other gift of gratitude could there be?

And at mealtime, he sent to Haṃsavega a remnant of sandalwood paste smeared upon his body, enclosed in a washed coconut shell wrapped in a white cloth; two garments that had touched his limbs; a waist-band called *pariveśa*, adorned with clusters of pearls as bright as autumn stars; an ear-ornament called *taraṅgaka*, which reddened the day with the light of an exceedingly precious ruby; and a great abundance of various kinds of food.
In this manner, the day passed away by degrees;
then the sun, his body greyed by the thick dust of the army stationed at the camp, descended into the western ocean as if to wash away his soiled limbs,
and departed for the quarter of Varuṇa to announce, as it were, the news of the gift of the royal parasol.

At the very outset, the earth with its continents appeared like one who had folded her hands in service before the king, as all the groves of lotuses were closing their buds; the twilight glow seized the world as if it were a respectful salutation with joined palms from the entire realm of living beings, consisting of devotion for the monarch;
and the eastern quarter turned dark, as if apprehensive of some offense committed by the Gaudas.
The earth spread a blackness as if from the mass of accumulated darkness, like the heap of ashes from the fire of the majesty of other kings who had been extinguished;
the quarters of the sky scattered a dense cluster of stars, beautiful with blooming *tagara* flowers, as if from a bouquet of blossoms offered at the evening court of the lord of the earth;
and in the sky shone the dust, pale as the ichor of Airāvata, which had rushed forth along its path, drawn by the fragrance of the rut of the scent-elephants descending upon his shoulders.

The lover of Rohiṇī ascended the vault of the sky, abandoning the western quarter as if it were assailed by a provoked tiger-king; the moonbeams, piercing the hearts of proud women like news of his departure, spread through the ten directions;
and the lords of the rivers, their inner natures agitated as if terrified by the expedition of a new king, became turbulent.

Thought alone entered the hearts of the kings, just as a mass of darkness enters the hollows of mountain caves; and sleep vanished from the eyes of the rival vassals like the night-blooming lily groves when the continuity of darkness has departed.
At this hour, the king, reclining beneath the expanse of a wide canopy, dismissed his attendants with the words "Wait a moment," and commanded Haṃsavega, "Tell me your message."
Having prostrated, he began to speak:
"O Lord, in former times, the Blessed Earth, having conceived through contact with the Great Boar, gave birth in the netherworld (rasātala) to a son named Naraka;
even in his childhood, the crest-jewels of the world-protectors became devoted to bowing at his feet."

And he, whose arm was exultant in wielding power over the three worlds, was such that even when the sun was glared upon by the curved side-long glances of the female cakravāka birds in the lotus-pools of his palaces, it did not proceed to its setting without his command, its chariot turning back in crimson fear;
and he, who took away this parasol—the outward manifestation of his royal status—while keeping the true heart within.

In the lineage of that great-souled one, after many great kings as lofty as Mount Meru—beginning with Bhagadatta, Puṣpadatta, Vajradatta, and others—had passed away, there was born a great emperor named Susthiravarman, the great-grandson of Mahārāja Bhūtivarman, the grandson of Candramukhavarman, and the son of His Majesty Sthitivarman, who was as steadfast as Mount Kailāsa. He was a mass of splendor whom the people called "Mṛgāṅka" (the Moon), and he was born together with self-confidence, as if with an elder brother.
And he who, even as a boy, out of affection caused the twice-born to accept all manner of gifts and out of enmity the enemies;

and in whom there existed that supreme sweetness of Fortune born from the ocean— which is exceedingly difficult to obtain— and likewise, who seized the conch-shells of the lords of armies, but not their jewels.
He took from the earth its stability but not its tax, and he assumed the dignity of the mountains but not their harshness.

To that king of auspicious name, by his queen Śyāmādevī, was born a son named Bhāskaradyuti— who also bore the secondary name Bhāskaravarman— just as the prince Bhīṣma was born to Śantanu by Bhāgīrathī.
From his childhood, he has held this firm resolve: "Apart from the two lotus-feet of the Lord, I shall not bow to any other.

Such a desire, difficult to attain even in the three worlds, can be fulfilled by only one of three things: by the conquest of the entire world, by death, or by friendship with a friend who is a peerless hero on earth, like a god himself, and whose fierce majesty causes the very quarters of the sky to burn. Furthermore, for kings, friendship generally depends upon some purpose to be served.

And what kind of body could it possibly be that, when presented, would enter into friendship with Your Majesty? For indeed, while Your Majesty is desiring to gather your glories, wealth is but an external limb;
and since you are seated upon your arm alone, there is no room for even the other limbs to offer assistance, let alone for an outsider.
What satisfaction could there be even in the proposal of giving a mere portion of the earth to one who devours entire villages and the four oceans?
Even the enticement of bestowing a beautiful maiden is utterly ineffective for one whose gaze is spoiled by the sight of the lotus-face of Fortune.
Thus, since every possible means has failed to achieve this object, let Your Majesty listen as I submit nothing more than a simple request.
For Prāgjyotiṣeśvara was indeed like Deva Ekapiṅga with Anaṅgadviṣ,
like Daśaratha with Gotrabhid, and like Dhanañjaya with Puṣkarākṣa.
Like Vaikartana with Duryodhana, or like the Malaya breeze with Mādhava,
he desires an unaging association.

And if Your Majesty’s heart is inclined toward friendship and you recognize that friends perform service through various means, then why do you sit idle? Let it be commanded! Let the Lord of Kāmarūpa enjoy a firm embrace from the Fortune of Prāgjyotiṣa—whose jeweled bracelets jingle against the fragments of gem-stones on her armlets as they clash with the points of his massive jeweled armlets, like Mount Mandara against Viṣṇu—and let her long at last caress his eyes with this moon-like face, which is a continuous, pure stream of the nectar of beauty and grace.
"If Your Majesty does not accept this request, what am I to say to my lord?

When he had thus ceased speaking, the king—already filled with great respect for the prince due to his previously known virtues, and now having that affection elevated to its highest pitch by the mention of the *ābhoga* umbrella—spoke respectfully as if feeling somewhat abashed: "Haṃsavega,..."

How could the mind of one such as I ever turn otherwise toward such a great soul, of noble lineage, a mass of merit, the foremost among the virtuous, and a friend even in his absence? For even the rays of the sun, though capable of scorching the entire world, become cool when they fall upon a lotus-pond that brings joy to the eyes of the three worlds;
and what am I, bought by a multitude of excellent qualities, to friendship?
The ten directions became the handmaidens of the sweetness of the virtuous;
for the sake of the night-lotus, whose resemblance was produced by its nature being exclusively pure and upward-turned, who has ever spoken of the cool-rayed moon as superior?
And such was the auspicious resolve of the prince.
He himself is mighty-armed, and he has taken up his bow against me; whom else but Hara, my friend, would he honor?
My affection has been increased by this resolve;
for even toward a haughty beast such as a lion, the heart feels great respect, how much more so toward a friend?
"Therefore, you must strive in such a way that this longing to see the prince does not distress us for long.
But Haṃsavega replied, "Your Majesty,
what else could possibly distress a noble person now, other than what Your Majesty has said?"
For the virtuous are indeed devoted to service;
even among them, let alone our own master’s lineage, there is this Vaishnava clan, which is characterized by pride in its own wealth.

Let Your Majesty observe the condition of a man who is being drawn toward service by extreme old age or misfortune, as if by a wicked woman; who is being impelled by greed or discontent, as if by a dissatisfied wife;
and who is being agitated by various desires born of youth or by improper intentions, as if by ill-behaved children.
He saw himself as one who, like an old maiden, was fit only for a supreme search; or as one entering a state of extreme great age;
or as one being assailed by an attack from all the planets, which were ill-situated in his own house like wicked kinsmen;
or as one being pursued by past actions, which were as filthy and difficult to abandon as long-standing servants.
Like a sinner entering a royal palace, which causes the entire body to burn like a fire of dried cow-dung;
like one whose power of all the senses is impaired by a mere false desire to seize the multitude of objects within the heart;
and like a garland of fresh sprouts withered at the very first upon the archway, being blocked by the door-keepers.
As he entered the gate, he was oppressed like a deer being struck by others;
he was repeatedly repelled by the blows of the hands of the circle of doorkeepers, like the trunk-skin of an elephant being pushed back;
and, out of longing for wealth, he bent his face downward like a sprout from a treasure-tree.
He felt distress at the arrow that, though far away, had been discharged from an exceedingly remote distance;
at it that, though lacking a barb, was being violently drawn and cast away as it struck his foot;
and at it that, though not the god of love, was meeting its destruction, consumed by the gaze of the Lord enraged by its untimely approach.
Like a monkey, his facial color remained unchanged even when rebuked with anger;
like a slayer of a Brahmin, his skull was rubbed clean by daily prostrations; and though devoid of touch, he performed inauspicious deeds.
Like Triśaṅku, fallen from both worlds, he remained with his head cast down day and night;
like a horse, he made himself easy to lead by means of the morsel of fodder;
and like one lying in a fast, he wasted his body while fixing his hope for life within his heart.
Like a dog, he turned his back on his own wife and wasted his body while maintaining his life in a base manner;
like a ghost, he received morsels of food offered upon unsuitable ground; and like a crow, he lived out his allotted lifespan in vain, consuming the splendor of men through the greed of his tongue.
He approached the king’s favorites, who were like trees in a cremation ground turned into human forms by the burnt ashes of a *piśāca*;
he was being deluded like a child by the chatter of royal parrots, whose sweetness was produced by their inverted tongues and whose passion was revealed only through their beaks;
and like a *vetāla* possessed by the power of a monarch, he performed no action whatsoever.
Like a painted bow, he was constantly bent by the sole act of superimposing false virtues; like a heap of refuse, his splendor was extinguished and he bore the dust gathered by the broom;
and like one afflicted with phlegm, he was daily provoked by pungent things.
Like a follower of the Sugata who, having conceived a distaste for existence through the realization that consciousness is empty of external objects, longs for the saffron robes;
like one who, even at night, is being tossed in all directions like an offering-ball to the Mothers;
and like one fallen into impurity, whose course of suffering is intensified by lying upon a bed of kusha grass.
Like a balance scale that has been weighted down at the back and thus bends even for the sake of water; like one abandoned by shame as if terrified by the merciless lashes of a cane-bearer's whip;
and like one forsaken by self-importance as if it had lost its place within a heart shriveled by wretchedness.
Of that fool who, like one enraged by the acceptance of despicable deeds, is bereft of all loftiness;
who acquires afflictions through faith in wealth;
and who, with the notion of his own advancement, increases his own humiliation.
Even though there was a forest fragrant with the scent of various flowers, he offered his cupped hands in thirst;
though he was a son of noble family, he approached him with extreme trepidation like a criminal;
and though he was handsome, his birth was as fruitless as that of a flower in a painting.
Though learned, he was like a fool whose mouth utters only corrupt words;
though capable, he was like a leper with both hands shriveled up;
and in matters of equal merit, he was as if being cooked without fire.
For one who is dying breathless amidst the leveling of the lowly,
treated as a mere blade of grass by insults,
and finds no relief from the wind of suffering;
Though blazing, he is devoid of devotion; though devoid of heat, he causes his kinsmen to suffer; though possessing no vehicle, he is unable to move;
and though fallen from dignity, he descends below.
Even though he was devoid of any virtuous essence, he sold "great meat" (human flesh);

even though he was free from pride, his conduct was that of one lacking self-control; even though he was not a yogin, he had brought his soul under the sway of meditation; yet, rising from his bed, he would prostrate himself like a shaven-headed monk who defiles his lineage, dancing day and night and making men of spirit laugh, a charcoal of a family burning his own kin.
What atonement can there be for this beast of a man who, upon obtaining even a blade of grass, bends his neck;
for this lump of flesh born solely for the purpose of filling a belly, the disease of the womb;
for this hireling who performs deeds of demerit?
What is the practice to be performed? Where must one go for peace?
What is the nature of life?
What is this pride of manhood? What indeed are these diversions? Of what sort is this craving for enjoyment?

The dreadful word "slave" drags everything down like thick mud; fie on that breath, let that wealth go to its destruction, and let there be no more birth for that prosperity! Homage to those blessed pleasures; here is my joined palms to that sovereignty—let that Goddess Śrī stay far away! May he, along with his retinue, bring auspiciousness, for his head shall go to the earth as it deserves: a eunuch devoted to the pleasure of his own mouth, a worm made of putrid flesh, uncountable as a hell, a walking footstool with his head greyed by the dust of others' feet.
The male cuckoo excels in its plaintive warbling; the peacock in its joyous cries;
and the large tortoise in its rubbing against the earth.
A dog in the practice of lowly flattery,
a flute in its modulations,
and the body of a courtesan in the pain of assuming contorted postures.
He was like straw among beings who are like rice-grains; he was like a chameleon among those who mock others; he was like a hedgehog among those who shrink from themselves.
He was a foot-massager for massaging the feet, a ball for striking with the palms of the hands,
and a neck-staff of a lute for striking with the plectrum.

"Even a wretched servant among mortals, or even a common earthworm, is better than a serpent; even a single grain of broken rice is better than a stalk of fine *kalama* rice. For a man of spirit, a moment of human dignity is preferable to the enjoyment of sovereignty over the three worlds for one who bows down.

Therefore, let Your Majesty take to heart that the Lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, having honored our request, will arrive as if in just a few days. Having said this, he became silent and soon departed after offering his salutations.
The King, too, spent that night with his heart captivated by the longing to see the prince.

For the great, the surrender of one's self is a spell of subjugation that requires no root-mantra; and at dawn, having bestowed a magnificent return-gift entrusted to his chief envoy, he dispatched Haṃsavega, while he himself,
from that moment on, set out toward the enemy with incessant marches.

Once, however, he heard from a messenger that Bhaṇḍi had arrived and was encamped nearby, having brought with him the entire military force of the Mālava king acquired through the strength of Rājyavardhana’s arm;

and upon hearing this, the fire of grief for his brother flared up anew within him, and his heart became faint. He entered, as it were, into the darkness of a swoon and remained for a moment in his own palace—having abandoned all activities, with his attendants silenced and stilled by the warding off of the doorkeeper—awaiting his arrival along with the royal retinue.

Then Bhaṇḍi, mounted on a single horse and surrounded by a few young men of noble family, appeared clad in soiled garments; he manifested his grief through a heart filled with the shafts of his enemies—seemingly protected from bursting by the many iron pins driven into it—and through a beard clinging to his chest as if out of respect for his master;
his sole remaining ornament was a lucky bracelet swinging on an arm-staff rendered flaccid by the cessation of physical exercise.
With his lower lip drying up—driven out by the force of long sighs like a charcoal from a heart being consumed by the fire of grief, its color faded by the betel-leaf used without respect;
with his face veiled as if by a cloth of tears, as though out of shame for the offense of remaining alive despite the separation from his master;
and entering, as it were, his own body with limbs that had grown weak through modesty.
As if vomiting, he rendered the heat of his arms useless through long-drawn sighs;
like a sinner, like an offender.
Like one who has been betrayed, like one who has been robbed, like one who has been deceived.
Like the elephant Vegadaṇḍa dejected at the fall of its herd-leader,
like a lotus pond bereft of beauty at the setting of the sun,
like the son of Droṇa distressed by the death of Duryodhana;
Like an ocean whose jewels have been stolen, he arrived at the palace gate;
dismounting from his horse, he entered the royal residence with downcast face and,
letting out a cry from afar, fell at the king's feet.
The lord of the earth, upon seeing him, rose and went forward with faltering steps; having raised him up and embraced him firmly by the neck, he wept piteously for a very long time.
When the force of his grief had subsided, he returned as before and sat down upon his own seat.
And when Bhaṇḍi had first washed his face, the king washed his own face.
When some time had passed, he inquired about the news of his brother's death;
then Bhaṇḍi related the entire account exactly as it had occurred.
Thereupon, the king said to him, "As for the matter of the royal fortune..."

"What? he asked again. "Your Majesty," he replied, "I have heard from the people that since Your Majesty Rājyavardhana attained divinity and Guptanāman was captured, Queen Rājyaśrī has escaped from her confinement and entered the Vindhya forest with her attendants at Kuśasthala."
"However, numerous people sent as searchers for her have not yet returned.
Upon hearing this, the king said, "What is the use of other trackers? Abandoning all other duties, I myself will go wherever she is;
you too should set out toward Gauḍa, taking the army with you."
Having spoken thus, he rose and went to the bathing grounds.

There, he took his meal together with Bhaṇḍi—the chief chamberlain, who had had the shaving of his grief-induced beard performed, who had bathed in the palace of the great warder, and who had manifested his favor by sending him bodily garments, flowers, unguents, and ornaments—and spent the day with him.

Then, on the following morning at dawn, Bhaṇḍi approached the king and informed him: "Let Your Majesty behold the army and its full equipment belonging to the King of Mālava, acquired through the strength of the arm of the illustrious Rājyavardhana."
Permitted by the king with the words, "Let it be so done," he displayed [the following]:

elephants numbering many thousands, like moving boulders with temples muddy from the frontal lobes matted with swarms of bees noisy with the fragrance of ichor flowing incessantly; like clouds descended to earth with deep thundering roars; like autumn days gathered into a mass, exuding the scent of forests of full-blown *saptacchada* trees;
and horses with the speed of deer, enchanting with circles of beautiful yak-tail whisks adorned with fine gold.
She beheld various ornaments that, emitting a flood of morning sunlight, turned the ten directions into many rainbows;

she saw necklaces that caused wonder, which were as delicate as the fragrance from the breasts of Mālava women maddened by love, and which, though flooding the horizons with their own streams of moonlight, were yet like stars; and she saw fly-whisks as pure as the mass of rays from the moon’s feet, appearing like her own glories.
A white parasol, its golden handle like a white lotus—the very garment of Fortune;
courtesans who had descended as if out of passion for the daring delights of many battles, resembling celestial nymphs;
and royal insignia such as thrones, couches, and stools.

Having observed the entire assembly of Mālava kings with their pairs of feet rendered motionless by iron shackles, as well as all the treasure-jars complete with their inventories and inscribed tablets and adorned with decorative crests,
the king commanded his officials to take possession of it all according to their respective jurisdictions. Then,
on another day, he set out with his horses to search for his sister and reached the Vindhya forest after only a few marches.
Then, as he was entering, even from afar, he saw the area filled with the grey smoke of forest-grain seed-vessels whose fires were spreading through the heaps of burning sixty-day-old chaff;
it was further marked by *vaṭas* (enclosures) surrounded by fences of cow-hides constructed from piles of dry branches,
and by tiger-traps fashioned from the dung of slaughtered calf-imitations.

The region was being illuminated by forest tracts where the axes of wood-gatherers from neighboring villages were being forcibly carried away by unrestrained forest guards, and where pavilions for the goddess Cāmuṇḍā had been constructed within dense groves of trees;

it was further characterized by small plots of paddy fields on elevated ground, which were being broken up by the loud shouts of farmers who, anxious to support their families due to the wilderness-like nature of the borders, practiced agriculture primarily with hand-hoes and were deprived of oxen.

With fields of very limited space, as hard as black clay or iron ore, where thick sprouts rose from stumps planted here and there; with dark, difficult-to-traverse growths abounding in *alambusa* creepers and never-departing *kokilākṣa* shrubs; with scattered rice-paddies being ploughed with great difficulty, their soil not yet fully broken by frequent coming and going; and with high platforms erected near the fields indicating the harassment caused by wild beasts.
In every direction, the shadows were marked by the fresh sprouts of roadside trees, grey with the dust from the travelers’ foot-stroking;

near the edges of newly dug wells adorned with clusters of *sāla* flowers common to the forest stood clearly visible stone images of serpents; there were huts constructed from seamless bamboo mats, resting upon rows of shallow bowls filled with parched grain and entwined by the curly antennae of insects; the ground nearby was strewn with the seeds of *jambu* fruits chewed by wayfarers, while the air vibrated with the thrill of swarms of *kadamba* bees rising on clouds of pollen.
Their thirst was quenched by wooden stools whose legs were gripped by bristling water-jars;

their fatigue was relieved by pitchers cooled by the cool sands of the moist ground; the chill of the water in their jars was intensified by the dark moss upon them and by the fragments of pale-pink sugar-candy drawn from the water-jars that made the quarters of the sky cool;
and they carried baskets of *pāṭala* flowers fastened to the mouths of their jars as garlands.

In some places, he seemed to cause the summer heat to be abandoned through the coolness of forest-entry water-stations (*prapā*), where the waters were being drunk by long lines of resting pilgrims; these stations had their sacrificial posts (*sthāṇu*) thick with clusters of fresh mango fruits—juicy yet drying—that were being tended by rows of flower-bunches whose sprouts bristled with spray. Elsewhere, he seemed to transfer that heat to the wood-gatherers who were burning the timber for making armlets, while the artisans (*vyokāra*) were busy collecting it.

And on all sides, there was a multitude of forest-dwelling householders from neighboring villages entering the woods for the purpose of gathering firewood; they carried provisions protected by elders stationed in nearby hamlets, their limbs were anointed with oil after strenuous labor with heavy timber, and upon their shoulders rested sturdy axes from which hung pouches of morning food; they wore rags as protection against the danger of thieves, their necks were bound with triple coils of black cane creepers twisted into nooses, their mouths were covered with leaf-wrappings, and they carried water in yellow skins; they led pairs of bullocks that were lowing in front of them.

It was filled with hunters roaming about outside, who had set up many traps, snares, and nets made of leather and woven from the sinews of deer; it was crowded with fowlers moving about carrying cages of captured birds such as partridges, francolins, and pigeons, with their bird-lime bags hanging from their shoulders and their whistles held in their hands; and it was thronged by groups of young snare-setters wandering about, greedy for the twigs and creepers smeared with the remnants of bird-lime.
Young hunters were sporting in bird-hunting, their dogs wagging their tails and cooing as they chased partridges hidden among clumps of grass;
there were bundles of *śīdhavya* bark-garments possessing the astringent hue of the throats of mature ruddy geese,
countless sacks of *dhātaki* flowers whose luster was like mineral pigments and which had not long been gathered, and abundant supplies of cottony *atasī* fibers and *paṭṭamūlaka* roots.

The horizon was filled with people carrying loads of honey from *mākṣika* bees, loads of beeswax that had not been processed into discs, loads of hanging tufts of *lāmajjaka* grass, barkless *khadira* wood, saffron, and abundant loads of *rodhra*—brown as the thick mane of a lion—with the villagers hastening along toward their nearby villages, their heads laden with baskets filled with various forest fruits gathered for sale, and their minds preoccupied with thoughts of trade.

And here and there, the land was being brought to the state of a poor, parched field through the arrival of long lines of carts—carts driven by yoked heroes, humpbacks, and laborers who scattered the dust of ancient times over heaps of dried dung; carts whose drivers were urged on with harsh voices, their faces grey with the dust upon the poles, and which produced the creaking of their restless wheels as they moved along.

Its vicinity was darkened by numerous sugarcane groves whose fences of tall bamboo were easily leaped over by deer that flew up at the mere stroke of a stick hurled by guards; and these groves had their lofty shoots snapped by hares, who were startled by the sight of white skeletons of deer driven into the ground, while their wide-spreading branches had been carefully nurtured with effort.

[The region was] surrounded by groves of *snuhā* plants as smooth as emeralds, separated by vast distances; crowded with thickets of bamboo suitable for making bows; difficult to enter due to rows of thorny *karañja* trees; and filled with garden-enclosures dense with clusters of castor-oil plants, *vacā*, *avaṅgaka*, *surasa*, *sūraṇa*, *śigru*, *granthiparṇa*, *gavedhukā*, and *garmut* beans.
Shadows were provided there by the spreading vines of *kāṣṭhāluka* creepers fixed upon high wooden posts driven into the ground;
and calves were tied to khadira-wood stakes driven into the floor of circular jujube-berry arbors.

In some way or another, [the place was characterized] by courtyards whose layouts were inferred from the crowing of cocks; by pits for quickly prepared bird-cakes fashioned at the base of plantain pillars; by scattered clusters of pale-red jujube fruits;
by walls constructed from fences made of bamboo-sheaths, dalana-grass, reeds, and *śara* grass;
and by circles and pavilions drawn with *kiṃśuka* flowers and yellow pigment, where charcoal was bound together with *balvaja* grass.
Abounding in heaps of *śālmalī* fruit-cotton, with stores of reeds, rice, lotus roots, pieces of lily seeds, bamboo, and grain, and having gathered seeds of the *māla* plant;

He beheld a forest village, filled with houses belonging to forest-dwellers that bore heaps of *kāśmarya* fruits soiled and withered by ashes, with mats spread out, abundant with dried *rājādana* and *madana* fruits, and mostly consisting of *madhūka* liquor and wine; it was provided with jars of safflower, pots, and granaries never lacking seeds of kidney beans, cucumbers, water-melons, pumpkins, and gourds; and it contained wild cats, mongooses, *māludhāna* snakes, *nakula* mongooses, *śālija* and *jātaka* birds, and other creatures being nurtured there—and he stayed right there.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Acquisition of the Umbrella," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the eighth chapter of the *Harṣacarita*: "By one who suddenly accomplishes the objects sought after by his heart's desire."
Even by fate is performed for the fortunate, like a prior service rendered.
Association with learned people and the joy of seeing lost beloved kinsmen.
To whom would the acquisition of great jewels not lead to happiness in their dwelling?
Then, rising on the following day, the king departed from that village and entered the Vindhya forest;
he roamed through it here and there for many days.

One day, as the monarch was wandering, the son of the forest-dwelling chieftain Śārabhaketu, named Vyāghraketu, appeared from somewhere—his head bound high with a wreath of *śyāmalatā* creepers dark as collyrium encircling his forehead.
He was perpetually bearing upon the surface of his forehead—a region that accompanied his rashness and which, with its three-pronged frown born of no cause, cast darkness like the night;
he was graced by an ear adorned with a glass-gem earring whose light turned it greenish-yellow, like the luster of a single parrot feather tucked behind it;
and from his slightly squinting eye, with its sparse lashes, there flowed a natural radiance of passion as if it were the blood of a hyena extracted by the application of elixir.
With a sunken nose, a flattened lower lip, and a protruding chin.
With his jawbones prominent due to his full cheeks and his neck slightly bent forward,

with the upper half of his shoulders sloping, he seemed to mock the vastness of the Vindhya mountains’ rocky slopes with his muscular chest, which had been expanded by the strenuous exercise of incessantly drawing his bow into a circle.
With his pair of arms, more powerful than the python, he was diminishing the length of the *śāla* trees on the snowy mountain;
on his forearm, which was made matted by small tufts of *nāgadamanī* creepers fastened with the hair of young boars, he wore a tin bracelet variegated with *godanta* gems;
though not pot-bellied, he appeared to be so.

His broad and formidable waist was made terrifying by a sword whose hilt was encased in a sheath fashioned from the skin of a beautiful snake, its scabbard variegated with the skins of various leopards and covered in a network of crooked antelope hides; the blade’s tip was bright and polished with a trace of quicksilver.
He possessed two massive thigh-staffs that seemed filled with flesh that had fallen away as his waist was being carved away by the onset of early youth.

He displayed a leanness that seemed to sprout forth from the weight of his quiver on his back—a quiver made of the skins of bears, filled with numerous arrows mostly of the *bhalla* type, bound with straps of variegated tiger-skin, and possessing wool as black as a swarm of bees.

He bore upon his left shoulder a bow made of heavy *khadira* wood, its tip adorned with the beautiful crest of a blue jay from the northern regions, its string fashioned from a tendril of *kharaprāṇa* thorns, and its surface decorated with leaf-patterns drawn in abundant peacock bile; and he displayed, as if a handful of pigments for the hunt, a rabbit with its head hanging down, its hind leg inserted through a hole made by a sharp arrow so as to form a *svastika* knot, its nostrils stained with streaks of blood as red as the *bandhūka* flower, the whiteness of its soft breast-fur clearly visible across its broad body, its neck tied to the tip of a sharp hunting-spear; and a partridge with its beak open and its copper-colored palate turned upward toward the bow.
With his face defiled by foul poison and his tip of the right hand occupied by Vikarṇa— who was like a black snake seized by the tail—
he appeared like a moving tamāla tree on a mountain slope,
or like a pillar of solid stone being whirled about by a machine.
Moving like a fragment of collyrium stone being split,
flowing like the very essence of iron melting from Mount Vindhya,
it was a pestilence for the herds of elephants.
The noose of Death for herds of deer,
the comet for the circles of lions,
and the Great Ninth Festival for the throngs of buffaloes.
Like the very heart of violence,
like the fruit of sin,
and like the cause of the Kali age.
Taking with him a young Śabara who resembled the lover of the Night of Doom, he arrived and,
having stationed him at a distance, made this representation: "O King," he said.
The master of this entire Vindhya range, the foremost among all the lords of the forest hamlets, is the Śabara army commander named Bhrūkampa.
This man, his sister's son named Nirghāta, is familiar even with the leaves of this whole Vindhya wilderness, let alone its regions;
let Your Majesty question him, for he is fit to carry out your command.

When this had been said, Nighāta, with his head bowed to the surface of the earth, performed a prostration and presented a partridge along with a hare as a gift. The lord of the earth, honoring him, personally questioned him: "My dear friend, are you well-acquainted with this entire region?"

"During these days, while you are habituated to staying in your quarters, some noble lady belonging to the commander-in-chief or one of his dependents may come within the range of your sight. But Nirghāta, esteeming himself highly due to the favor of the king’s address, bowed and made this request with great deference: "Your Majesty, even female deer generally do not roam about here unobserved; how much less women? And surely no woman of such a form exists, much less one who is defenseless."
Nevertheless, by the command of His Majesty, an effort is now being made every day toward his search with undivided attention;

for at a distance of only half a *gavyūti* from here, in a great grove of trees growing at the foot of a mountain range revered by sages, there dwells a mendicant named Divākaramitra, a follower of Pārāśarya, surrounded by many disciples, who lives by the mountain river—if he might find some news of him.

Having heard this, the king reflected: "It is indeed reported that the venerable Grahavarman—whose name is auspiciously invoked—having passed away, had a childhood friend who was a learned follower of the Maitrāyaṇīya school; having abandoned the three Vedas, that Brahmin’s son, possessing realized meditative concentration in the Buddhist doctrine, donned the saffron robes even while still young.
And generally, even a friend, when seen, produces great consolation in people;
for virtues are desirable to everyone."
"To whom would the state of being a sage not be worthy of respect?
The Blessed One, the mistress of Dharma, inspires reverence even in a simpleton; how much more so in a learned person who steals the hearts of all men?

Therefore, our hearts have long been curious regarding a sight of him. This most auspicious opportunity has presented itself incidentally; we shall behold this person whose audience was sought with such great effort."
And he said aloud, "Friend, point out that place; there dwells that mendicant.
Having spoken thus, he set out to go, with the path being shown by that very man.
Then, as he proceeded by degrees, there appeared for him, who was free from all impediments,
*karṇikāra* trees in bud and abundant *campaka* trees.
Abounding in trees bearing abundant fruit, with *nameru* trees weighed down by the burden of their harvest, and clusters of *nalada*, *nārikela*, and trees with dark green leaves.
The surroundings were filled with *harikeśara* and *sarala* trees;
rows of *kurubaka* trees were bristling with the hair-like buds of their clusters;
and the ten directions were being smeared with the loveliness of the tender shoots of red *aśoka* trees.
The days were turned grey by the spreading pollen from fully blossomed filaments;
the surfaces of the tilaka trees were strewn with their own pollen-dust;
and the hiṅgu plants were swaying.
Abounding in betel nuts,
with priyaṅgu trees tawny with clusters of blossoms,
and producing joy among the people through the sweet humming of bees gathered in swarms upon flower-clusters turned golden by pollen;
Where the itching of the temples of elephants was being relieved without hesitation by the trunks of *mucukunda* trees whose trunks were darkened by the bees intoxicated with honey;
where the ground was made beautiful by lawns entirely covered by the young of black antelopes, leaping about fearlessly and restlessly;
and where the sunlight was obscured by rows of *tamāla* trees as dark as the time of universal dissolution.
The *devadāru* trees were bristling with clusters of blossoms;
the rows of *jambu* and *jambīra* trees were overspread by a network of swaying betel-vines;
and the skies were kissed by circles of *dhūlīkadamba* flowers, white with the pollen of their blossoms.
The ground was sprinkled with thick drops of honey;
the sense of smell was satisfied by the gathered fragrances; and the hollows of the *kuṭaja* trees were turned into nests by hen-sparrows that had recently laid their eggs.
Where the chatter of young sparrows was rendered sweet by the movements of the female birds;
where the beaks of cakora birds were eager for the wandering of their mates;
and where the ripe, tawny pīlu fruits were being fearlessly devoured by numerous bhuruṇḍa birds.

Where the young fruits were stripped from the *sadāphala* and *kaṭaphala* trees by parrots and other birds that had plucked them free of their husks; where young fawns lay comfortably on stone slabs as tender as *śaileya* grass; and where multitudes of monitor lizards rolled about with full confidence within the hollows of the roots of *śephālikā* shrubs.
Free from the terrors of predators, where families of mongooses sport without agitation, and where the emergence of flower buds is swallowed by flocks of sweet-voiced cuckoos;

Where herds of young camūra deer were chewing the cud in mango groves; where flocks of blue waterfowl sat at their ease; and where cow-elephants, suckling their calves, were watched by ruddy cows that remained motionless even as they observed them.
The drum-like flapping of the ears of herds of elephants was lulled into slumber by the sound of waterfalls cascading from the mountain slopes nearby;

the roar of the ruru deer was equaled by the sweet strains of songs from nearby kinnarīs; and the snouts of young boars were stained with the bright yellow juice of turmeric rubbed upon them by the exceedingly joyful hyenas.
Where mongooses were howling in the thickets of *guñjā* shrubs; where bracelets of *jātīphala* nuts had fallen asleep upon the *śālija* trees;
and where swarms of young monkeys, enraged by their teeth, had torn open the cocoons of *pāṭala*-colored moths.
The *lavalī* creepers were being scaled by langurs greedy for *lakucha* fruit;
circles of sand-water basins had been constructed; and the currents of mountain streams were diverted by the force of rows of crooked water-wheels.
With water-pots hanging from their thick branches and trunks, with vine-arbors made lush by empty alms-bowls suspended from cords and loops,
and with images of the Pāṭala-mudrā Caitya fashioned upon nearby huts;
Their regions were defiled by water turbid with the dye of saffron-colored robes;
they were like masses of clouds, filled with the clamor of flocks of peacocks;
and they were like the Vedas, dense with the manifold divisions of countless branches.
With bodies as dark blue as great sapphires, they were as if made of rubies; robbing the eyes of all people, they were as if composed of darkness;
with their great trunks raised aloft, they were like the Yamunā rivers.
Dark as emerald jewels, like the pleasure-mountains of spring,
appearing like mountains of collyrium covered in sprouts,
they were like sons born of the Vindhya forest.
Like masses of darkness from the netherworld having burst through the earth and risen up,
like the re-entries of the rainy days,
and like partial incarnations of the dark nights.
Like palaces made of sapphire belonging to the forest deities,
the trees descended into the path of his vision before him;
thereupon, it occurred to the king’s mind that the Venerable One must surely be not far away.

Having descended to the mountain river and performed his ablutions, he stationed his cavalry force in that very spot—the forest depths of which were deafened by the simultaneous neighing of the horses released for their moment of rest. Then, assuming the modesty appropriate for an audience with ascetics, and supported by Mādhavagupta on his right arm, he proceeded on foot to travel, followed only by a few kings at a distance, while his heart was fixed on the right hand.

Then, amidst those trees, it was announced from afar by various people—Vītarāgas, Ārhatas, Maskarins, Śvetapaṭas, Pāṇḍurabhikṣus, Bhāgavatas, Varnins, Keśaluñchanas, Kāpilas, Lokāyatikas, Kāṇādas, Aupaniṣadas, Aiśvarakāraṇikas, Kāraṇḍhamas, Dharmaśāstrins, Paurāṇikas, Sāptatantavas, Śaivas, Śābdas, Pāñcarātrikas, and others—who, having come from various regions, were leaning against tree trunks here and there, seated on stone slabs, dwelling in bowers of creepers, hidden in forest thickets, or sitting in the shade of branches, frequenting the roots of trees; who were intent upon their respective doctrines, some reflecting, some reciting, some doubting, some resolving, some instructing, some disputing, some practicing, and some explaining, while others had entered into discipleship.

It was attended by even monkeys who were exceedingly well-disciplined, performing acts of devotion at the *caityas* and devoted to the Three Refuges as supreme lay followers; by parrots skilled in the teaching of the Śākyas, expounding upon the treasury of the Dharma; by mynas endowed with the tranquility that comes from the instruction in the precepts (*śikṣāpada*); by owls who displayed the preaching of the Dharma and had acquired the light of wisdom through constant listening; and even by tigers whose very nature was cooled by the birth of the Sugata’s ethical conduct (*śīla*) and who abstained from eating meat.
With several lion cubs sitting confidently near his seat, the supreme sage appeared as if seated upon a natural lion-throne;
his sprout-like feet were being licked by the tongues of wild deer as if they were drinking his tranquility;
and with a young pigeon perched in the palm of his left hand eating wild grain, he seemed to propitiate his beloved friend, Maitrī, as if with an ear-lotus.
Causing delusion among the people by the streaks of light from the nails of his other sprout-like hands,
he filled a peacock that stood with neck outstretched— like an emerald water-jar being filled with streams of water—
and himself scattered grains of *śyāmāka* rice here and there for rows of ants.

He was wrapped in a very soft robe of saffron-red cloth, appearing as if anointed with the thick rays of the morning sun; with the radiant glow of his body—pure red and resembling the luster of a freshly polished ruby—he seemed to be teaching even the quarters of the sky how to don the saffron robes, for they had been turned pale-red by his light.

Out of modesty, he gazed downward with eyes that were like gently closing white water-lilies, smooth, white, and serene, as if raining down nectar to restore life to the tiny creatures crushed underfoot by people.
He was Avalokiteśvara, the supreme follower of the Sugata, as if fashioned from the very atoms of every syllable of all the scriptures;
though unswerving, he was devoted to asceticism,
like a light that reveals all objects exactly as they are to those seeking vision.
It was as if it were worthy of being approached even by the Sugata;
as if it were worthy of being propitiated even by the Dharma; and as if it were worthy of being clarified even by serene faith.
It was as if pride itself were being honored,
as if the state of being worthy of worship were being worshipped,
and as if the self itself were being longed for.
Like the object of meditation for meditation,
like the object of knowledge for knowledge,
it is the birth of recitation.
The rim of self-restraint,
the essence of austerity, and the body of purity.
The treasury of virtue,
the abode of trust, and the entire wealth of good conduct.
He was the perfection of skill,
the limit of compassion for others,
and the very cessation of happiness.
He beheld Divākaramitra, who was in the middle of his life;
and having conceived great respect for him due to his exceedingly peaceful and profound appearance, he saluted him respectfully from afar with his head, mind, and speech, all simultaneously.

Divākaramitra, however, being by nature full of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), was especially delighted by that extraordinary distinction of the king’s form—never before seen, befitting a superhuman world, surpassing all, possessing the majesty of great power, radiant, and noble—and by his profound courtesy which revealed his high birth; thus he grasped him simultaneously with both his eyes and his mind.

Although he was of a heroic nature, he rose up with great agitation; gathering his upper robe slightly as it trailed unsteadily from his left shoulder, he raised its hem and—being skilled in the initiation of granting manifold assurances—honored the king with a gentle and sweet voice by bestowing the gift of health. Cherishing him like a venerable guest who had arrived, he greeted him with words of welcome and invited him to sit upon his own seat, saying, "Please, be seated here."
And he said to the disciple standing at his side, "Venerable one,
bring water for washing my feet in the water-pot. But the king thought, "Truly, for those of noble birth, kindness is a bond of restraint that is not made of iron."
"It is indeed fitting that the honorable Grhavarma, who is devoted to virtues, has so often praised his merits," he said aloud, "and, O Blessed One,
for me, who am already graced by the merit of your sight, this further favor bestowed by your noble self appears like a double boon."
Furthermore, for one who has been accepted by the very clarity of your vision, the ritual conduct of offering seats and the like is like an act performed by another's hand;

indeed, the ground itself is a sufficient seat before those such as you. And for me, whose entire body has been washed by the consecration of the nectar of your conversation, even water for the feet offered in a limited measure is useless.
"Be seated, sirs, as you please; I shall sit with you," he said, and having spoken thus, he sat down upon the very ground.
"For in truth, the supreme ornament of those who possess power is an excess of humility."
Considering that "the jewels and such are merely a burden of stone," when the king, though entreated again and again, did not accept his words, the Venerable One returned once more to his own seat.

His heart rendered motionless by the fetters of his pair of steady eyes fixed upon the lotus-face of the king, he remained for some time, as if washing away the impurity of the Kali age with the stainless rays of his teeth; and as if exhaling the fragrance arising from his diet of roots and fruits, he addressed the creeper-grove, white with clusters of blossoming flowers and lovely with its scent: "From this day forward, this cycle of existence is not only blameless, but worthy of worship, for its true essence has been revealed."

What wonder indeed is not beheld by those who live, since this form, arrived unexpectedly and brought before our very eyes, leads such as us to infer through heart-felt celebrations the merits accumulated in previous births?
Even in this life, O beloved of the gods, you have granted us the fruit of our penance and hardship, by revealing yourself whose sight is so difficult to obtain.
Nectar has been drunk by my two eyes until satiety; my mind is now free from longing. Without great merits, the eyes do not find rest upon a virtuous person such as you.
That is a truly auspicious day on which you were born;
that is a truly noble mother who gave birth to you, the long-lived one who brings life to the entire world of living beings;
and those merits are indeed meritorious whose fruition you are.
Those atoms are the fruits of your well-performed austerities, which have been gathered by you in every state;
that is the auspicious good fortune upon which you rely, by which that noble state of manhood becomes established for you.
It is the truth that even in me, who seeks liberation, faith has arisen again at the sight of this fortunate one; though we did not desire it, we have beheld the flower-armed god,
and today the eyes of the forest deities have been fulfilled.
Today the birth of these forest trees has become fruitful, since you have come within their range;
for by your nectar-like speech, they have indeed achieved the very purpose of sweetness.
Yet, even when reflecting upon it, I cannot imagine who could have been the preceptor of such discipline in your childhood.
The earth was entirely void until the birth of this long-lived one,
for fortunate is that king in whose lineage he has appeared like a pearl-jewel;
and since such a meritorious person has somehow been obtained, our minds are restless with the thought, "How may we perform what is pleasing to him?"
Of the roots, tubers, and fruits common to the entire multitude of forest-dwellers, or of the water of mountain streams, who are we?
This wretched body of ours, however, has been made a means for the service of others; it remains our only treasure for the sake of honoring dear guests.
There exist within me several drops of knowledge that are entirely under my own control;
yet, affection does not consider their utility.
If it does not obstruct some small matter, nor if it involves words that need not be guarded, then let your honor speak what is to be told; for our hearts long to hear all of this.
"By what weighty task has this worthy one adorned this ground, which is unfit for wandering?

What is the limit to this hardship of roaming through this desolate forest? And why does this body of yours, a mass of auspiciousness, appear as if scorched by heat, though it does not deserve such suffering?"

The king, however, spoke with even greater respect: "Noble sir, by this very speech of yours—which showers forth a sweet flow like nectar that sustains the heart, and which displays such courtesy—you have fulfilled everything. I am fortunate that you, who are worthy of honor, consider me thus, even though I am one who requires no service."
And let the wise one determine the cause of this great affliction from wandering in the forest;
for me, whose entire circle of beloved kinsmen has perished, my only remaining bond to life is my youngest sister.
She too, separated from her husband and wandering through this Vindhya forest due to fear of humiliation by her enemies, somehow [reached it].
Abounding in the strength of many Śabara barbarians,
thick with countless herds of elephants, and filled with immeasurable fear of lions and śarabhas;
He entered the forest, where the paths of travelers were blocked by large buffaloes, which was harsh with exceedingly sharp arrows and kusha grass,
and treacherous with hundreds of pits.
Therefore, we wander incessantly through this forest day and night to search for her, yet we do not find her;
may the Preceptor also tell us if, while wandering in the woods, that news ever reached the ears of anyone.
Then, having heard that, the venerable one, as if seized by anxiety, spoke again: "O wise one, no such news has ever reached us;
for we are indeed unworthy recipients of such pleasant tidings and gifts from you."

Even as he was speaking thus, suddenly another monk, who appeared to be of middle age and was in a state of agitation, approached him with palms joined in reverence; moved by compassion and with eyes welling with tears, he said: "Venerable Sir, Reverend One, a great tragedy is occurring!
A young woman, though previously of auspicious appearance, now utterly overwhelmed by powerful calamity and helpless against the force of her grief, is entering the fire."
"May the Blessed One honor her, whose life-breath has not yet departed;
may he favor her with appropriate words of consolation,
for it is never before known that even a suffering worm or insect has fallen outside the range of the Noble One’s compassion."

The king, however, suspecting that she was his own sister, his heart as if melting with grief out of brotherly affection and trembling violently, somehow managed—with a throat seized by stammering, faltering speech, and eyes welling with tears—to ask: "O son of Parāśara, how far away is that woman of such a kind? Does she still live after such a time? And when asked by you, did she say, 'Who are you'?"
Whose daughter are you?
From where have you come?
For what purpose have you entered this forest?
"And for what reason do you enter the fire? I wish to hear the whole account from the beginning—how you came within the range of my sight, or what you were like in appearance.
Thus addressed by the king, the mendicant replied: "O noble one, listen."
Indeed, having paid my respects to the Blessed One this very morning, I wandered at will along this riverbank with its soft sandy soil for quite a distance.

Then, in a thicket of forest creepers near the mountain stream, I heard the piteous and deeply distressing wailing of women—a sound like the humming of female bees distressed by a frost-bitten lotus pond, or like the continuous, piercing resonance of the strings of a lute being tuned. Moved by compassion, I went to that place.

And I saw a certain man whose fingers were dripping with blood from being mangled by fragments of stone; whose eyes were narrowed by the agony of arrow-shards lodged in his heels; whose feet were motionless due to the swelling caused by the fatigue of the road; whose ankles were bound with birch-bark to relieve the pain of wounds from thorns; who suffered from a fever born in his calves as they limped from exhaustion and the friction of the wind-blown dust; whose knees were chafed by the tangled mass of *kharjūra* fibers; whose thighs were split open by *śatāvarī* roots; whose delicate silk garment was torn by *vidārī* creepers; whose tunic and ragged cloth were ripped by the sharp points of thorns on formidable bamboo branches; whose tender palms and bellies were scratched by the bristling thorns of *badarī* vines bent down in their greed for fruit; whose arms were worn out by digging up bulbs, roots, and fruits with deer-horns; whose mouth was parched and bitter from the absence of betel, having chewed upon tender *āmalakī* fruits; whose eyes were swollen and reddened from gathering *kuśa* grass and flowers, and were smeared with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) as an ointment; whose locks of hair were cropped short by *kaṇṭakī* creepers; one who had made young sprouts serve as a parasol; another who carried a fan of plantain leaves; another who held water in a cup made of a lotus leaf; another who had made a bundle of lotus stalks his provisions for the journey; and another who carried a jar of mango oil in a coconut shell placed within a fold of fine Chinese silk.

She was surrounded by a dense throng of women—some mute, some hunchbacked, some dwarfed, some deaf, and others of barbarian stock—who were all crippled and rendered speechless by the lingering remnants of their grief;
she who, even in this hour of calamity, was not forsaken by a splendorous beauty born of noble lineage that seemed to smear its radiance upon her;
and whose body was being veiled within by the fresh sprouts of nearby forest creepers reflected therein, as if by tender wounds of sorrow.
Her feet were red as if with the lac-dye of her own blood, which flowed from wounds inflicted by the sharp sprouts of *darbha* grass;
she bore a face that, though shaded by a lotus petal held by another woman with its stalk pointing upward, was nonetheless lusterless;
and she surpassed even the sky in its exceeding emptiness.
She was like one made of clay due to her lack of consciousness, like one made of air due to the abundance of her sighs,
and like one made of fire due to the continuous stream of her torment.
She was like water through the streaming of her tears,
like the sky through her lack of support,
and like lightning through her flickering instability.
She was like a personification of sound due to the profusion of her lamentations;
she was like a celestial *kalpa* creeper fallen into the great forest, its pearls, silken garments, jeweled flowers, and golden leaf-ornaments all cast away;
she was like the Ganges descended to earth, her limbs rendered helpless by falling at the head of the Supreme Lord.
With the sprouts of her feet greyed by the pollen of forest flowers,
she seemed like the form of the morning moon longing for another world,
displaying the beauty of her large white eyes through the shedding of her own waters.
Like a lotus plant in the Mandākinī river withering away,
like a night-lily closed in exhaustion from the touch of the unbearable rays of the sun, she passed her days in sorrow;
like the flame of a lamp at dawn betrayed by its burnt wick, her body was exceedingly emaciated and pale.
She was like a wild female elephant submerged in a great lake, guarded by the efforts of elephants stationed at her side;
she had entered the thicket of the forest as well as the state of meditative absorption, and stood beneath a tree as if standing upon the brink of death.
She had fallen into the lap of a nurse amidst great misfortune,
yet was cast away by her husband with ease;
she had been purged by wandering, yet remained endowed with life.
Distraught by her mass of disheveled hair and by the means of death; discolored by the dust of the road and by the pains of her limbs;
scorched by the fierce heat of the sun and by widowhood.
Her face was held down by her hand and by silence;
she was gripped by her dear friends and by resentment; and likewise, she was abandoned by her kinsmen and by her amorous graces.
With her pair of ears and her own self liberated;
with her ornaments and all worldly undertakings abandoned;
and with her bracelets and her desires shattered.
With female attendants clinging to her feet like needles made of darbha grass sprouts,
with her beloved fixed upon her heart as if it were his own eyes,
and with long sighs of grief that seemed like her hair.
With their bodies and merit exhausted,
with tears falling from the eyes of the elderly women,
and with only a small remnant of attendants and life remaining;
Sluggish in opening her eyes, skillful in shedding tears,
and constant in her anxieties.
Fragmented in the directions,
emaciated in the body,
and coarse in the breath.
Filled with suffering,
empty of sentient beings,
and occupied by exhaustion.
She was empty at heart, motionless in her resolve,
yet shaken from her fortitude.
Moreover, it is the abode of calamities, the receptacle of anxieties,
and the station of instabilities.
The support of all misfortunes,
the dwelling place of despondencies,
and the abode of calamities.
The object of misfortune for the unfortunate,
the cause of agitation for those who are agitated, and the ground of compassion.
I reflected on the other shore of dependence upon women, and marveled that even such a form as hers could be touched by afflictions;
yet, when I drew near, she, despite her condition, bowed her head with great respect and prostrated herself before me.
But I, impelled by powerful compassion and desiring to address her, again reflected in my mind: "How indeed shall I address this noble lady?
'Dear child' implies excessive intimacy;
'Mother' is a mere flattery."
"Sister" implies self-conceit;
"Queen" is a term of address for one's own attendants;
"Princess" is explicit.
"Upāsikā" (laywoman) implies a mere wish; "Svāminī" (mistress) implies the acceptance of the status of a servant; "Bhadre" (lady) is appropriate for other women.
"O long-lived one" is unpleasant at that stage; "O auspicious one" is contradictory at that time; "O moon-faced one" is not considered appropriate by the wise.
"O child" is accompanied by a lack of respect;
"O noble lady" implies the infirmity of old age;
"O virtuous one" is contrary to the [expected] fruit.
The word "you are" is common to all;
however, "who are you? is unfamiliar [to her], and "why do you weep? causes her to remember the cause of her sorrow.
To say "Do not weep" without removing the cause of grief is not fitting; on what basis can one say "Take heart"? And "Welcome" is stale.

While I was thinking, "It is false that one sits in comfort," a certain woman from among those women, appearing noble yet overwhelmed with grief, rose up; she drew near, bowed her head which was streaked with a few grey hairs toward the ground, and burning my feet with teardrops that indicated incomparable anguish of heart, she addressed me with most piteous words: "Venerable sir, the life of renunciation is generally compassionate toward all living beings."
The followers of the Sugata are unwearied because they have undertaken the initiation for the destruction of the suffering of others;
the teaching of the Blessed Śākyamuni is the ancestral home of compassion;
and the Jain doctrine is the goodness of the virtuous, intent upon the essence of benefiting all people.
And dharma is the means for achieving the world beyond;
moreover, no accumulation of merit is proclaimed by people in this world that is superior to the protection of life.
Young women are by their very nature grounds of compassion, how much more so when they are overwhelmed by calamity?
And this virtuous person is a field of success for those who utter words of distress,

since our mistress— due to her father’s death, her husband’s absence, her brother’s exile, and the loss of the rest of her circle of kinsmen— is without support because of her exceedingly tender heart and childlessness;
and she is naturally high-spirited yet has been humiliated by base enemies.
Her delicacy was tormented by this hardship of wandering through the great forest, and her heart was rendered despondent by these manifold calamities, one after another, brought about by cursed fate.

Unable to endure this terrible suffering, disregarding her elders whom she had never before defied even in a dream, setting aside her constant affection even during jests, ignoring her dear friends who were entreating her, and utterly despising with her mind that group of servants whom she had never before looked upon as anything but her own—she is entering the fire;
save her!

"May the Noble One also employ his speech, so skilled in instructing the means for removing unbearable grief, upon her," she said most piteously. Raising her up, I, deeply distressed, spoke softly: "Noble Lady, it is as you say; this grief of hers, whose virtuous disposition is beyond the reach of our words, can—if it may be saved—even for a mere moment. If it can be so preserved, then this request of mine will not have been in vain hereafter."
"For my teacher is like another Blessed Sugata standing right before me; when I have related this account, that most compassionate one will surely come and,

with the well-spoken words of the Sugatas— which pierce through the veil of the darkness of suffering— and with his own skillful speech, weighted by various scriptures and illustrated by apt examples, he will raise her, who is of virtuous character, onto the path of awakening."

Having heard that, she fell again at his feet, crying out, "Noble sir, do not hasten! Then, approaching with haste and weeping, he reported this most piteous and distressing occurrence—the death of many young women who were helpless and wretched—to his venerable teacher.

Then the king, having understood that speech of the mendicant—which was mixed with tears even though his sister’s name had not been mentioned—his mind humbled by grief, his doubts dispelled by the very description that corresponded in every detail, felt as if he were burned in his ears upon hearing the condition of his sister; and he said to the teacher of the Śramaṇas: "Noble sir,..."

"Surely this sister of mine—belonging to this ignoble person of extremely hard heart, exceedingly cruel, and ill-fated—has been brought to this state by her fortunes, which act as causeless enemies toward this wretched girl; my own heart, as it breaks, reports this very thing. Having said this, she spoke also to that ascetic: "Noble sir, rise!
Show me where she is."
"Exert yourself to acquire the merit of rescuing many living beings; let us go,
if perchance we may find her still alive," he said, and as he spoke, he rose up.

Then the Master, followed by his entire assembly of excellent disciples, descended from his horse and proceeded on foot toward that place, as if drinking it up with his rapid strides. He was pursued by the entire body of vassals who were dragging their cavalry behind them, while the son of the Śākyas pointed out the way before him.

Having gradually approached, he heard the various cries appropriate to the moment uttered by a great multitude of women, hidden within a thicket of creepers, who were about to die: "O Blessed Dharma, run quickly!"
Where are you, O Goddess Earth, the family deity?
Why do you not comfort your suffering daughter?

O Lord, where indeed has the prosperity of the Puṣpabhūti family gone into exile? Why do you awaken this widow, your own daughter-in-law, who is now protectorless, belonging to the lineage of Mukhara, and distressed by manifold afflictions?
Do not do this, O Blessed One!
O Sugata, when your devotee is burning with fever, you are like the moon that has fallen asleep;
O King of Dharma, you who show partiality toward the abode of Puṣpabhūti,
why have you become indifferent?
O Vindhya, friend in adversity, even to you this joining of palms is in vain; O Mother, great forest,
do you not hear this woman crying out as she has fallen into calamity?
O Patañga,
be gracious! Protect this devoted wife who is without refuge— O you who are protected by effort, O ungrateful one, O outcaste in conduct!
Why do you not protect the princess? What has been determined by the [auspicious] marks? Alas, Queen Yaśomatī, who consists of love for your daughter!
O King, you have been robbed by the thief of cursed fate; O Pratāpaśīla, you do not rush to the aid of your daughter while she is being consumed by fire.
O Great King Rājyavardhana, your affection for your offspring has become slack;
you do not hasten, for your love for your sister has grown faint.
Alas! Cruel is this state of a ghost; depart, O wicked fire, you who are merciless in the slaughter of women—do you not feel shame while burning?
"O brother Vāta,
I am your slave;
quickly announce the burning of the queen to the King, who brings joy by relieving the suffering of afflicted people."
O utterly merciless dog-cooker of grief,
you who grant one's desires,
O demon of separation who bestows suffering!
You are content in the lonely forest; whom shall I cry out to? To whom shall I speak?
To whom shall I go for refuge? To which direction shall I turn?
What shall I do, unfortunate as I am?
Gāndhārī,
Piśācī Mocanikā, you who have seized the noose of the creeper!
O kalahamsī, abandon this quarrel over grasping the tip of a branch;
why do you strike your own head beyond this point?
O auspicious one,
O beautiful lady, why do you still weep with unrestrained throat?
The company of friends is departing;
O fair-limbed Śabarikā, how will you remain in this inauspicious camp of corpses?
O Mālāvatī, you too shall fall before Tanūnapāt; though as delicate as a lotus stalk,
you have withered away.
O mother Mātaṅgikā,
you too have accepted death;
O child Vatsikā!
How will you dwell in this city of the dead, which is so utterly undesirable,
when you have attained such dignity through this devotion to your master?
O Virājake,
you are radiant; O princess, you who are well-acquainted with the resolve to sacrifice one's life in times of calamity through the act of leaping from a precipice, O bearer of the water-pot!
Blessed are you, O Ketakī;
for where else could there be such a good mistress?
O Menakā, may the Lord grant me the status of a servant to the Goddess in birth after birth; and may the Fire-god, burning my body, burn it away in the midst of victory.
O Vijayā, fan the fire!
Sānumati,
Namatī, Indīvarikā, Divaṅgantukāmā,
and Kāmadāsī— these are the names.
Give me space to circumambulate the fire;
O wandering one,
prepare the sacrificial fire.
O Kirātiki, scatter a profusion of flowers;
O Kurariki,
prepare a funeral pyre heaped with kurubaka buds.
"O Camaragrāhinī, take up the fly-whisk;
O Narmadā, you must endure once more these playful jests fashioned as sport, O Subhadrā, you who laugh without restraint."
May it be well with you on your journey to the next world,
O village woman who delights in virtues beyond the common; go to a happy rebirth.
Vasantikā, give way; the umbrella-bearer asks leave. O Queen, grant him your glance.
"Your beloved Vijayasenā is giving up her life;
here is Muktikā, the director of the drama, wailing aloud nearby;
and Patralatā, the highly esteemed betel-bearer, falls at your feet, O Princess."
Kaliṅgasenā,
this is the final embrace; press me firmly with your chest, Vasantasenā, for my life-breaths are departing.

Mañjulīkā, how many times have you wiped this burning eye of mine, stained by thousands of most unbearable sorrows? And how many times, Yaśodhanā, have you wept while embracing me in such a semblance of a body? For the most part, it is merely a manifestation.
O Mādhavikā, why do you still reproach me?
What state is this? The time for consolations has passed, as has the time for the conciliatory gestures of my friends. O Kālindī, [this is the end] of the supplications of my companions.
O you who are like a madwoman,
you have already yielded to the prostrations of your beloved;
O wife of the cakora bird, loosen your grip on my feet.
Kamalini,
what has not been gained by this repeated reproaching of fate?
For a long time, the pleasure of union with your circle of friends has been attained.
Noble Mahattarikā Taraṅgasenā, salutations!
Friend Saudāminī,
you have been seen.
O Havyavāhana, bring the flowers for worship; O Kumudikā, give me the blossoms; O Rohiṇī, lend me your hand to ascend the funeral pyre;
O Mother Dhātrī!
Be steadfast;
such indeed are the ripenings of the karmas of those who commit evil deeds.
This is my salutation with joined palms to the feet of the Noble Ones.

O Mother, why at this moment of death, when I am about to set out for the next world, does this powerful tumult arise within me? Why is my heart filled with such joy, and why do my limbs thrill with horripilation as they break into a dance? What is it that you have resolved to do?
O dwarf woman,
my left eye is throbbing;
cease in vain, O friend crow, perching on this milky tree moment after moment before me, whose merit is exhausted.
O deer-eyed one,
what is this neighing like that of horses from the north? Whose is this lofty parasol that is perceived here through the gap between the trees, O radiant lady?
Kuraṅgikā,
by whom has the name of my lord— whose name is auspiciously invoked— been uttered, as if it were nectar, O Queen?

"By good fortune, you prosper through this great festival of the arrival of the god Harṣa. Having heard this, he quickly approached and beheld Rājyaśrī, who was fainting and preparing to enter the fire.
And with his hand, he anxiously touched the forehead of her whose eyes were closed in a swoon.

Then, by means of that most beloved brother’s cooling touch of the hand—which, as it were, dripped the spreading essence of the medicinal herbs bound upon his forearm, capable of reviving the dead; which seemed to vomit forth the inconceivable power of the jewels in his bracelets like nectar through the rays of his moon-like nails; which appeared to bind upon her head the moonstone crest-jewel dripping with cool spray at the rising of the moon; and which, with its finger-like lotus-stalks, so exceedingly cold, seemed to extinguish her burning fever and restore life from some unknown source—Rājyaśrī suddenly opened her eyes.

And so, embracing the neck of her brother—who had arrived suddenly, whose coming was impossible to conceive and whose sight was unexpected—like seeing one seen in a dream, she was overwhelmed by a mass of grief that manifested at that very moment and pervaded her entire being; shedding a thick torrent of tears from her eyes as if released through two channels from the mouth of a river, she cried out again and again, "O father! O mother! O friends! in a voice that grew louder and louder.

Though her face was covered by her brother’s hand as he consoled her, saying, "Child, be steadfast," she— her grief intensified by the weight of the genuine sisterly affection that had arisen within her— cried out at the top of her voice for a very long time:
"O auspicious one!..."
"Follow the word of your elder brother and guru," she was entreated by the teacher; yet [she replied],
"O Queen,
do you not see the King's condition?"
Although entreated by the royal circle with the words, "Enough of weeping," and although petitioned by the attendants with the plea, "O Mistress, look upon your brother," she [remained silent].
"Daughter, rest and then you may cry out again," she was thus being restrained by her elderly kinswomen; "dear friend," [she continued].
