Though she was being consoled by her friends with the words, "Why do you weep so much? Be silent; the Lord is deeply pained," she remained as she was.

Her throat oppressed by a flood of tears that issued from the discharge of the many long-accumulated burdens of suffering, her heart filled with a heavy weight of grief, she wept piteously for a very long time in a loud voice;
and when the force of her grief had subsided, being drawn away from the vicinity of the fire by her brother, she sat down at the foot of a nearby tree.

The teacher, perceiving that Harsha was thus gradually recovering, felt his respect for him increase all the more; having passed a moment as if it were very brief, he took by his own hand the water brought by a disciple who had been signaled with a secret sign, and bowing low, offered it in lotus leaves for the washing of the face. The king also, having accepted it respectfully, first washed the eyes of his sister—which were copper-red from incessant weeping and filled with a long-standing torrent of tears, resembling a red lotus—and afterwards his own.
When the king had washed his face, the entire world became silent on all sides, as if painted in a picture;
then the lord of men spoke very softly to his sister:
"Child, pay homage here to this venerable monk."

"This is the second heart of your husband and our preceptor," said the king. At these words, as the princess bowed with tears once more brought to her eyes by the shock of hearing news concerning her husband, the teacher—his eyes moistened as his long-guarded flood of tears broke forth despite his efforts to restrain them, and turning his gaze slightly away—sighed deeply. After remaining silent for a moment, he spoke with gentle words and a sweet voice, showing great courtesy: "O mass of auspiciousness!"
Enough of weeping for so long; the world of kings has not yet ceased its lamentation,
so let the necessary ritual of bathing be performed.
"Having bathed, you must go back to the earth itself.

Then the king, conforming both to worldly custom and the command of his preceptor, rose and bathed in the mountain stream with his sister; he then returned to that very spot and, having first fixed his attention there, remained by her side and fed his sister—who was overcome with grief and had only with great effort been induced to take food—along with her attendants.
Immediately thereafter, she herself took her meal;

and having eaten, she heard from her attendants the entire account in detail, beginning from the time of her imprisonment: how she was brought from Kanyakubja to Gauḍa by a nobleman named Gupta under the pretext of protection; how, upon her departure, she heard of the death of Rājyavardhana and consequently abandoned all food; how, overcome by hunger and exhausted by wandering through the Vindhya forests, she conceived a sense of world-weariness and prepared to enter the fire—all these events she heard from her retinue.

Then, having approached the king— who was seated comfortably under a tree on a secluded spot, accompanied only by his sister, with his attendants standing at a distance— Ācāra slowly sat down and, after remaining there for a short while, began to speak briefly:
"Your Majesty, please listen."

We have something to relate: for this king of stars, the moon—the ear-ornament of the night—overcome by the intoxication of youth and disregarding his many wives who were most fickle in their first bloom of youth, became excessively lustful and abducted Tārā, the lawful wife of Bṛhaspati, the priest of Indra;

and having fled from heaven, he wandered through delightful regions, sporting with her, whose eyes were like those of a startled cakora bird, who was full of passion, and who was charming in every way.
After a long time, and somehow out of respect for the speech of all the gods, the Lord of Speech returned her to him;
yet he burned incessantly in his heart at the separation from that woman of noble form, whose fire was fueled by no other source.
Once, however, as he was rising from the mountain of sunrise, he beheld his own reflection cast upon the clear waters of the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.
Upon seeing it, Tārā—her cheeks flushed with a smile—remembered her beloved;

and he, his mind tormented by the madness of love, though dwelling in heaven, became unwell. With eyes whose pupils were white as if from drinking the flood of luster from all the groves of night-lotuses, he shed drops of tears.
Then, as they fell into the ocean, pearl-oysters swallowed them all at once.

And Vāsuki, the lord of the venom-spitting serpents dwelling in the subterranean realm (rasātala), somehow obtained those [pearls] that had become pearls within the cavities of their bellies; and with those pearls, which displayed a multitude of stars even in the depths of Pātāla, he fashioned a single-string necklace and gave it the name Mandākinī.

And by the power of the Blessed One Soma, the lord of all medicinal herbs, that necklace became an absolute destroyer of poison; and because it was born from cool nectar, it removed the torment of all sentient beings through its mere touch. For this reason, Vāsuki always wore it to pacify the heat of his venom. After some time had passed, a monk named Nāgārjuna—who had been brought to the depths of Pātāla by the nāgas themselves—begged for and obtained that single-string necklace from that king of the nāgas.
Having emerged from the subterranean realm, he gave her to his friend, the sovereign of the three oceans and lord of men named Sātavāhana;
and she, through the succession of disciples over time, has somehow reached our hands.

Although this act of offering might seem like an insult to those such as yourself, nevertheless, it should be accepted by your long-lived self—whose body must be protected, who is wise, and who is engaged in guarding the multitude of all living beings—for the sake of protection against poison, regarding her as a medicinal herb.
She loosened that single-string necklace, the Mandākinī, which was fastened to the edge of the hem of the monk’s robe as he stood nearby;

and as soon as it was being unfastened, its great circle of rays— pervasive with light, spreading forth with clear brilliance, and finding its opportunity— simultaneously whitened the faces of the quarters, so that the groves of *ketakī* trees seemed to blossom from their very roots out of longing for the creeper-like necklace,
while the night-lilies, jagged with emerging petals, seemed to awaken.
It was as if the forest were leaping with throngs of lions whose heavy manes, shaken about, filled the circle of the quarters;
it was as if the forest deities were laughing, their laughter painted across the woods by the radiance of the rays from their white teeth;
and it was as if the groves of *kāśa* grass were in full bloom, unrestrained in their loud laughter of loosened filaments and flower-buds.
It was as if agitated by herds of *camarī* yaks, appearing white as they whirled about in a frantic frenzy with their young tails;
it was as if spread abroad by the mountain river’s flood, surging with frothy and most tremulous waves;
and it was as if the full moon had risen, delighted at attaining another host of stars, pervading the quarters with its circle of blossoming rays.
The day seemed as if washed clean, its horizons grey with the dust of forest fires;
and the faces of the women, once soiled by tears, appeared as if washed anew.

But the king, his eyes being overwhelmed by her thick, forward-reaching rays, could only with great effort look upon her—who fulfilled every hope—as he repeatedly opened and closed them, seeing her like a rowed-up mass of spray from the trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
It was like the autumn moonlight released from the clouds and drawn into a single streak;
like the path of the young moon’s journey marked with visible footprints; like the garland of the Seven Sages fallen from their hands and come to rest;
and like the digit of the moon belonging to Śiva, whose power and splendor as an ornament of the entire world had been surpassed.
She was like a radiance emerged from the ocean of milk, embraced by the quality of whiteness;
she was like the Gaṅgā, which relieves suffering and has descended through a succession of many great mountain ranges;
and she was like a vanguard banner for the arrival of the state of Maheśvara, with its shimmering, flickering silken cloth constantly quivering.
Like the row of teeth of the approaching Lord Śiva, white as camphor;
like the self-choice garland of the Fortune of the World, capable of fulfilling the most excellent desires;
and like the smile of the Earth’s passion for his eyes, difficult to discern because it was shielded by her own sprout-like hands.

Beholding this [rosary], which was like a counting-bead string for the royal dharma of one engaged in the practice of the treasury of mantras, and like a tablet for recording numbers that served as an ornament to the ocean-like treasury of Kubera, he was filled with wonder in his mind for a very long time.
The teacher, having lifted it up, bound it upon the king’s shoulder at a pleasant spot;
then the king, displaying his pleasure, replied, "Noble sir,
men are generally unworthy of such jewels."
This is either the perfection of the noble one’s asceticism or the grace of the deities;
for who am I now to judge even my own self, much less to decide upon acceptance or rejection?
From the moment I beheld him, our hearts have been captivated by the multitude of his abundant and venerable virtues, and we have become dependent upon him.

"This body is dedicated by me until death for the service of the Noble One; you may do with it as you wish regarding what must be performed. After some time had passed and the conversation concerning the description of the single-string necklace had concluded, Rājyaśrī—having gained the confidence of the people—summoned her betel-bearer Patralatā and whispered something softly into her ear.
Having displayed her humility, Patralatā addressed the king: "Your Majesty,
the Queen requests that you know she does not recall ever having spoken even a loud word before your noble self, much less making a formal request."
For this unbearable intensity of grief, issuing commands as if from a malevolent fate, loosens the self-restraint of women;
for indeed, a husband or a son is the support of women,
yet for those destitute of both, life itself— acting as fuel for the fire of sorrow— is nothing but a lack of decorum.
"Furthermore, even though his efforts toward death were thwarted by the arrival of the Noble One,
let this person, who is not a vessel for merit, be favored by the permission to take up the saffron robes.
Having heard this, the lord of men remained silent.
Then the teacher spoke with great composure: "O long-lived one,
grief is indeed a synonym for a demon, another form of agitation, the youth of darkness, a particularization of poison, the inexhaustible leader of the city of the dead,
and a fire whose nature is lack of peace."
This is the inexhaustible King Consumption;
this is Janārdana, the abode of misfortune; this is the mendicant who has turned away from merit.
This lack of awakening is a form of sleep; this is a derangement characterized by lethargy;
this is a leader accompanied by inauspiciousness.
This group of planets is frequented by the ignorant;
this type of luminous phenomenon arises from disharmony; this provocation of wind arises from [excessive] oiliness.
From the mind arises fire;
from moisture comes the agitation of passion;
from the vital essence comes desiccation.
From passion comes the transformation of time.

Therefore, how could the hearts of even the learned—though they shine with the lightning-flashes of faultless knowledge, are profound in their grasp of the hidden depths of dense knots of difficult texts, hardened by extensive poetic narratives, and vast from bearing many scriptures—not be unable to withstand the onset of this? How much less so the hearts of women, tender as fresh jasmine blossoms and weak as the fibers of a juicy lotus stalk? For it is a great disease that constantly flows; a great wound of the heart; one that has gained entry and spread through the thick darkness of manifold defects; a thief of life; a cause of emptiness; a destroyer of the assembly of the great elements; skilled in wasting away the entire body; a universal sovereign of vices; abundant with the afflictions of emaciation, labored breathing, and delirium; a long-lasting malady; a malevolent seizure; a comet portending the destruction of the whole world; expert at snatching away life; devoid of auspicious luster; and like a thunderbolt falling from a cloudless sky. It is for these reasons that even the hearts of the wise cannot endure its impact. How much less so the hearts of women?
This being so, O Satyavrata,
tell me: what is to be done here, and who is to be blamed?
Before whom is there loud wailing, or is all heart-rending suffering proclaimed?
One who possesses the nature of a mortal, being undeluded, must endure it all with eyes closed.
O virtuous lady,
by whom can these ancient laws be altered?

Wandering day and night, the exceedingly long ropes of the water-wheel mechanism that assembles birth, old age, and death for living beings—expert in observing the activities of the internal organs presided over by the five great elements and the five families; all-grinding, treacherous, and established by the King of Dharma; skilled in calculating the portions of life—these water-clocks of Time flow away in every dwelling, not tolerating even a single moment.

In this world, the command of Yama, which strikes down the life-force of all living beings, moves swiftly like Caṇḍikā; the drums of the Lord of the Dead, skilled in proclaiming the departure of every creature, resound incessantly;

and in every direction and in every city, the agents of Time wander in groups—men who are as dark-bodied as the hue of the Kālakūṭa poison, whose eyes are red like heated iron, and who carry the nooses of Death in their hands.

In every house, there wander terrifying messengers, making the air ominous with the sharp clanging of the bells of Yama struck by their hands; they blow through every direction terrible blasts of death’s breath to summon the multitudes of all living beings. The vultures’ eyes fall upon the banners of the Lord of Pretas, grey with the smoke of many funeral pyres; the streets are filled with thousands of bier-carts for the dead, variegated by the disheveled tresses of mourning women crying out in grief, while the camps of the cremation grounds resound with the "ki-li-ki-li" cries of young jackals. These are the thoroughfares where the caravans of travelers set forth toward the dwelling of the next world.

The tongue of the Night of Doom— black as the embers of a funeral pyre, smeared with blood, licking the heights of the sky, and greedy for devouring the entire world as its morsel— licks up the lives of living beings;
likewise, the insatiable hunger of Death, the Lord who devours all creatures, has never learned contentment,
and the river of impermanence flows with extreme rapidity.
The assemblies of the great elements are momentary;
the wooden beams of the skeletal cage of the embodied beings' limbs are fragile throughout the nights;
and the atoms that construct the body are prone to disintegration, rendered helpless by the onset of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

The cords and threads of the snare that bind the soul are easily severed; having thus ascertained that this entire universe, including the self and the Lord, is perishable, you, O wise one, ought not to allow the expansion of darkness into your tender mind to such an extreme degree.
For a single moment of discernment serves as the support for steadfastness;
moreover, even though your grief has long since passed, surely this eldest brother of yours, who is like a father, must still be looked upon by you as a guru.
Otherwise, who would not highly esteem such a virtuous resolve on your part regarding the taking up of the saffron robes?

For the blessed state of renunciation is indeed the supreme means for quelling the fever of the entire mind; this is truly the highest goal for those who possess self-mastery. Yet now, O illustrious one, you shatter my heart's desire.
"Whatever he commands must be carried out—
whether he be called brother, elder, affectionate one, virtuous man, or king— in every way one must abide by his command," having said this, he ceased speaking.
When he had ceased speaking, the king said, "Who else but a noble soul would speak thus?

For you are pillars of support for the world during the calamities of adverse fate that arise without being solicited; you are beings whose forms are moist with affection, destroyers of the darkness of delusion, and lamps of righteousness."
However, affection, when indulged by being granted its request, desires even an unattainable wish;

excessive love instills audacity even in the steadfast; and extreme endearment, once the heart has been overcome by lightness, renders one devoid of the discrimination between what is proper and improper, so that cravings for self-interest teach boldness even to the modest.
Noble men protect the bounds of their requests like the oceans;

furthermore, this body of mine was already surrendered by you, who are worthy of honor, to me as hospitality from the very beginning without being asked. Therefore, I beg a small favor of the Venerable One: this sister of ours is young and afflicted by many sorrows, and she must be constantly cherished, even at the cost of neglecting all other duties.

And we, having become obedient to this arm which is intent upon bringing about the destruction of the enemy clan that committed the crime of murdering our brother, have made a vow in the presence of all the world; unable to endure the humiliation of our previous insult, we have surrendered ourselves to wrath.
Therefore, let my noble brother also employ himself in my service for some time.

"Let this body be given to the guest from this day forward, for as long as this person lightens the burden of his vow and consoles the subjects who are overwhelmed by the grief of their father's death; meanwhile,
[let him do so] through the righteous discourses of your honor."
By means of stainless instructions that bring about wholesome awakening,
by teachings that bestow ethical discipline and tranquility, and by the visions of the Tathāgatas which serve as the cause for the abandonment of the afflictions;
I wish for her to be awakened only after she has come to my side;
however, she will accept the saffron robes along with me once my purpose is fulfilled—
for what indeed do the great not bestow upon those who seek them?
The ocean of fortitude, Dadhīca, fulfilled the Lord of the Gods even at the cost of his own bones;
and how many times has the Lord of Sages, out of compassion and disregarding his own existence, not offered himself to dull-witted beings?
Beyond this, you yourselves know far more.
Having spoken thus, the king became silent;
but the venerable one spoke again: "Noble ones do not utter their words twice;
your virtues have already been accepted by my mind—this offering is for you."
"But the employment of this person, who is otherwise of no use, depends upon one possessed of merit, whether for a task small or great.

Then, being delighted by that man whose friendship he had thus welcomed, the king stayed there for that night; at dawn, having dismissed him after satisfying him with gifts of garments, ornaments, and other things, he returned with his sister and the teacher toward the camp situated on the banks of the Jahnavī, taking about a few marches.
And even as he was recounting to his friends the story of his acquisition of royal fortune, the sun also crossed the vault of the sky;
the day, dear to the cakravāka birds, contracted like a lotus-pond turned brownish-yellow by thick honey-paste;

and the sun, with its rays, withdrew from its own body the nets of light—which were scattered across the Lokāloka mountains, reddened with the hue of fresh blood, and which resembled the sacrificial *yajus* mantras vomited from the mouth of the enraged Yājñavalkya, yet which were now once more shrouded in sin.
Gradually, the sun, radiant with its thickening rays of crimson glow,
appeared like the crest-jewel innate to the binding of the turban on Duryodhana, fierce with its body smeared in fresh blood-red unguent after being uprooted by the hollowed palms of Bhima;
and it was like the skull-bowl of Brahmā, tawny with the blood filling the veins of the shaven heads cast down by Śiva when he was intoxicated by the giving of alms to Rudra.

A blood-red lake, difficult to cross, was filled with thousands of channels of blood flowing from the hollows of the throats of wicked Kṣatriyas, which had been hewn by the axe-blade of Paraśurāma—his anger provoked by the murder of his father and sharpened upon the broad, formidable shoulders of Kārtavīrya; it resembled a pool of gore that obstructed the way.

A fire, its mass of flames hidden by fear, took on the appearance of a circle of severed heads with hands and feet tucked away; it was drenched in blood as it was cast down and extinguished by the cage-like talons of the great Garuḍa, and it rolled through the sky like a tortoise.

Like a mass of flesh with its inner core of blood, it was brought to a state of fragmentation; like a slope of Mount Sumeru, it was marked by the cooking of sacrificial porridge for the sorcery intended to slay the Asuras, as it was cast away by Dākṣāyaṇī, distressed by the passing of the appointed time.

With its interior blackened by the boiling of blood, it was an exceedingly narrow cauldron, terrifying from the smear of blood from the bodies of elephants and Dānavas that had recently fallen into it; it remained visible for a moment like the expansive orb of the face of Mahābhairava.
The twilight hour appeared like a *vetāla*, hanging from a row of clouds radiant with the reflection of the sun’s orb mirrored in the waters of the ocean, as if clutching a heavy load of raw flesh;

and the lord of the waters, his stream of water colored by the blazing glow of the twilight, became once again—as in ancient times—red-hued like the mass of blood from Madhu and Kaiṭabha when crushed between the thick thighs of the Primal Being (*Purāṇapuruṣa*).
Immediately upon the conclusion of the twilight hour, his own family fame, parched with thirst to drink his immeasurable glory, was like a goblet carved from the stone of the Pearl Mountain.

The night brought forth a white-rayed moon for the lord of men, like the imprint of the seal of the command of the first king, who was intent upon establishing the Kṛta Yuga, brought by the Goddess of Sovereignty; and like a messenger from the White Island (Śvetadvīpa) sent by the Future, who had set out to conquer all the continents.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Harṣacarita*, composed by the illustrious Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
